summary: The Food Inspector took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi seeds were adulterated. The trial court acquitted the respondent, but the High Court in appeal reversed the acquittal and convicted him. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'insect ' is defined in the Oxford Dictionary as "small invertebrate segmented animal having head, thorax, abdomen, and three pairs of thoracic legs usually with one or two pairs Of thorcic (1) 1973 (Prevention of Food Adulteration Cases) 257. The word "worm" in the same dictionary is defined as "a slender, creeping, naked, limbless animal usually having a body divided into segments and several pairs thereof". According to that dictionary an article of food must be unfit for human consumption because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insect infested or on account of any other cause". [468B] 1.2 The word used in the definition section 2(1)(f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal ; , and the conclusion that the article was "adulterated" is a correct statement of the law.

The appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law, because the presumption in his case could be drawn against him. The appellant contended that he was an agricultural labourer and was therefore not liable under the Act. Held, that the presumption under section 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrains Dealers ' Licensing Order, 1966 cannot be drawn. It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a "dealer and that is the essence of the order. The fiction in the second sub para must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , referred to. The presumption under para 3(1) could not be drawn from proof of storage only. It was obvious that subs. (2) speaks of storing for sale and as a 'dealer although the word "as" are mentioned in sub paragraph, it must be held that the appellant was in fact carrying on agricultural operations.

The respondent was a monthly tenant of the appellant. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit, and the rent was paid in the succeeding year on 16th March 1926. In 1951, the respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land described in Schedule to the plaint, on the allegation that the defendant was a regular tenant under the plaintiff or his predecessor. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the decision was affirmed by the District Judge. On appeal, the High Court held that the notice to terminate the tenancy was invalid as not amounting to a lease as defined by the Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The agreement between the parties was certainly not to create a monthly tenancy. It is one thing to say that in the absence of a valid agreement, the rights of the parties would be regulat ed by law in the same manner as if no agreement existed at all; it is quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which is palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case. [273 D] (2) The question whether payment of rent to the Receiver was tantamount to payment to the plaintiff himself, though this question was left open by the High court on the previous occasion. [272 E F] (3) The relationship of landlord and tenant between the par ties came to an end on the expiration of the second annual lease. As there was no holding over by the defendant since then as contemplated by section 116, Transfer of property Act, there was, therefore, no subsist ing tenancy at any time after December, 1926, and consequently a tenancy from month to month came into existence in accordance with the provision of section 106, Transfer Of Property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926.

The appellant, Trilok Chand Jain instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the respondents, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati, w/o Shri Pindi Kumar Gulati. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the Court records relating to the Income tax Assessment of the defendants, M.Dagi Ram and Smt Budh Wati Gulati w/O Shri Phaniindi Lal Gulati Lal Gulti, for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1971 72. The Income Tax officer to whom the summons were issued sent the record in a sealed cover alongwith a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an income tax assessee could be made. It considered the first question in the following four situations: (a) Where the documents, records etc., in respect of which privilege is claimed were filed by an assessee or a third party after April 1, 1964, in respect for assessment years 1962 63 and 1963 64 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922; (b) where the documents. records, records, etc. in respect thereof were filed on or before April 1 1964, but before April I,1964 in respect o assessment years, 1964 65 onwards; (c) Where, the documents record, etc., were filed or by an assesee or a second party after 4th April 1965, butbefore April 1.1964 in regard to assessment years 1963 63 and 1962 64 in respect off the said years taking places under the IncomeTax Act, 1961; and (d) where, the document, records and documents were filed before April l, 1964 in respect Of assessment years upto and including assessment year 1961 62 in proceedings of the said assessments taking place u/s 143 for the aforesaid assessment years. The Full Bench while considering the second question, dealt with the following situations: "1. What is the position of law relating to privilege prior to 1964? 2. What was the effect of production of certified copies relating to income tax assessment records, and how far certified copies can be admitted in evidence ?" The circumstances under which these questions arose, briefly put, are as follows: (i) Where documents, record etc. were filed, by an assesses or a Third party after 1st April 1964, and before April 31,1964, in regard of assessment years ending on and including the assessment year 1962 63 onwards; and where the document records, record, documents etc.

The respondent was a minor and was in hospital. He made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died on May 3, 1946 without an issue. Seinha also died soon afterwards on February 25, 1947, without leaving any issue. The respondent filed a suit for partition and possession of the property which he claimed as an heir under Muhammadan Law, challenging the gift as invalid. To the suit he joined his two sisters as defendants who submitted were entitled to a 3/16 share each. He also submitted that the first three defendants (the appellants) were entitled only to the remaining 4/16 shares as heirs of Seinabai and accepted on her behalf by her mother. The trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept it. After the death of Seinsha, the present suit was brought by Kunhamu an eider brother of Mammottty for partition, possession of a 6/16share of the properties which he claim as an heirs under Muhammadans Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or by his executor. The plea taken in the suit was that when succession opened out on the death Of Mammothty, his widow Seinaks was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was no issue and the remaining 3/4 was divisible between him and his two sister sisters, Kunhamunu getting twice as much as each sister, these shares according to him were unaffected by the invalid gift in faVour of SeInaba and accepted by her father. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the gift was void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that neither express acceptance nor transfer of possession is necessary for the completion of a gift when the donor is himself the guardian or the de facto guardian or 'quasi guardian ' provided there is a real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee, and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment is sufficient evidence of such an intention.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The Act provided that the trustee of every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. Section 76(1) provides that the Government may make rules to carry out all or any of the purposes of this Act and not inconsistent therewith. The respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana Temple at Mulki, challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was without jurisdiction. Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76(2) of the Madras Act 19. The Commissioner had to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious endowment. The percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate, and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The High Court was therefore right in holding the Commissioner 's order upholding the claim of the respondents temple on this part of the case must also be set aside. The order of the High court is set aside and it is directed that the case do stand remanded to the High. The case will be sent back to the high Court for disposal according to law and in the light of the observations made in this judgment.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice issued by the High court. The High Court held that no appeal lay to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner for bearing the case piecemeal. In appeal to this court, HELD : An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appealed against as a matter of right under section19. [512C] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. Baradikanta Mishra 's case was not applicable to the present case. The appeal is therefore dismissed as not maintainable. [511F] Barabadakata Mishra vs justice Gatirushna Misra, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206, distinguished. Barbakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikrunna Mishra; , referred. Bardakanta Kumar Mishra vsJustice Gatikaushna, A C.A. No. 15 of 1975, dt. 2 4 1975, referred to and distinguished. The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High 'Court affecting its right, the mere order issuing the notice is not appealable. [ 512B] Barbadakrishna Mishra vs Judge, Orissa High Court, ; and Baradkanta Mishra v Justice Gitikrushnna Mishra A.l.I.,R.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone plus a fine of Rs. 500. On revision, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Held, that the words " unless a different intention appears" in section 6 A of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949, are comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphy transmitter ' this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only went wrong for if that section was not on the statute book at the time of the alleged commission of the offence. The words "unless a different intent appears" mean " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another it amends the subject or proposal of it though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. Held further, that section 6 (1 A), inserted in the Act XVII of 1933 by the amending Act of 1949, is either covered by the provisions Of the , or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. The word " text" in its dictionary meaning means " subject to or theme ". When an Act amends the language of another, it amends, the subject and theme of it, though sometimes they may expunges unnecessary words with altering the subjects. The repealing Act does not indicate any intention different from that envisaged by the said section.

The appellant was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait, he executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty some time in April 1928 on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The last entry in the Hatchitita was made in March 1929 and the total amount borrowed up to that date came up to Rs. 3,801. Adwaita died in March 1930 and after his death, Satish Chandra Roy became the managing shebait and continued to act as such till his death in 1940. There was an adjustment of accounts between Nanitash and the creditor in whose favour the Hundita was executed, and a sum of Rs. 5,068 having been found due to the 128 creditor, Satish Chander gave him a renewed Hatchi for that amount. The instalments not having been paid in either of the cases both the decrees were put into execution. In Execution Cases Nos. 76 and 77 of 1936 arising out of Money Suits Nos. 261 and 262 of 1932, the properties mentioned in Schedule Ka were sold and 991 were knocked down to Srimati Oramba Sundari Dasi who figures as the appellant in the appeals before this Court and who, it may be noted, was the wife of Aghore Nath Roy, a son of Adwaitita, the former managing Shebaits of the debutter estate. The High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court on the strength of a certificate granted by the High Court under sections 109(a) and 110 of the Civil Procedure Code, HELD : (i) The object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of the decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled, and in case of default in payment of any of the instalments, the property restored to the Judgment debtor under clause (c) would be put back into the possession of tho decreeholder. [991 D] (ii) The High Courts have not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decreeholder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b). But it does not agree with the learned Judges of the High Courts that in making a new decree under clause(a), of section 36(2) and giving the judgment debtors consequential relief under clause C) of the sub section, the court can at all enter into the question as to what the ostensible purchasers at the executing sale, Or the person whose title they are to be adjusted and worked out when a decree hat was reopened has been dealt with exhaustively in the several clauses of section36(2).

The respondent company instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent. per annum on the ground that it was due to the firm in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the firm as pucca adatias. The appellant contended that the transfer was not made in accordance with Order XXI, r. 16, and therefore, the application for execution could be made by them as persons claiming under Habib & Sons. Held, that the application was competent to execute the decree passed in favour of the respondent company by virtue of the assignment in writing executed before the decree came into existence and the only way in which the transferee could claim that the decree was transferred or agreed to be transferred by the document under consideration and the appellant was entitled to a declaration that she was an assignee of the decree. The application for the execution was not competent as the respondent had not stated any particular date on which the transfer of the suit property was made. Kangati Mahanandi Reddi vs Panikalapati Venkatappa & Anr., A.I.R. , and Bhagwant Balajirao & Ors. vs Rajaram Sajnaji & Others, A. I. R. , referred to. Held further that the respondent could not claim to be a transferee of the original decree under section 232 of the Civil Procedure Code because the transfer in writing was by assignment in favour 'of the respondent and therefore the application made by him prior to 1923 were not made within Order XXI r.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods. On April 20, 1957, the respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows"W ' Type 'T.H ' type 'T 'H ' Window ' and "Composite Winds" of certain sizes "in accordance with the specifications, designs, drawing and instructions in writing referred to in r. 1 hereof and Class 11 of the conditions of contract and with such materials as are provided for by and in all other respects in accordance with such conditions so far as applicable". The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. The Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the terms of the tender were not decisive and the court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the Respondent. HELD : (i) The object of the respondents was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to he fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. 'The rate quoted by the respondents is based on the current price of mild steel billets, and that the price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. The contract undertaken by the 'respondent was to prepare the window leaves according to specifications with Glass plain or Ground as decided in Charge. [508 H] (ii)The High Court was right in holding that the contracts were a works Contract and not a contract for sale. [511 E F] (iii)The object of respondent was to entering into a work contract. The primary undertaking of the Respondent was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves.

The appellant was a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. On November 15, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram Pal and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. Ram Avtar lodged a report with the police against Shanker Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. Later on that day he was arrested by the police. The appellant contended that he was not present along with Shanker, when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the goods. The trial court accepted the contention and quashed the charges framed against him. On appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: There is no infirmity in the judgment or order of the Calcutta High Court as might induce us to interfere. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. [ 279 C] The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he is present along alongwith Shanant Lal, when he brought washeher plates and demanded price of goods from Ram Avtar.

The petitioner, an Allopathic doctor by profession had himself drafted and filed a writ petition in the High Court of Kerala challenging the reports of the Kunzru Wanchoo and Sikri Committees appointing a fact finding Commission to inquire and report about the numerous train accidents from 1970 onwards and for several other directions to the Union Government and the instrumentalities connected with the administration of the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not properly implemented. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunozru Wanchoo & Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railway with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, inefficiency in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts, robberies and murders of passengers, ineffective checking and supervisory system, want of replacement equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It has been averred that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level Crossings are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level crosses with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the railways and control at the gate is also being improved. It was further pleaded that periodic review is undertaken about manning of unmaned level crossing of new level cross ingings in consultation with appropriate State Governments. Initially it used to be the obligation of the respective State Governments to provide for such level cross promotions at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way is of the train in preference to traffic on the road. As that arrangement was not working well, with effect from April 1, 1966, a Railway Safety Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. From 1978 potentially hazardous unmanaged level cross remarks with a Volume of traffic were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. It had been alleged that unmannerned level crossing crossings with a length of traffic more than 5000 train vehicle unit units or defective approach visability are being menned in an phased manner, at the costs of the petitioner and his assistance crystalising the issues for determination by the Court was filed, leave to amend the writ petition. The petition was opposed on behalf the Railways contending that the Railway Safety work Fund has not been properly implemented; that there were nearly 120000 bridges on the Railways out of which 195 are important bridges and nearly 9400 are major bridges; that un manned Level crossings were gradually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operation. Relying on the Sikri Committee Report of 1978, it has been submitted that the State Governments appeared to be aware of their responsibilities in this matter and about 2/3 of the funds of the Safety Works had been utilised by March 31, 1982.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 in respect of their proprietary jagirs. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration should be allowed as they were prevented for sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeals. The Tribunal rejected the applications holding that they were time barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41, rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since in view of section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act which provides for restoration of an appeal or application made under regulation 20 shall be filed within 30th days from the date of the date on which the order is passed, the Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications were time bar. HELD: The language of Regulation 20 applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a cases where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or an application is called for hearing, the Tribu nal may decide the same on merits. [143 H] In the context of section 20 and in view Of the express language of section 18(1) of the jag Abolition Act it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case when the appellant did not appear in person, or through an agent or pleader. It is also open to it to the Tribun nal in such a case to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits even though there was default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal.

The appellants, two descendants of Dinanath Sao brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinnath Sao from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Telibandha and for accounts. The appellant 's case was that Telivancorebandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Ji as early as 1857 by Dinanath, Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath, Saoo of this village of Totlibandha but also dedicated the village Telilegraphbandha to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The Trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village and it was therefore liable to be removed. On appeal the High Court agreed with the trial court that the dedication had been made by one Dinanath but held that the mere use of the word 'Malik ' so clearly and unambiguously passed the absolute interest that examination of the context was not necessary. The High Court also held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temple and it could be removed without going into the other questions as regards the character of the property or whether the defendant had committed breaches of trust. On a construction of paragraph 2 of the Panch Faisala, the learned judges of the High court held that it did purport to revoke the dedication and to allot the village to the members of one branch of the family with only a moral obligation to look after the temple but this later Award had all along remained a dead letter and did not affect the Panch Majibil Award of 1896. The main controversy before us was whether by the Punch Faisla Award of 1796 an absolute dedication of the Village TeliFEPOSA was made in favour Of the respondent temple or whether it was superseded by the award of Shri Hariram on May 14, 1898, which was accepted by all the co sharers as the actual settlement of their own and on the basis of which a suit brought to challenge the validity of the earlier award was dismissed as compromised.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Lucknow Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. The first charge was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The text of the resolution was this "The Action Committee is of the opinion that the chief Justice is acting in the dis charge of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a highly partisan manner" under the control of the High Court. The second charge was with respect to the contumacious conduct of which the appellants were charged. The High Court held that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associating with the passing of the Resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of 'Criminal Contempt '. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [603B] In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 was entered into a joint family with the object of partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators; namely, three appellants Nos., 5, 6 and 7 herein. On or about 2nd July 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the said registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah, the district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. On November 28, 1977 the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made signed the award. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration; that the limitation for the registration of the award had already expired; that in this case the award was in the court of the learned Munsif from 28th January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The period that is to say from 28st January 1978 till the return of the Award to the arbitrators on 24th of November,1983, the award is in the Court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977. [123B] 2. Section 23 of the provides that if owing to urgent necessity or unavoidable accident, any document executed, or copy of a decree or order made, is not presented for registration till after the expiration of the time hereinbefore prescribed, the Registrar, in cases where the delay in presentation does not exceed four months, may direct that on pay. 123 ment of a fine not exceeding ten times the amount of the proper registration fee, such document shall be accepted for registration. Sub section (2) of Section 25 provides that any application for such direction may be lodged with a sub Registrar. who shall forward the same to the Registrar. Therefore the cumulative effect of sections 23 and 25 read together is that total period of eight months is available for registration if the conditions are fulfilled. The High Court had held that in the instant case the only period which should be excluded was from 26th July, 1978 till 20th December, 1982. [124C D] 3. Section 25(1) of the stipulates that the time for registration is four months from the date of its execution. The award was made on 28th November 1977 and it was presented for Registration to the Sub Registrar on 25th November 1983.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting of the premises. The appellant agreed to vacate and the respondent let to him a portion of his new building which 219 was riot far from "Fida Ali", Villa '. The trial court held that subletting was lawful in spite of section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bom. 57 of 1947). He also held that the appellant did not occupy the premises as on the same terms and conditions on which he occupied the old premises in "Fiida Ali vsilla" ; , followed. Held, further, that under section 15 Of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, the landlord had the right to evict the tenant on account of sub letting and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. The non obstante clause in section 10 of the , which prohibits subletting and makes it un lawful for a tenant to assign or transfer his interest in the Premises let to the landlord, was void because of the provisions of section 16 of the Contract Act and section 23 of the Indian Contract Act. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co. (1924) L.R. 52 I.A. 126, referred to. Held further, also that the non obstante clauses in section 15(1) Of the Act were not intended to be used as a guide for enforcing an illegal agreement and therefore the plea of waiver could not be raised because as a result of giving effect to that plea the Court would be enforcing an illegality and infraction of a statutory provision which cannot be condoned by any conduct or agreement of parties.

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, were found tampered with, the marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. The appellant Board 's writ petition challenging the notification was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Board it was contended that the Act empowers the Divisional Board to deal with the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted under the Act and Regulations and that the Standing Committee is an alien body to the Divisional Boards is to do violence to the scheme of the Act, and Regulations. It was further submitted that the impugned notification was vitiated for the reasons that the Committee itself did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examinees/parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest. Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Examination Standing Committee of the Divisional board itself a statutory body acted on behalfof the Divisional Commissioner and is not a delegate of the Regional Board. Truely, it is regulatory in character and the powers were exercised by the Committee and recommended to the State Govt. to compulsarily retire the respondent and it amounts to taking a decision on behalf o the High Courts. [798C D] 1.2 The Examination Committee, if relies upon such evidence to come to the conclusion that tho examinees, their parents or guardian are parties to fabrication and whether their complicity was established from record and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached by the Standing committee or the Enquiry Officer. Once a matter is established beyond reasonable doubt it must be taken for all purposes of law to be a fact, as there is no room for a distinction between what is found by inference from the evidence and what is held as a positive face. [781E F] 1:3 The finding of the learned Judge Sugla, J. that the resolution passed by the Board was not based on any evidence is clearly illegal and cannot be sustained. The question, therefore, is whether the conclusions reached by him were based on no evidence and the conclusions are in different hand writings, which would show the non application of the mind to the facts and it violates the principle of natural justice also does not apply to the case. [784E F; 798A] 1 :4 The finding that the examinationees/guardian were parties lo the fabrication cannot be upheld for the reason that the regulation itself postulates that if the Committee disagrees with the Inquiry Officer then only it is obligatory to record reasons. [783F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the findings of the Committee are based on cogent evidence and in this case all the requirements are lacking.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge found the appellants guilty under both heads of charges and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500. On appeal by special leave: Held, that before it can be made applicable there must be proof, it was said, that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal means and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The word "obtains" is used in sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code. The other words "corrupt or illegal mean" find place in section162. Apart from "corruption and illegal means", it does not follow that there is no overlapping of offences. The offence as defined in clause (d) does not come with. In the meaning of bribery, is to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. A speedy disposal of corruption cases by special courts, the benefit of in vestigation by higher police authorities are some of the provisions intended for the protection of public 189 servants prosecuted under the Act while they are subjected also to increased disabilities, namely, a longer term of imprisonment as punishment and the application of the presumption referred to in sub clause (3.). Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh vs The State of Vindhya Pradesh, ; , distinguished. Brennan vs peek, Cr. Appeal No. 81 of 1953, followed.

The appellant Bank, a surety for the respondent Bank, filed a suit against the respondent bank for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. against the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor and defendant 2, the surety. The principal debtor also passed letter of continuity of the bond and the promissory note executed by the principal debtor in favour of the Bank. The surety executed a demand promissory note, Ext. 81 in favour to the Bank on September 16, 1957 and on the same day the principal creditor also executed a letter of guarantee in favour thereof. The respondent bank wrote to the surety letter Ext.32 dated December 24,1957 calling upon him to pay the outstanding balance of Rs 70,879/ in cash credit account of principal debtor as in the circumstances mentioned in the letter the balance was required to be recovered from the surety and on personal guarantee of the surety, the sureties executed a bond Ext. 83 in favour by the Bank and the principal amount was required for recovery from the respondent. Some correspondence ensued between the bank and the surety whereby ultimately the Bank filed the suit for recovery against defendant 1, the legal representatives of the principal debtors and defendant2, the bail surety. On appeal by the surety the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal applicant 's security of goods by way of pledge and that though the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd., but the godown was to be maintained under the lock and key of the bank, it was to he responsible for safe custody and keeping of the pledged goods. It also held that as the surety 's guarantee was not discharged from his liability under the guarantee, the respondent would not be discharged from its liability under guarantee. In appeal by certificate, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the bail bond had been lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank. [924A] 2.1 The surety ' has made an application that in compliance with the decree made by the trial court he had paid the entire amount and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amount and that this Court should give a direction to the bank as part of this judgment that the amount be returned with interest at current rate to the respondent surety. An explanation has been added to section 144 by the 928 Amendment Act of 1976, the relevant portion of which reads as under: "Explanation For the purposes of sub section (1) the expression "Court which passed the decree or order" shall be deemed to include where the decree, or order has been varied or reversed in exercise of appellate or revisional jurisdiction, the Court of first instance.

The appellant was the son of a member of the family. The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers, and 22 to 39 were included in the jagir portion. As a result of these regrants the jagirdars thought that they were entitled to take possession of the "patelki inam" lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. After the resumption proceedings were followed by the proceedings of 1917 and 1917, and the appellant was granted a sanad in respect of these two plots. The order made by the Government further stated that the aforesaid lands would be recorded in the name of Amritrao as his "p Patelki inam lands". On August 28, 1922, the Government excluded the " patelki Inam" lands from the resumption proceeding relating to the jagir on the footing that they had been granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government. The appellant 's suit in 1942, claiming that the Government had no jurisdiction or authority to resume and regrant them to respondent No. 1 was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the lands were granted by it as remuneration or wages for services rendered by him to the jagirs. Held, that the grant of " pate Patel inam" of 1 1/2 bighas per netan was in its origin a grant by the sovereign authority which the Nizam confirmed in accordance with old judicial usage; and the order made on August 28. 1922, did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect thereof. The settlement was valid and binding on the jagdars who agreed to be bound by it.

The respondents claimed that they were governed by the customary law of Cutchi Memons in Madras and Bangalore. They claimed that cutchi Memon sect amongst Muslims was governed by Hindu Law as to inheritance and succession only. The Deputy Controller held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said estate only concluded the issue before him, viz., that the rules of Hindu law including the rules as to joint family property and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary customary law governing Cutchi memons in Bombay and Bangalore and therefore they were entitled to prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The High Court held that the Khojas who had settled down in Cutch, Kathiawar and Bombay were converted as a caste to Islam some three or four hundred years ago, but had retained on their conversion the Hindu law as to succession and inheritance. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to Cutchi could not be said to be in accordance with Muhammadan Law and that the custom of adoption recognised in the (1) A.I.R. (2) Bom. 2 48, Madras in favour of the respondents ' family properties as being governed by Mohammedan law; (ii) that the doctrine of sons acquiring interest by birth in ancestral properties did not apply to Cutni Memons and therefore the High Court was right in its view that the said Khoja Memons were governed under Hindu Law. HELD : The High Courts had rightly treated the Khudkas as being a class of Hindus for purposes of the Hindu Wills Act, XXI of 1870. [234 F] (1)(a) The question whether the custom recognised in section 3 of the is to adopt the text of the Koran as law any further than it has been adopted in the laws and usages of the Muhammadans who came under their sway, was open to objection, since such a rule could rest only upon proved customs, that no custom of that kind had ever been proved and that Scott, C.J., had based his conclusion only on the case law. [235 D] (b) The High 'Court erred in holding that the customary rule of succession recognised in Madras was applicable to the Khoias as it was governed under the rules. [236 F] In the instant case the High Courts were right in their view that they had not before it, as appears from the decision itself, any evidence as to the customary custom which the Cutchi had settled in Bangalore followed. Its second section provided that any Cutchi may be declared by a Muslim to be a Khoja widow, he held that in the absence of proof of a special custom to the contrary, that question also must be governed by Indian law. The conclusion which was arrived at on consideration of the decisions referred to above is that the Kahhatas and the Cutch Memons retained, despite their conversion considerable portion of their personal law and that they discarded the rules, as to coparcenary and the son 's interest in the property of his grandfather.

The appellants manufactured fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputes that the various kinds of fabric which are produced or manufactured at an intermediary stage and, thereafter, subjected to an integrated operation process for the manufacture of different fabrics. Indeed, on a writ petition filed by the appellants, the Delhi High Court held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the purpose of weaving the said same into fabric will be liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided in the Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49, there cannot be such fictional or deemed removal without the specification of the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The language of rule 9(1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises relatable to the place of manufacture or production of the excisable Goods. [707B] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants are liable for payment of duty on the yarn which is obtained in an intermediate stages of an integrated manufacturing process of manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of the commodity at an inter unit stage to be removal from such place or premises of manufacture. It is true that under rule 9 (1) there is a provision for specification by the collector, but the question is what has to he specified by the Collec tor. [700C] 1:3 The words "place of removal" in Rule 9(2) refer only to one interpretation.

The petitioner filed a suit for declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents in the suit from finalising and approving the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for the reliefs prayed for by him; (ii) the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred; and (iii) the power of the Civil Courts to try a suit in which the validity of the proceedings under Chapter IVA of the , is called in question. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. [544C] 2.1 In cases of the instant nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, a writ petition lies before the High Court. In such cases a suit is hardly the remedy which can be availed by them. If suits of this nature are allowed to be entertained, the very object of the several provisions of Chapter IV A of the . [544D E] H. C. Narayanappa and Ors. vs The State of Mysore & Ors., ; at page 753 has observed that the jurisdiction is impliedly excluded from entertaining suit of the nature. The juris of the High Courts is impliedly ousted from entertaining a suits of present nature, and the jurisdictionof the civil court is impliedly con tended. [545E F] H C.

The appellant was charged under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that Miss Eylene (P.W. 2) used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. She developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963 Miss Eene was married to one S. N. K. Lal who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital, and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. The appellant asked Russel Niel to bring to him the appellant 's house of N.K. Lal at about 7.30 or 745 P.m. The girl told S.P. Mukatdhari Singh turned up and recovered the currency notes from the pocket of the appellant. On being questioned, the appellant told the D.S.P., that he never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel ' Nathaniel. The D.I.G. Police, Mr. M. P. Singh who recorded his statement and called two witnesses to witness the proceedings. S.D.P Mukatadhari Singh examined seven currency notes of denomination of Rs. 100/ each. The numbers of those currency notes were noted and Russel nathaniel was then instructed to pass on the money to the appellant, but the appellant did not ask for bribe. The charge against the appellant was also under section 161 I.P .C. and section 5 (1)(D) of Prevention of corruption Act. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charged framed against him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 6(2) of that Act. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of the appel lant under section S 5 (2) Prevention of Criminal Corruption Act and section I. P .C., and also the sentence to undergo imprisonment for one year and to payment of fine or imprisonment in default. In support of this appeal, HELD : The order of sanction dated December 10, 1963 shows on the face of it what were the facts constituting the offence charged and that a prima facie case was made out against the appell lant. It is manifest that the decision of the Judicial Committee has no application to the present case for the order of sanctioning in that case was much more cryptic and materially different. [185 E F] Gokulchand vs The King, A.I.,R. 1948 P.C. 82; Gokulchand V. King, , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by a Special judge who sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. No separate sentence was passed under section 6(1)(c) of Act. The appellant unsuccessfully appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The charge framed against him related to the same transaction stated that on or about May 12, 1952 he had accepted Rs. 100 as illegal gratification from V. section Doraiswamy as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to whomsoever in seeing that a speedy settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway was subsequently the Eastern Railway. The sanction also clearly stated that Mr. Bokil had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice, the appellant should be put on his trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Act. Held, that the sanction accorded by Mr.Bokil was a valid sanction. The sanctioning authority had not applied his minds to the fact that before according sanction he went through all the relevant papers and after being satisfied that sanction should be given he accorded his sanction. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R 75 I.A. 30, referred to.

The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 against the appellant tenant for eviction on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The appellant contended that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b) as grounds for eviction of the tenants by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. It was further urged that since the interest of the remainder man may be prejudiced, the landlord with a life interests in the property cannot evict the tenants on these grounds. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction. HELD: The rights between section M.

The respondent decree holder in the execution proceed ings in this very case between the same parties which came to this Court on an earlier occasion. The appellant contended that after the coming into force of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (the Act) the respondent was entitled to enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force. HELD: Under the general law, trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of groves, and grove land. [34 F G] The proposition is well settled that trees before they were cut, formed parts of the 'land" and an "intermediary 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncutti trees are deemed to be parts of land. And, an inseparable portion is always excluded in the entire. [35 F G; 36 A] In view Of this very legal position it is impossible for us to accept this opinion in view of the definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the Act which says "intervary grove means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such". This means that "grove land" and a "interrimediary" 's broves are treated equated and roves are on lery collections of the trees in plot of land, so as as to exclude cultivation in they. The respondent decree holders were therefore entitled to succeed. [36 F G].

The six accused persons were charged with offences punishable under Sections 302, 324, 323, 341, 148, 149 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution sought to establish its case by examining as many as six eye witnesses besides other evidence, documentary and oral. At the trial however four eye witnesses, PW3 Devassykutty, PWs 6 and 7 salesman and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The Trial Court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6, namely Rajan, Preman, Viswan, Sura and Shajan were found guilty of offences under Sections 143, 147, 148 and 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against them by the Trial Court was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it is directed that issue notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and quantum of sentence. The four appellants were released on bail. The High Court acquitted two of the accused and convicted the remaining four only. The appellants preferred an appeal against their conviction and sentences passed against them. In the appeal before this Court it was contended for the appellants that the trial court had wrongly relied upon the evidence of PW4 Biju, who had been believed by both the courts below and without any motive for commission of the crime, and that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the four accused had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause the death of the deceased. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.P.C. [93B] 1.2 In a case like this to determine as to which of the appellants is guilty of a particular offence. On a consideration of the circumstances of the case, the type of weapons with which they were armed and nature and seat of injuries, it cannot be said that any one of the four appellants, who alone stand convicted by the High court had inflicted injuries intending to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. [94C] 1:3 The existence Of an unlawful unlawful assembly was a necessary requirement for invoking section 149 I P.C., and it is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by him were not sufficient in ordinary course to cause such death of one of them. The existence, of an assembly is necessary postulate that where the existence of such an unlawful rioting is not proved, the convic tion with the aid of Section 149 cannot be recorded or sustained. [92D] 1 :4 In a trial like this, to determine whether all the four persons had shared common intention in causing such death or any such bodily harm as is shown by the prosecution witnesses, it must necessarily result in the failure of the charge under section 149 IPC.[93E F] 2:5 The existence or otherwise of an ' unlawful assembly ' is a requisite postulate for invoke Section 149. Where the existence,of such an assembly was not proved the conviction with the help of Section 34 I. P. C. cannot be sustained and the same would be the position with regard to the conviction of all the appellants for other offences with the assistance of Section 148 IPC also.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company, having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of 5 per cent less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. When it came to filing of the return for the assessment year 1969 70 (year ending 30.9.1966) and 196869 (year ended 30. 9.1967), the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs, 925,257 but filed a nil return saving that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis. The I.T.O. completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For these assessment years, 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' plea that it is maintaining its account on cash basis. He held that it had not been following any particular method of accounting regularly in the past years, that it did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coptry. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past year relating to the asses see reveal that the method of accounts adopted by the assessee must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income Tax Officer. On a reference made at the instance of Revenue, the High Court answered the question in the negative i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. The appellant company filed these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in answering the question against the appellant. [102F] 1.2 In the instant case, the very concept of "receipt" as espoused by the assesse is untenable and unacceptable. The order of remand made by the Tribunal was thus unnecessary.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The conviction was set aside by the High Court on appeal. Held, that there should be corroboration of the approver in material particulars and qua each accused. The time gap between the preparation of the knife and murder is great and it is possible in such circumstances that the appellant might have cemented and not proceeded with the commission of the offence. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (1924) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, referred to. Bhsuboni Sahu 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which we express no opinion but so far as the appellant is concerned it was not sufficient that there was corroboration of his story and it was therefore not sufficient to connect him with the murder under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. Bhoboni Sahu v The King, (1923) L R. 76 1. A. Mad 308, re Rajagopal vs Baskerville, ; , referred to and distinguished. Bhunoni Sahu V. King, A.I.R., Cal. 308 and re Rajagopalan, A, I.L.R , approved. Bhopuboni Naik vs The Queen, (1878) L L. R. 75 I. A, Mad. 309, disapproved. Bhumoni Sahu, vs The State of Orissa, ; and re Gopal Rajagopal, A I.I.,R. , referred not to. Held further, that though the conviction was unsustainable the law being that there must be corroboration in material facts and qua the appellant.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On or about December 11, 1962, the appellant was charged in the Court of Special Judge for an offence under section 5 (2), read with section 5, (1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act, and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The case of the prosecution was that on July 8, 1961, the Electrical Executive Engineer accompanied by his Head Clerk, the appel lant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramprit Singh P.W. 2 was the lessee of the Mills. The Executive Engineer met P. W. 2 in the mill premises and told him that the outer seal of the meter, technically called the body seal, was tampered with. Thereafter the Executive Engineer cut the inner seal, technically known as the loop seal, of the Electricity Board and fixed two fresh seals on the meter one in the terminal 'and the other in the body of the same meter. The appellant demanded money and P.Ws. 2 to 9 gave him eighteen rupee currency notes, the serial numbers of which had been previously noted down by the Magistrate, P. Ws. 2 and 9. The Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.,W. 16, accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the Special Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that on the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the language of section 2(2), Prevention of bribery Act or section 21 of the Penal Code, and that the sanction of the Government was required under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code where any public servant is accused of an offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . HELD: (i) The appellant was not therefore a "Public servant" but he was merely a "person who was appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. [687 E] (ii)The appellant could be deemed to be a public officer within the expression of section 21, Indian Penal code in view of the language used in section 81 of the and therefore the appellant cannot be deemed as a " Public servant" under section 21(1)(d) Of the Prevention Act. [688 F G] (iii)The question whether sanction of Government was necessary under section 198 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, is one which must be decided on its own facts. The word "officer" in the context of section 81 means that there must be some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government. He is either himselfarmed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so armed.

The appellant was prosecuted for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Prevention of Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Essential Commodities Act, 1962. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence of India Rules, 1962, is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and the rest of the order of conviction maintained. [273 D] Rule 141(1) of Maharashtra Foodgrains Prevention of Restriction on Purchase 'and Sale Control of Movement) Order 1964, is not ultra vires. Section 3 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r . 141(3) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of Indian Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [272 E] In the present case, the order was not challenged much less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, Penal Code and sentenced to death. The incident took place at about 5 p.m. on October 20, 1970. The deceased Kunwar Singh was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. They were proceeding on their bicycles and as they reached a spot near Barhpur Block, Violet was alleged to have shouted "the Vakil has come". Sia Ram fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. All the accused thereafter ran away. The other lawyer Om Prakash Pandey contacted the District Magistrate and the Superintendent of Police vainly attempting to have the dying declaration of Kunwar Singh recorded. A person called Soney Lal, also alleged to be an eye witness lodged the First Information Report at the police station at about 6 p. m. on the same day. The Superintendent of police K. N. Daruwala reached the spot of occurrence shortly before 6 pm. R. N Singh, the Sub Inspector, held an inquest on the dead body of Kunwar singh and sent it for postmortem examination. Dr. Rizvi who performed the postmortem examination found a firearm wound on the left upper chest of the deceased. There were abrasions and scorching marks around the injury. The evidence of the doctor who performed postmortem examination showed that he had received a gun shot from the gun as one result of the injuries sustained by him. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia, Ram and Violets. It dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government except in regard to Shri Ram whom it convicted under Section 302 read with section 109. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate commission of crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active complicity is the gist of the offence of abetment under the third paragraph of section 107. [629 H] (2) The words of VioThatlet are at best in the nature, of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design. [625 A B] (3) In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission or of the crime. Mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the said alleged abettor is not sufficient compliance with the requirements of section 106. A mere proof that a crime charged can not have be committed without tho interposition Of the alleged abetment is not necessary.

The appellant was charged with committing the murder of one Vishwanath for helping Deoram Maruti Patil and bringing about his acquittal. The Sessions judge found that the prosecution witnesses were not speaking the truth and that the version given by accused 2 was the probable one. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is well settled that common intention within the meaning of section implied a pre arranged plan and the criminal act was done pursuant to the prearranged plan. The said plan may also develop on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence. If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, it should come to a definite conclusion that the person, had a prior concert with one or more other persons, named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. A few illustrations will bring out the impact of section 34 on different situations. [683 E F] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab ; , followed. (ii) The judgment of the High Court cannot stand. [684 B] Mohan Singha Singh vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , referred to. (iii) It was not correct to say that when three of the four named accused, who were charged under section 307 read with s.149, were acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointly along with one of the said named persons.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, was granted import licence for the supply of MSCSC defective sheets and coils on 30th May 1984. The foreign supplier shipped the material in three consignments and the goods arrived at the Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984. On 21st August, 1984, the petitioner 's clearing agent filed six bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, the bills of Entry were returned with the remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax". This was endorsed on 24th August,1984. The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner, that it to say, by the order of the Income Tax Authorities, the goods could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. On 30th March, 1988, the Income tax Department issued a notice to the peti tioner for the payment of duty, the liability of the peti tions to pay the duty was the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. The duty as is prevalent now is Rs.5,000 per M.T. and 10% C.V.D. at Rs.325 per M.,T. plus addl. duty 45% and C. V.D., at Rs 325 per M,T. + addl, duty 45%. The total duty on the consignment was assessed as Rs.26,20,109.55. 624 On 21th August 1984,the petitioner ' s clearing agent moved six bills for ex post clearance. But, the bill of entry were returned without the remark "pleases obtain no objections from the IncomeTax Authorities". This action was challenged by the petitioner under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April, 1989, this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective Sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S.SEA PRIMROSE" will be released forthwith on petitioner ' paying customs and other duties as leviable on 21.8.84. In addition to the above payment, the Petitioner will deposit Rs. 5 lakhs and furnish surety (which may consist of ITC bond but excluding cash/bank guarantee/NSC/FDR) to the satisfaction of the Collector of Customs. " The petitioner ' asserted that duty at a particular rate prevalent at a certain date was not payable.

The appellants were the managing director of a bank. The property was attached by the Collector under the Bombay Land Revenue Code on July 27, 1942. Notice for sale was issued on November 24, 1942 and the proclamation on December 24, 1943, was published under sections 165 and 166 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939. On January 16, 1943 M. B. Jakati sold the property to defendants 8 to 10 who were respondents 2 to 4. The appellants applied for postponing the sale which was rejected. The auction sale was held on February 2, 1943 and was confirmed on June 23, 1943. The purchaser was section N. Borkar, defendant No. 7, now respondent No. 1. On February 10, 1944, M.B. Jhakati sold his property to respondents 8 to 12 who were defendants 2 to 1387. The sale was confirmed by the Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies on June 3, 1943 but the purchaser was not a party to the suit and the appellants filed a suit for partition of the joint family property alleging inter alia that the purchase by respondent No 1 of bungalow was not binding on the joint Hindu family as it was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of respondent No 2 which were characterised as misfeasance " The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the S.C.R. (2) that even if the debt had been not avyvaharika the institution of the suit for Partition operated as severance of status between the members of the family and therefore the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end and consequently in the auction sale, the share of the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser; and that what could legally be sold under section 155 of the Act was the right, title and interest of the defaulter i. e. of the father alone which could not include the share Of the other members of joint family. Held, that the liability of the appellants to discharge the debts of the husband 's father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the son to pay the debt of the mother and which does not come to a end as a result of partition of joint Hindu Family property. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a consequence of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avy avyVaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals".

The petitioners, who were both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends.
