They are alleged to have been found guilty of an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. and were convicted by the Metropolitan Magistrate for offences punishable under sections 8 B and 8 B of the Act. The petitioners challenged the orders of the Committee before the High Court which quashed the orders directing the filing of complaints and the criminal proceedings initiated against them before the Metropolitan magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the Delhi Administration. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the Committee should send a report recommending suspension of the D.C.,P. (North), S.H.O., P.S. Samepur (Badli) and S.I. Incharge Police Post, Tis Hazari; and (2) the petitioners in this case hold the Committee in great respect and that they never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the Committee. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The orders of Delhi Administration directing the filling of complaints should be quashed and the petitioners are persons who fall under section 8 B. [521E] 2. Mere non issue of notices to them under section8 B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8B. [525F] 3. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section 9B of the . It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by section 8 C of the , before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end of the inquiry. [426C D] 4.

The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the Act on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the tax was not laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised by Entry No. 56 but upon "fares and freights", which are different entities, and in support of the contention that there is a difference, reference was made to Entry No, 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "faff and freight 's". The petitioners contended that the Act was not ultra vires the legislature. Held: (1)(a) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. (b) The word "accept" shows that the incidence of the tax is upon passengers and goods, though the amount varies in the case of goods because the freight must necessarily differ on account of weight, bulk and nature of the goods transported. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers or goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. (c) The tax under section 3(1) is not a tax on fares and freight charges attributable to routes outside the State except in one instance which is contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 and to which reference will be made separately. (d) The words "if passengers are carried or goods transported without the charge of fare or freight, the tax has to be paid as if fare or fares have been charged. This clearly shows that there was a clear classification made by the Constitution itself. No discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out and all operators are equally affected by the Act.

The appellant company served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen in February 1974 alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1st July, 1974, Ext. E 2 viz., heavy loss caused by non availability of tin plates, persistent power curbs and mounting cost of production were not the real reasons for affecting retrenchment but the real reason was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment is not bona fide and that the non availability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real motive being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l). Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have taken this view and they are of the opinion that the view taken therein is correct. [567F] 1.2 In the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. The spectre of common law doctrine that contract of personal service cannot be specifically enforced or the doctrine of mitigation of damages does not haunt in this branch of law. The relief of reinstatement with continuity of service can be granted where termination of services is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived deprived workman of his earnings. If the normal rule in a case like this is to award full back wage, the burden will be on the appellant employer (l) [1971] 1 Law Journal, 327; Susannah Sharm vs Sacrifice for the survival of an industrial undertaking cannot be an unilateral action. It must be a two way traffic. The management need not have merry time to itself making the workmen the sacrificial goat. If sacrifice is necessary, those who can afford and have the cushion and the capacity must bear the greater brunt making the shock of sacrifice as less poignant as possible for those who keep body and soul together with utmost difficulty. F The appellant wants us to give something more than full back Wages in this case which the Labour Court has awarded. There is nothing to show whether the Managing Director had made any sacrifice; whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether the managerial coterie has reduced some expenses on itself. If there is no such material on record, how do we expect the workmen, the less affording of the weaker segment of the society, to make the sacrifice, because sacrifice on their part is denial of the very means of livelihood. [568C E] 1:3 The appellant is making profit since 1976 77. The unit is looking up. It has started making profits. The workmen have already been reinstated and therefore they have started earning their wages. It may, however, be recalled that the appellant has still not cleared its accumulated loss.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the confession exhibit PH was not admissible in evidence as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the same is inadmissible in evidence. HELD: (i) The statement of PW 1 recorded by him during investigation of a case cannot be treated as devoid of force. [434 D] (ii) It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation (see in this connection H. Rishbud & Inder Singh vs The State of Delhi, ; , referred to. (iii) In view of the decision of this Court in Nazir Ahmed 's case it was the accused and none else who was responsible for the murder of Churi deceased before the visit of the accused to the house of Shri Mahajan. [427 E] (iv) It was not necessary to dilate upon this aspect of the matter because the question whether a confession recorded during the investigation of the case by a second class Magistrate not specially empowered under section 164 is admissible in Evidence, was considered by this Court. [334 F G] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Ors., ; , followed. (v) The decision in Nazir Ahmad 's Case also covers the case in hand and that on the principles there applied, here to oral evidence given by PW 2, mother of the deceased, shows that the accused had been illtreating Churi. It is not necessary for this Court to dilate on this aspect because it was of the opinion that a confession recording by a first class Magistrate (1) [1964] 4 S.C.R. 435 not specially authorised during the course o f an investigation under Chapter XIV of the Criminal Procedure Code, can also be led at the trial.

The plaintiff 's father Tarak Lall and Tarak had two brothers and Naku. The mortgage was exe cuted on the 12th June, 1936 in favour of one Mst. Gyarsi for a consideration of Rs. 80,000. For convenience I will call this suit the mortgage deed though this is not a suit on the mortgage. The mortgagee sued in 1938 and obtained a preliminary decree for sale on the 17th February, 1939, for a sum of Rs 89,485 12 plus costs. The decree was made final on the 22nd December, 1989. In execution the mortgagee proceeded against the proper ty of the plaintiff alone (as Tarak 's son) and during the pendency of the execution, assigned her rights in the decree to the Hooghly Flour Mills. The Mills continued the execu tion and on the 11th March, 1943, the claim was satisfied in this way. An order of the Court was obtained sanctioning sale of a part of the mortgaged property, 20 Round Tank Lane (which belonged exclusively to the plaintiff) to the decree holder for a certain sum of money. The sanction of the court was necessary because the judgment debtor Hari Lall (present plaintiff) was a minor and the only benefit they got out of this Rs. 79,744 4 from each of them. In addition to this Rs, the plaintiff asked for (1) "a declaration that the properties mentioned in Schedule A ' belonging to the defendants stand charged with the repayment of the sum of RS. 80.507 7 8 being the aggregate amount due and payable by the two defendants"; and (2) "Decree under Order XXXIV, Civil Procedure Code in proper form". Schedule A contains a list of the rest of the properties which belong exclusively to them. The plaintiff claims on the basis that each of the three mortgagors was liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. According to him, the bulk of the Rs.80,000 was borrowed on what I have called the suit mortgage to pay off previous debts which had been incurred by the parties on earlier mortgages. The amount which went towards satisfaction of the defendant 's portion of these earlier liabilities was only Rs. 1,19,116 11 0 in satisfaction of his claim and costs then outstanding. The mills executed a reconveyance of the remaining properties to the mortgagors in release of the mort gage on the same day. In addi tion to this amount the plaintiff demanded Rs. 2,500 from each one of the defendants. The balance of Rs 1,18,116 was retained by A. 5,000 and C jointly mortgage their three estates for Rs. 10,000, the total aggregate sum due at the date of the suit from the three of them, and Rs. 11,519 11 0. In this way he asked for a declaration of charge and for a decree under Order XXXII, Civil Proce dure Code in terms of Schedule A. Held, that though the claim is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance asked for the relief to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer of Property Act. The suit was therefore maintainable. Mohammad Sher Khan vs Seth Swami Dayal (1917) I.L.R. at 586 and Taibai vs Wasudeorao, A.I.R., , referred to.

The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka Univer sity. The Govt. by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil). The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment) Rules 1973. According to these rules total marks for qualifying examina tion were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33. 3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions, but the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. In view thereof, it was an admitted fact that if marks for interviews were kept on 15% or 16th of the aggregate marks, and merit lists are prepared according to the Rules then both of them were bound t be selected. [495E F] Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court, in appeal, confirmed their conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution evidence on record should be rejected as when on 10th July 1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11 4 1983; (2) the confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The confession of the co accused is not substantive evidence against the other co accused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State of Bihar, ; this Court observed that in dealing with a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.W. 10 stated that he had been convicted in three cases of murder and several dacoities. It appears that by then he had some pending cases against him where final reports were later given by the police. His wife who was a material witness has not been examined in the case. Obviously, as the jail records did not show that P.Ws. 5, 12, 15, 40 and 57. In his own statement recorded under section 164 of the Code on 13 4 1983, Yadav denied to have made any statement fol low ing his apprehension. Even accepting the prosecution story that Yadav made this statement, he appears to have been convicted as alleged can the same be utilised against Sadanand is the next aspect for consid eration. Obviously when Yadav was beaten up, he must have been anxious to ensure to ensurethat the assault stopped. His plea in such a situation would neither be voluntary nor natural. It would not be proper to rely upon the same for any purpose. [417F G] Kashmira Singh vs State o Madhya Pradesh, ; , referred to. (3) The confession is admissible under section 3 of the Act.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited and its main business was to invest money in manufacturing concerns. The last company was Ruston and Hornsby (India) Private Limited, and its principal business was distribution of products of a manufacture concern known "Cromptonson Parkin" (Works) India Limited and service and repair to the said products at its workshop. The third company was Konyon Greaves Private Limited. It carried on the business of manufacturing oil engines and pumps. The fourth company was Cromapton Park Insulatedon Park Co. Ltd., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were nine awards, though the main award dealing with the main controversy relating to wage and dearness allowances was common. It appears that wages and Dearness Allowance prevalent in the four companies had been continuing since 1950 when the last award was made between the parties. The main dispute which gave rise to the references was with respect to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The references included other items also but they were not concerned in the present appeals with those items. Of the four Companies who were the appellants before 364, Greaves Cotton and Co., was the first company and its subsidiary business was dealing to invest moneys in manufacturing concern. The second company was Greaves cotton and Cromeppton Gardeninson Pvt. Ltd. and its branch office was to manufacture oil engines, pumps and pump sets. The three companies were controlled by the first Company, namely Greaves Jute Cotton and Compton parkinson (Work) India Ltd., and service repair to their products at their workshop. There was a dispute between the four appellants companies and the respondents workmen, which were referred for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal by nine references orders on various dates between April to December 1959.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Annappa and against whom the present appeal was directed, applied to the Mamlatdar alleging that the mortgaged property was Devasthan Inam and praying for the cancellation of the transfer in favour of the mortgagees. The application was rejected on the ground that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of annappa to the mortgagees and that inasmuch as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse possession. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. Annamappa vs Daim (1904) L.R. 32 Ind App. No. 22 of 1945, relied on. The Rajinada passed by Shiddappa did not purport to file, the same on behalf of an application for Letters of Administration in respect of an area in question and conferred certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupant as laid down in the Code but did not take away the rights of other occupants. It was true that no specific reference was made in the judgment to section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code but the actual decision in that case, quite clearly indicated the court 's understanding of the law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 74 Of the Code. In view of the observations of the Judicial Committee in Khiarajmal vs Daamim (I) , the conclusion of the Division Bench in the Letters Patent Appeals was correct and the principal contention urged before the High Court must be repelled.

The respondent company, a company incor porated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers, despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur wherefrom sales there of these goods were effected in the State of Uttar Pradesh. During the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the aforesaid Notification but a specialised article used for copying purposes its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed in the aforesaid notification. The Sales Tax Officer, (Section IV), Kanpur, did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and held that carbon Paper was a part of the typewriter and taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6%, and ribbon was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A word which is not defined in an enactment has to be understood in its popular and commer cial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs. In Attorney General vs Winstanley ; , Lord Tenterden started as follows: "Now, when we look at the words of an Act of Parliament, which are not applied to any particular science or art, we are to construe them as they are understood in common language. " In Grenfell vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue (1831) 2 S.T.C. 302; State of Orissa vs Gestetner Duplicators ; , referred to. (2) The word 'paper ' in the common parlance or in the com criminatory sense means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing purposes. " [838E F] (3) In the instant case carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/X 1012(4) dated 1st July 1966 issued under section 3 A of the U.P.

The respondents were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946. In 1951, the partners of the appellant Mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Kiccha in the district of Nainital. The respondents filed a suit to recover damages from the bank for wrongful dismissal. The trial court held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1 to 4 had disobeyed the order of the management, they were properly dismissed by the management. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that both the concerns i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The appellant came in appeal by special leave against the order dismissing the respondents ' appeal. Held: (i) The two factories are distinct entities situated at different places and, to import a term conferring a right on the employer to transfer respondents I to 4 to a different concern is really to make a new contract between them. The decisions cited at the Bar do not in the least sustain the appellant 's broad contention. In the present case, as the two factories were situated at distinct places and to import the term conferring an option on the employers to transfer the respondents I t to 4 from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of this case. (ii) The question whether a person employed in a factory can be trans ferred to some other independent concern started by the same employer at a stage subsequent to the date of his employment. (iii) The appellant was an employee of the respondent bank. The Bank transferred him from one branch to another branch of the bank situated in different towns. As he refused to comply with the order, he was dismissed.

The appellant company was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provision for certain other matters in relation thereto. It was an obvious social welfare legislation in tune with the Directive Principles of State Policy contained in Articles 41, 42 and 43 of the Constitution. The Act extends to the whole of India and comes into force on such date or dates as the Central Government may appoint, different dates being permissible for different provisions of the Act and other necessary provisions have been made in this Chapter. The special contribution is required to be such percentage not exceeding five per cent of the total wage bill of the employer, as the central Government may specify. It is also provided that the employer 's special contribution in the cases of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions Of both Chapters IV and V are in force shall be fixed at a rate higher than that in the ease of factories and establishments situate in areas where the provisions o the said Chapter are not in force. The employees, ' State insurance Act,1948 was enacted in 1948. Chapter VA provides for the establishment of the Employees ' State ' Insurance Corporation for administering the scheme of Employees ' ' State A Corporation for administered tho scheme of employees in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended and it includes among other items, (i) payment of benefits and provision of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and where the medical benefit is extended to their families; (ii) payment by the principal employer of a special contribution throughout the Union. The contribution payable in respect of an employee shall comprise contribution payable by the employer called employees contribution and contribution payable under Chapter IV in the Case of factories Or establishments situated In areas in areas which the provision of both Chapters V and V is in force; (iii) payment, of benefits or provision of Medical treatment and service to insured person and where medical benefit was extended to his families. The appellant company challenged the constitutional validity of Chapter VI A of Part V A on the ground that it contravened Article 14 of the constitution inasmuch as it did not contemplate rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) When extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant provisions (1 ) , 23 and 24 in List III of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitu tion are in operation, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter; (2) The scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution was levied from all employers wherever they be, in the present case, the scheme is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro li quo. [1090C D] (3) The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It could not be considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contribution and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1191E F] Basant Kumar vs Eagle Rolling Mil/s, ; , followed. (4) The benefit provisions will sooner or later be extended to all areas. Therefore, the amendment provides that employers of regions to whom the benefit clauses are not extended must also make their contributions though at a lesser rate.

The petitioners demanded regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna. The management denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such, there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a continuous long time. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim. In this petition for special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that: (1) The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him; (2) The petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work available for them. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle that regularisation of daily rated workers and payment `to him ' of the ' pay equal lo that of regular workman arise only when a daily wager is doing that the same job as the regularly workman and therefore there being no vacancy available in the establishment for absorption of the peti tioners and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite thereof, there being an appointment made by respondent No. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate. The property was set out in Schedule A to the plaint and besides a claim was also made to certain other items of movable and certain other tenures, but this suit was decreed as prayed for and the property was sold in execution of the final decree and was purchased by the mortgage decree holder on September 24, 1931. The appellants ' claim to have purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The contesting defendants were the Azamabad Tea Co. Ltd., who too had been impleaded as defendants. The National Agency Co. resisted the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs ' suit was liable to be dismissed by reason of the provisions of 0. VI r. 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and that in consequence the appellants were precluded from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that the suit was not maintainable. The High Court upheld the contention of the appellants and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale was not held to be real to no more than what the High Court has decreed. (ii) The High Courts have decided not to reject the claim based on this ground. (iii) Though the plaintiffs did not agitate or press before the courts below any special right based on the purchase of Ashfaq 's share through Pir Baksh, they could not be held to have been raised before the trial Court and hence their interests could not he affected by the dismissal of the suit.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad. The trial court convicted and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) had not been complied with, and that the omission had the effect of vitiating the entire proceedings ending in the trial of the appellant. Held, that the failure to comply with section 360 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was a mere irregularity which could be cured by the provisions Of section 537 of the code. The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions thereof. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor, (1923) L.R. 59 I.A. 206, referred to. In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 had been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that such person was done. The mere irregularity involved as must always be the case, a breach of one or more of the very comprehensive provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. Abdul Rahim vs The Emperor, , referred to and distinguished. In the present case the omission complained Of in the present was not material because the omission on the part of the police officers concerned or of the Magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, had caused prejudice to the appellant in the interest of justice, the court may reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with the provisions.

The respondent Municipality, after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), to show cause why it should not be directed to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of such direction for the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in the Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda, as shown in the plan annexed to the notice. The appellant replied that the effluent was being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha Channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad. In 1944 it was felt that as the water of some of the wells in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent, which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas, still further away from the city which lies on the western side of the railway lines. It was pointed out that during the last 3 or 4 years periodical surveys of the water in the city had been taken by the appellant and these tests had shown that the water was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluents being discharged through the existing channels, that all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the respondent were available for inspection by the Municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The Special Officer decided issues No. 4 in the affirmative and held that the question whether the discharge was mala fide, arbitrary, capricious and that the same had been issued without the respondent Municipality sufficiently applying its mind, the Special Officer was of the opinion that it wag out of the purview of the present enquiry. He accordingly directed the appellant to arrange for the discharged of the sewage through a drain for pumping water over a period Of nine months as shown by the municipality. The appeal filed by the Municipal Corporation was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question of whether the nuisance in question existed was one which ought to be set aside. [395 D] (ii) The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. Under sub section (3), however, the appointment of a Special Officer is considered necessary because the dispute between the Municipality & the partyconcerned required investigation and report from the Officer. [397 E] (iii) The words "to hold an enquiry into the matter" clearly suggest that the Special Officers must enquire into the entire matter where a party objects absolutely to the notification and the requisition contained therein.

The appellant was charged with the offence of attempting to recover possession of railway stores which were found unauctionable. The prosecution relied on the evidence adduced and principally on the report of Jaswant Singh along with his oral testimony, the Magistrate found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the appellant had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he had bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained possession of the same. HELD: (i) The onus of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. [189 F] (ii) In most cases the burden of proof is discharged by lead evidence about identifying marks On the goods and some peculiarity Of the goods cannot be found. [188 D E] Moyalal Rostagir vs The State, ; , referred to. (iii)The onus of proving that the articles belong to any particular railway administration it has to establish that the article were the property of a railway administration. Evidence to the effect that the goods conformed to the Railway Standards fails short of such proof. [ 189 F] M Royalal Ro stagirv vs The Union, ; referred to and distinguished. (iv)The evidence in the case did not establish that goods were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act.

The appellants had leased out the demised premises for 11 months from May 1, 1964 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The demised premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '). Section 13(1) thereof postulates that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract no court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord, whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act" unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the Court any one of the grounds enumerated in Clauses 'a ' to 'k ' thereof. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respondent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop premises. The findings recorded by all the courts are that Smt. Anandi was the tenant. The appellants during her life time had not carried on the business with her till date of her death. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt Anandi paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control) Act 1976 by which Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introduced to section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means (a) The person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and (b) In the event of death of a person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the cases of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. Anand i Bai, therefore, they are entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. The respond ent landlord 's appeal against the order of the Trial Court was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave.

The appellant Board maintains a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum and that the services of the workers of the company are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. HELD: The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should have looked at the profits made without considering provision for taxation in the shape of income tax and for reserves. [44E F] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. In the instant case the decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the board. The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the respondent Board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate held that the appellant was not entitled to live with her husband on the grounds that as he was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligation, she could not persuade herself to live in with him and thus inflict on himself a life of perpetual torture. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court dismissed the application. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant wife that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the wife to refuse to live alongwith her husband and hence the wife is not entitled tO maintenance if she refused to live. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decision in Velayudhan vs Sukmari a Single Judge of the High Courts was purely obiter. It would appear that there was a clear finding by the Magistrate which had been accepted by the High court, that the wife failed to prove by convincing evidence that her deceased husband was impetent and was, therefore, unable to perform his marital duties, found himself bound by the decisions of the Madras High Court in Jaggavarapu Basawamma 's case. [704C D] 1:2 The decision of the Bombay High Court is not a good law and are accordingly overruled. [700F] 1 :3 In the instant case, the appellant had very rightly pointed out as follows: "If the maintenance of a wife is supposed to include only food, shelter and clothing having regard to the conjugal rights and if the just cause on which wife can refuse to stay with the husband and yet claim maintenance, can have reference only to the comfort and safe of the wife then it might reduce the wife 'to the status of a domesticated animal. [607C] 1.4 The decision given as far back as 1907, while construing the proviso appears to be both prophetic and pragmatic in its approach and it is rather unfortunate that subsequent decisions have not noticed this important principle of law decided by the Bombay high Court. [808E F] 2:1 In the present case, there was no dispute because the appellant did not arise out of the proceedings under section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 made no difference because if the wife had a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the husband that she is likely to be physically harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband 's parents or relations, such an apprehension also would be manifestly a reasonable justification for the husband 't refusal to live With her husband. [908H; 909A] 2 :2 The appellant had not been able to prove that his wife was impecotent. In view of this finding of fact, the question of law posed and decided by this Court in the aforesaid case must be held to be no longer good law for the purpose of deciding the present appeal. [900B C] 2.3 The decisions of High Courts given prior to the Amendment of 1949 would no longer be good law after the introduction of the Amendment which gives, as it were, a completely new complexion to the intendment and colour of the second proviso to section 488(now Explanation to the second sub section (3) of section 125 and widens its horizon.

The plaintiff, a Municipality, was the owner of certain premises in the State of Saurashtra. The suit property was described as "Rate" and the defendants were the Union of India and the State Government. The plaintiff claimed damages for wrongful occupation of the Parade Ground from 1st January, 1964 till they vacate the wrongful encroachment and hand over possession to the plaintiff. The defendants denied that they were trespassers or liable to pay damages and rent in respect of the suit property. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they had proved their title to it. In appeal the High Court allowed the appeal of the Union and held that even assuming that by virtue of the Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 the title to Rate Ground had come to be vested in the Municipality there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land in question, that its right over the suit lands was never recognised by the Union Government or the State Govern ment and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show, that as early as July 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the Government of India. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff has not shown possession of the Suit building within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit is also liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Article 65 of the is applicable in this ease as the suit in question was filed on 3rd April, 1964 and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect thereof on the ques tion of title, the Trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that Article 66 of the Constitution is applicable to this case since the suit has been filed on threerd March 1964 but the Act had come into force on 1st Janu ary, 1964. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The suit notice under section 80 Civil Proce dure Code is a copy of the proceedings of the Board of Officers of the defence Department in which they have described detailed inventory of Defence department assets, accommodations, installations, furniture and connected stores pertaining to Saurashtra state forces in Bhavnagar. [226B] The resolution No. 33 dated 19nd January,1948 which is relied on does not make any distinction and it refers to only lands and not buildings. It refers to lands and buildings. Since a number of Municipalities made representation to the Government to reconsider the same, the Government reconsider the entire case and decided that the right to sell plots of land given under Resolution No 37 dated lnd January 1948 by the State was transferred or vested in tho Municipalities concerned. [227C D] The procedure to be followed for giving this land in sale or on rent shall generally be followed according to the rules of Government, that is to say public auction shall be made. If the approximate value of the land to be given on sale or lease comes to Rs.25 per sq. metre or it is more than that the sale or the lease land shall be considered final after permission of the revenue department of the Govern ment for sale or leased lease is obtained.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The Special judge convicted him of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. In appeal by special leave the appellant contended that he was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code and therefore a public servant be fell within the definition of a public servants contained in section 2 of the Act. Held, that the contention must fail. The appellant was an Officer within the terms of section 1(9) and therefore, a public Servant within the expression of section 2 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act II of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Lah. (2) I.L.R., approved. Ram Kishan vs Delhi Administration, A I. R. , referred to. The true test in order to determine whether a person is an officer of the Government is: (1) whether he is in the service or pay of the government and (2)(iii) whether the duties he is performing are of an exalted character or very humble indeed. As has been stated in Bacon 's Abridgment at Vol. 6, page 2, in the article headed "Of the nature of an officer and the several kinds of officers": "The word "officium" implies a duty, and in the next place, the charge of such duty; and that it is a rule that where one man 'bath to do with another 's affairs against his will, and without his leave, that this is an office, and he who is in it is an Officer".

The respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise and Taxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share of the respondent in the said property was notified for June 14, 1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale the respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, being Suit No. 472/13 6 77 against the State of Punjab and the collector cum Deputy Excise and the Taxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Excise Collector cum Deputy excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the Respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of the land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his half portion was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The Respondent then filed an appeal to the District Judge, Patiala, being Civil Appeal No. 554/5.9.79. The Additional District Judge dismissed it with costs but the High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the property used for residence was exempt under clause(ccc)(cc) of proviso to Section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent order restraining the state and the District Collector cum Excise and Excise Taxation Commissioner. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was allowed by the Single Judge of the High court holding that since the appellate court applied totally a wrong law in deciding the appeal, it allowed the respondent 's second appeal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 60(1) has no application to attachment and sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said provisions are concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provision of the aforesaid Act. [847C D] 1.2 The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sold in execution of a decree of a civil court, but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery, would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said section. There is no provision in the Act corresponding to cl. (cc) or of the Proviso to sub Section (1).

The respondent was the owner of certain agricultural lands. The land acquisition proceedings were initiated by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963 and March 19, 1965 respectively. The Special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000. This compensation was received in April, 1964 by the heirs of Rashid, who had merely exercised a right to sue for further compensation which was merely a hope or a chance that the compensation might be enhanced, that such hope or chance could not be elevated to the status of an assets or property and as such not asset or property chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment and as a result thereof no property escaped assessment. The respondent as well as the High Court proceeded on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands formed part of the estate of the deceased and passed on his death for, it was on such basis that the High 'Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands such property (meaning lands) had been undervalued in the original assessment and that as such it had escaped assessment to duty. On appeal by certificate, the appellant contended: (i) that the accountable person had only a claim to get an extra compensation which could not he called 'property ' and whether that claim amounted to a right of property capable of sale in open market was a highly debatable question and a mistake which had to be discovered after lengthy discussion and debate could not therefore be said to be a mistake apparent on the record; (ii) that land acquisition proceeding and land references in Civil Court not being part of assessment record a mistake discovered by reference to such other record was not a mistake manifest from the record of the case and (iii) that even assuming that any asset or properties chargeable to Estate duty had been escaped assessment, the notice was illegal and without jurisdiction because such escapement was not due to any omission or failure on the part of accountable person to disclose fully and truly material facts necessary for making the assessment. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there were no two separate rights one a right had to receive compensation and other a right which could have been elevated to his status of any asset/ property and, as such, it had jurisdiction to issue the notice. [331B] 2.1 In the instant case, since the lands were lost to the estate by the deceased before the relevant date, namely, the date of death, it would be the right to receive the compensation under the Land Acquisition Act that will have to be evaluated under the Estate Duty Act. The only right is to receive an additional or further compensation. Upon acquisition of his lands under the land Acquisition Act, the claimant has only one right which is to get compensation for the land acquired by the Government, which is the fair market value on the date when the relevant notification and it is this right which quantified by the Collector under section 11 and by the civil court under section 26 of the Land Acquisi tion Act.

The appellant, a Director of the Bank, was elected as the Directors of the bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. His election was not called in question according to the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act 1960. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of the Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur, issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of that Bank as per the provisions of section 73FF and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 1167 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The notice stated that the appellant had borrowed a loan of total Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 7,000) from the Bank and he kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986, and being elected as Director of that bank on 18.8.1986. Till then he was working as the Director of it. The appellant 's appeal against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of Cooperative Societies on 15.2 1988 holding inter alia that section 73F(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act, 1960 came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21. 10.86 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21.11.1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7.12.1987 was served on the appellant on 8.1287. The Assistant Registrar, Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7 12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter on 31.1 .1986 and he became defaulter under section 73(FF) of that Act. The appeal against this order was also dismissed by a Cooperation and textile Department, State of Maharashtra, Bombay holding that the dues calculated on 31 1.86 became recurring dues every following day and on 12 5.1986 when section 73 F came into operation the outstanding dues continued even on 18 8.6.1986; and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21 10.8 1986 when he was elected, he was defaulter under Section 73FF(1). The order dated 30.8 .89 was served by the appellant to showcause why he be not removed from its Board of directors. The orders of the Asstt Registrar dated July 7. 12.87 were served on him on 8th December 1987. The Appellant 's writ petition challenging the above order was rejected by the Cooperation & textile Department on 30.9.89 holding that section73FF became applicable from 6.81986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.1986 i.e. the date when he had been declared elected as Directors. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the Appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 78(2) of C.P.C.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's representation to the State Government was rejected. The State Government issued orders reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition before the High Court. A Division Bench allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's Order dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from Service. Allowing the appeal partly, this Court, HELD: The reduction of pension by 50% was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [189F] M. Narasimhachar vs The State of Mysore, ; , followed. In the instant case, the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent `s pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. It appears that the attention of the High court was not drawn to these Rules. [190F] In M.M. Narasimhaacharchar vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents from the premises in dispute on the ground that they had applied for permission to sue the District Magistrate, Moradabad under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit with costs on the 25th March 1955. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court upheld the contention of the appellants that the permission granted by the Commissioner was invalid in law as it was not admissible in evidence; and that the notice given by the appellants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was also invalid in view of the provisions contained in section 3 (4) and section 16 of the Act. On the question whether the permission was valid or not, HELD : The High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the width of the revisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 of the . [556 B] In the present case, the order passed by the District Magis trate granting or refusing to grant permission to the appellants to bring the suit was a nullity. The High ' Court was therefore not justified by introducing a new limitation pertaining lo questions of jurisdic tion in determining its scope. [560 F G] The words used in sections 188 and 191 of the Sea Customs Act (1878) were very wide enough to empower the Commissioner to correct the error committed by the district Magistrate in making an order brought before it; quite clearly if the District Judge had wrongly refused to act, and that would give the Commissioner jurisdiction to exercise his revisional power. [561 F] The present case was not one of those cases where the plea raised before the civil court went to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order was a mere nullity.

The President of India, who was alleged to have assaulted her, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of article 317(1) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) Article 317(2) of 'the Constitution confers power on the President to remove the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission for reasons mentioned in sub clauses (a), (b) and (c) is not relevant for our purpose; (ii) article 317 provides that the Chairman, or any member of the Public Service Com mission can only be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court has on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145; and (iii) the order of removal can be passed after the High court has on enquiry reported to the President that the chairman or such other member ought to be removed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President under article 317 is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that an inquiry has to be held by this Court in accordance With the procedure laid down in that regard under Article. 145. [648B] 2. The purpose of article 316(1), is to ensure independence of members of the public services Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. The Judges of the Supreme court can be removed by their office only in accordancewith the procedure provided by Article 124(4) which is made applicable to the Judges of High Courts, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and the Chief Election Commissioner by articles 218, 148 and 324 (5) Members of Public Service Commissions are, in one sense, given a higher degree of protection by the elimination, as far as possible, of political pressures in the matters of their removal.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939) against the respondent temple for the management of an idol installed in the temple. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellants ' suit holding that the deity installed therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. The respondent preferred an appeal before the High Court against the decision of the Subordinate Judge which was heard by the Division Bench referred to above. The High Court reversed the decision and held that the temple and the deity install therein being private endowment fell outside the four boundaries of the statute and the Respondent was fully justified in passing orders for their management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Under the Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal a family deity in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and his descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the Chairman. [830 F] 1.2 The essential distinction between a private and public endowment is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or class of unascertained people. This being the essential distinction both between a public and a private endowment is the nature of a public or a private trust. [ 830 A] 1:3 The essential difference between a Private and a public charitable endowment is (1) where the origin of the endowment cannot be ascertained, the question whether the user of the temple by members of the public is as of right; (2) The fact that the control and management vests either in a large body of persons or in the members of a family or a specified individual, then the endowment can only be regarded as public, intended to benefit the general body of worshippers. [ 831 C] 1 :4 In the instant case, the High court has not properly construed some of the important features contained in the documents and the evidence and has in fact overlooked certain important aspects which completely negative the fact that a dedication was of a purely private nature and the intention of founder was merely to instal the idol in the temples.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into various contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys had agreed to finance contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. " The appellant was also authorised to sue for, recover and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaLhotra, to conduct and defend proceedings in consultation with him and to take steps in his name and on his behalf. Malhotra promised and declared that "all powers hereby granted are and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorney 's against us whether for principle, interest, costs, charges or otherwise remain outstanding and unpaid. " Intimation of the power of the Attorney was given by the appellant to the military authorities for payment. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under the bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained by him against Malhotra. The appeLlant filed objections in the execution proceedings. On September 11, 1952, the objections were dismissed. On December 12, 1952 the appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhat Mal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the appeLtlant was the assignee of that bill and decreed the suit. On appeal by the High Court, the sole question in this appeal was whether the power Of attorney dated July 13. 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies payable under the Bill in favour 'of the appellant. HELD : The law on the subject admits of no doubt. In Palmer vs Carey, ; , referred to.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. [438E] (2) The receipts of Rs 27,949/ by M/S Gillands Arbundnot & co. Ltd. cannot be said to be either interest on the securities; income from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered "income from other source" and brought to tax under section 56. [441F G] (3) The respondent was not represented before this Court. [442H] (4) The expression "salary" in section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High court. [443C D] (5) The income from a house property cannot be held to be neither interest on securities; the income from property would be exempt from tax or if it is not exempt under what head the same has to he brought to taxation.

The Bihar Legislature passed the Bihar Act, 1950, which was later amended by the Bihar Amendment Act of 1951. The validity of this Act was challenged on the ground that it violated articles 19(1)(g) and 31 of the Constitution as they prohibit the Mussalmans from performing the religious practice of the community to sacrifice the cow on the occasion of Bakr Id. HELD: (i) The impugned Acts, if enforced, will compel them at once to close down their business and will, in effect, amount to a complete denial of their right to carry oil their occupation, trade or business in spite of the mandatory provisions of article 19(6). [682 C] (ii) The Bihar Act makes no distinction between she buffaloes, bulls and bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which are useful as milch or breeding or draught animals and those which are not and indiscriminately prohibits slaughter of she buffaloes. [690 D E] (iii) The provisions of the impugned Acts were not enforceable by any court of law but nevertheless they were fundamental in the governance of the country and it was the duty of the State to give effect to them. The impugned Act, therefore, contravenes article 19 (1)(f) and is to that extent void. [678 F] (iv) The ban on slaughter of her buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (Cattle and buffaloes) which were useful as a milch cattle was reasonable but of those which were not useful was not valid.

The respondent, a public limited company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager and Assistant Manager, was suspended by the appellant company on December 5, 1955. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the orders of suspension and termination dated December 5. 1955, and December 7, 1955 respectively and asking for certain other reliefs. The preliminary objections taken were these: (1) that the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent because he was an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order; (2) that as regard being had to the context and the entire body of the standing orders, the aforesaid view of the High court is not correct; and (3) that in any case, the Standing orders did not make a distinction between `employees ' and ` workmen ' and there may also be employees who have no tickets. Held, that the respondent was an 'workman ' within the definition of the Central Act and an 'employee as defined for the purpose of the said Standing Orders. The Standing Orders in question were not objected to as being defective or incomplete by workmen, and they had been approved by the appropriate authority and they must be construed with reference to their subject or context. In the present case, however, the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental muster, he was not an ' employee ' as defined under the Standing order. The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in Standing Order No. 2(a) should be read as " whose name and tickets numbers, if any, are included In the depart mental musters " occurring in Standing Orders No. 1 and should apply in the case of those employees only who possess tickets and whose ticket numbersare capable of being entered in departmental musters; they are not intended to exclude employees who do not possess tickets or to whom tickets have not been issued and consequently whose names only are so entered.

The appellant, an undertaking owned controlled and managed by a Government Company, was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into Production. The dispute between the work men and the Company could not be resolved amicably and consequently a reference was made under the which came up before the Ninth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel project could not he treated as a separate Establishment because under the Act a company is itself an establishment so that all units of a Company like Hindustan Steel Ltd. will constitute one establishment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even the establishment employing less than 20 persons would be a part of the principal establishment consisting of the factory and, consequently, the point raised had to be decided on the basis whether under the proviso to section 3 the Alloy steel Project is to be treated as an establishment separate from Hindustan Steel Limited or it had to he treated in a separate unit because, under the , a company was itself an "establishment" so that only all units Of Hindustan Steel Company Ltd. would constitute one Establishment and since this Project had not been earning any profits the Tribunal directed payment of bonus at 4 per cent of wages prescribed by the Act. HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed an obvious error, as it ignored the indications which are manifest from the language used in the Act, and in view of section 1(3) of the Act the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because alloy steel project was owned, controlled and run managed by Hindustan Steel.

The appellant State of Haryana issued a notification under Section 3(1) of the , levying cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industries and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of water pollution. The Cess Act was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a avowed object to control the pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urban isation. The Act provides for the constitution of joint boards, the details of which need not detain us. The cess Act sets out in detail the functions and powers of these Boards. Chapter VI of the Act requires the Central Govern ment and State Governments to provide funds to the Central Government and the States Boards respectively for imple menting the provisions of the . The Cess Acts are intended to ensure that the domestic and industrial affluence are not allowed to be discharged into water coars without adequate treatment. This Act is intended to regulate and control pollution but a fiscal measure to raise revenue for augmenting the resources, of the Pollution Control Boards. There are also certain provisions relating to constitution of Joint boards the details whereof need not detained us. Section 3 of the Cess Act which may be termed as charging section states that there shall be levied and collected a cess for the purposes of the and utilisation thereunder. The levy and collection of cess provided under the Cess is on water consumption by persons who carry on certain industry specified in the Schedule. The appellant State and the Haryana High Court have taken the view that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products" and that it could not be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining table for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It was further of the view, that in interpreting the word 'vegetable ' one has to keep in mind the object for which the Cess act was made. The High Court also took the view (1) that sugar industry is one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and since the object of the pollution Act and the Cess Acts were intended to control water pollution, and since it was based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it This Court in State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc. ; , with reference to the meaning given to the same word occurring in a.
