The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Appellate Authority passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Before the High Court, it was contended by the appel lant that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ' and that the practice of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate or Doctor which had nothing commercial about it was not business within the meaning of section 10(3)(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1960. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'business" occurring in section 10 (3)(b)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice ously described as learned, liberal or noble. [14A] 2.1 The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the background of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context in which the term should be understood generally. On the other hand, it is a well known principle of construction that meaning of words and expressions used in an Act must take their colour from the content in which they appear. [15B C] 2:2 The expression business ' in section 12(1) (a)(iii), is used to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the purpose of livlihood or profit '. In a broad sense it is taken to mean something that occupies tho time attentionand labour of an men for purposes of lvlihood or profits '. [16C D] 2 :3 The word 'business has not been defined in the Andhra pradesh Buildings (lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1960. It is a word of large and wide import capable of a variety of meanings. It was so used that it could be given a narrow meaning which the appellant wants to give to that expression. It would indeed be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10 which bars the eviction of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not section 10 of the Rent Control Legislation. [17F] 2(a) The expression "business" in section 2(3) (b)(ii) is not used in the wider sense so that it is confined to commercial activity. It has not, therefore, been a sound principle of construc tion tn interpret expressions used In one Act with reference to their use in another Act; more so, if the two Acts in which similar word is used are not cognate Acts. Neither the meaning nor the definition of the term in one statute affords a guide to the construction of the same term in another statute and the sense in which that term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which such the term ought to be understood ordinarily generally. [18E F] 2 K. B. D. 256, referred to.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which the appellant was the partner on the condition that interest would be payable @ 7/9 per cent per month and that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The suit was filed in the court of the First Civil Judge, Kanpur. The evidence was concluded before the civil judge, Kanpur, and thereafter by an order dated 12 May 1964 of the High Court at Allahabad the suit was transferred to the High 'Court in its original civil jurisdiction. The High Court heard the suit and decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. At the trial the issues were first whether the respondent deposit ed the sum of money with the appellant under an agreement that it was payable on demand or whether it was a case of loan of Rs 4,000. The entire controversy in the suit is whether it Was a case where money was deposited under an Agreement and that it Was payable on demands and whether it wag a case for an ordinary loan of RS. 4 lacs. The respondent contended that Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was the relevant Article because if was a ease of money deposited under the agreement that the same would be paid on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit filed within three years from the demand. Held: (i) The High court was right in decreeing the suit. (ii) The letter exhibit A 5 bears the date 29 September, 1942 and is contemporaneous with the entire transaction between the appellant and the respondent; (iii) The document was contemporaneous with it the entire transactions between the parties; (iv) The evidence showed that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him on 27th February, 1986. He made an application to this Court under Article 32 in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 292 of 1986 challenging that order of detention. In the earlier writ petition, several contentions had been raised but Mr. Jethmalani confined his submissions only one aspect namely, that the period of parole was from 15th May, 1986 till February 22, 1987 should not be added to the period for which speci fied in the impugned order under section 2(1). The Court dismissed the writ petition on 22nd April, 1987. In paragraph 2 of the judgment it was stated: "In reply to para 4, it is submitted that the summons as required by the detenu 's advocate in the letter dated 12th April, 1986 were not supplied as there were no written summons served on the petitioner. I say that after the completion of the search of the residential premises of the petitioner on 27.2.1986, the petitioner was taken into custody around 2.00 p.m. on 27rd February,1986 and he was produced before the Magistrate and an order was made requiring him to be produced next day in the Court. By the time the order of deten tion came to be passed the petitioner had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him. At the relevant time, the detenu was under trial in the said criminal case. On such facts it was the contention of the peti tioner that the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. This Court rejected the contentions advanced on behalf of the detenu. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact remains that only one contention had been urged. There is absolutely no basis for the alle gation in paragraph 2. [848B] 2.1 In the writ peti tion which has been settled by Mr. Desai, such allegations have been made. It is common experience that when those several contentions are advanced in the pleadings, counsel chooses to press one or some out of the several contentions at the time of the hearing. The judgment indicated that only two point was argued. The averments in paragraph 3 of the writ Petition accepts that position. It, therefore, follows that Mr. Salve made submissions confined to one contention which had not been raised in the earlier Writ Petition but arose out of proceedings in court therein relating to the effect of release on parole.

The petitioners, who were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department, challenged the orders of the Central Government on various grounds. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. It was further urged that since they belonged to the categories of casual labourers and are being exploited by the Union of India, they were not entitled for the same benefits which the ordinary employees are enjoyed. The petitioners also contended that even though some of them have been working continuously for more than a year in the Department and some of the petitioners have been engaged as casual labourers for nearly ten years, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above. The Central Government rejected the contentions of the respondents and directed the Union to prepare a scheme on rational basis for absorbing as far as possible the casual labourers who have been in continuous service for more or less than six months. The Union of india, however, filed a writ petition in this Court for the issue of a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the Union Government to pay to the petitioners wages to them same salary and allowance and other benefits as are being paid to the regular and permanent employees of Union of lndia in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union Public Service Commission to regularise the service of the casual labour who had been in continuously working for morethan six months, and also to pay wages to the workmen who were employed as casual labourer belonging to the several categories of employees referred to aforesaid. The Court, while issuing notice to the respondents, directed the Central Govern ment to prepare the scheme on a rational basis. The scheme was followed by another order bearing No. 10 4/83 R dated 26 7 1984 which prescribed the rate or rates of wages payable to casual labourers in the Telecommunication Wing of the Department. The relevant part of the order reads thus: "No. 28 II/77 SR/STNST Office of the Director General Posts and telegraphs, New Delhi 1, 15 5 1980 To . . . Subject: Increase in rate of daily wages for the casual/ semi skilled/skilled labour. Sir, The employment of the Casual semi skilled or unskilled labour in similar grade: Provision has been made in the recruitment rules whereever possible to give preference in recruitment for corresponding semi skilled and unskilled workers. " The petitioners were not satisfied with the above reply received by them. They therefore filed the present writ petitions and the first of them bearing Writ Petition No.

The assessee, a public notice under section 22(1) of the Income tax Act, was issued requiring every person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as well as the Tribunal rejected his contentions but the High Court, on a reference under section 66(1), held that the notice issued by the Income Tax Officer was valid in law. Held, that the notices under section 34(1)(a) of Income tax were not invalid and the consequent assessment also so far as it related to the period during which action could be taken was the extended one of 8 years. The notice under s.22(1). was therefore invalid and consequently the subsequent assessment equally so far. Held further, that in view of the decision of this Court in Harakchand Makanji & Co. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, , the notice under S.23(2) was valid and the consequential assessment also bad to be quashed. The assessee might file a return showing an income below the taxable minimum but the return in law is not a mere scrap of paper. It is a return which shows no assessable income. A return showing income below that taxable limit can be made even in answer to a notice under sec. 22(2).

The first petitioner is a registered Central Trade Union claiming to represent about 85 per cent of the officers working in various nationalised banks. Peti tioners 2 to 4 are principal office bearers of the first petitioner and are officers of different nationalised banks, who are not workmen, is to be appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India on the Board of each of the Nationalised Banks. The petitioners contend that Clause 3 of the Scheme in terms of which the circular was purported to have been issued is ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless the said clause is so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read, the said Clause does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. The Central Government by its own practice prior to the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi, directed that the said circular be amended in accordance with the provisions of the scheme and the Scheme insofar as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board. The first petitioner challenged the Circular dated 23 8.1982 issued by Joint Secretary, Government of lndia, Ministry o/ Finance, Depart ment of India. The said circular was quashed by this Court in Union of India vs R.S. Seita & Ors., ; and Union of india vs M/s. P.K. Sejani & Ors. , , on the ground that it violates Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the legislature is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act, "control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the nation in conformi ty with the national policy and objectives". [855E F] 2. The purpose of the legislation is to promote the banks and to provide for nationalise banks in consonance with the National Policy and objectives. It is with this object in view that the Act has envisaged a truly representative Board of Directors chosen by election where election is feasible or by nomination where that mode is more appropriate. But the legislature has left it to the Central Govern ment to specify by a scheme the manner in which the election or nomination is to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give the best form of representation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. It may be possible to appoint a representative of the depos itors by election instead of nomination.

The respondent was imposed penalties in respect of certain assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of penalties imposed. The Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) By the provisions of section 254(1) of Income tax, 1961 powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate tribunal to stay proceedings relating to the recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. At the same time it is significant that under section 220(6) power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income Tax Officer only when an appeal had been presented under section 246 which will be to the appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Tribunal. There is no provision in section 220 under which the Income. tax Officer or any of his superior departmental officers can be moved for granting stay in the recovery proceedings of penalty/tax. [681 D] (2) The power of staying by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It has further been observed that "where the legislature invests an Appellate Tribunal with powers to prevent an injustice, it impliedly empowers it to stay such proceedings which may result in causing further mischief". [691 F] (3) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Assistant Commissioner with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers fully effective. In the instant case, when section 220 confers appellate jurisdiction, it expressly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of head constable and posted as Station Officer at Sidholi. On February 27, 1953, he made an application to the Superintendent of Police for his conduct, but the Superintendent dismissed him from service with effect from the said date. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad, praying that the order of dismissal be quashed on the ground that it was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities and that as no case, as required by the said sub paragraph, was registered against him in the police station, the order was invalid. The High Court held that the enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. Held, that the departmental trial was not vitiated by any irregularities and the departmental proceedings were illegal. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries does not affect the question, if substantially the subject matter of the mag ministerial inquiry and the Departmental trial is the same. In the circumstances it would be hypertechnical to hold that there was no magisterial enquiry in respect Of the matter which was the subject of the departmental enquiry. The relevant provisions of the Police Regulations read: Paragraph 486: "When the offence alleged against a police officer amounts to an offence only under section 7 of the police Act, there can be no mag ministerial enquiry under the Criminal Procedure Code. In such cases, and in other cases until and unless a magisterial Inquiry is ordered, inquiry will be made under the direction of the Superintendent in accordance with the following rules."

The appellant, a highly qualified ophthalmic surgeon feeling aggrieved by the promotion of respondents 4 to 24, who were promoted on different dates to supertime grade II, sought redress of his grievance praying for a mandamus that he may be deemed to have been promoted from February 18, 1971 failing which more out of frustration and less by any justification he seeks quashing of the promotion. The principal contention was that their promotions are in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. It was further contended that as these 28 posts were in Specialists ' grade and the strength of Specialists Grade posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to super time grade II is required to be filled in, it can only be filled by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists ' Grade, i.e. category 'C ' under 1963 Rules. The appellant contended that the 19 unspecified Specialists (Class I posts) and unspecified posts were meant only for promoting category 'D ' and 'E ' officers on probation on September 9, 1966, in specialists grade and that the strength was reduced to 28 whenever any posts out of those 28 posts added to Supertime grade 11 is required. The respondent contended that since these 28 post were in specialist ' grade ' posts and unsspecified posts, 28 posts in number can be filled from amongst the unspecified specialists; that as the uns specified Specialists " grade posts and unidentified Specialists" grade posts, 29 posts in numbers could be filled only by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly not by transfer. The Central Government accepted this contention and directed the appellant to consider his eligibility for promotion from September 1971 and if found eligible he should have been appointed from that date. The matter was referred to the State Public Service Commission who held a meeting on October 9, 1967. The State Public Services Tribunal held that the promotions were in contravention Of rule 8(3) of the Rules; that the appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to super Time grade II on February 8, 1971 and that his refusal to accept promotion at Simla was not justified; that he was fully eligible for being considered for promotion to the post from September 9. The High Court also held that since the initial constitution of service on September9, 1966 any future promotion to super lime grade II from departmental candidates could be from amongst these 28 originally belonging thereto specialists only; that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into a specified post and assigned to a speciality it can be made only in by promotion; that since there was some substance, though there was none, in the contention on behalf of the appellant that whenever unspecifiedSpecialists ' post is converted into an unspecified post it can merely be filled In either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not in a way going to be benefited by the invalidation of their promotion. [52E] 1.2 The appellant being conscious of this position tried to circumvent it by saying that the post at Simla offered to him by way of promotion in super time Grade II was a teaching post for which he was not qualified and, therefore, his refusal was not valid. [53F] 2.1 In passing a contention of the Appellant that all 28 posts must be filled into by promotion, it is not open to him to urge that the Post at Simla offer to him was not correct. It is futile to contend that in declining promotion to he appellant when some post were converted from unspecifiedspecialists ' posts into different specialities and were filled in by those who were qualified to be promoted in the respective speciality in which each one of them was promoted.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to generate great changes by banishing big concentration of Naturs bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. Naturally the State enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others, peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures Rules is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' as section 2(2) having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. 'Permissible area ' [section 2(3)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and be in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' ' [Section 2(4)] and then he must make available to the State such excess as called surplus area [section 10A]. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants, and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is a big holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of laws will go to feed the surplus pool. With this end in view, the Act has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High Courts have upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the legislation suggests an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer to later. Suffice it to say that the law is interpreted a radical agrarian measure; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasants proprietors.

The appellants, who were the sons of one Amarshah, instituted an action in the Court of the Additional District Judge Chanda for a decree for possession of property immovable (including the Zamindari of Dhanora) and movable specified in the Schedules annexed to the plaint. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Under the terms of the Chanda Patent it is declared that the tenure shall be indivisible, and non transferable (save to the nearest male heir the transfer in such case being subject to the approval of the Chief Commissioner) the land shall pass from such proprietor or such other person to and vest in the State for the purposes of the State free of all encumbrances. The compensation is to be determined in accordance with the rules contained in Sch. 3 and such question has not already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction, the Compensation Officer shall proceed to enquire summarily into the merits of such question and pass such orders as he thinks fit. [316 F H] In adjudging the plaintiffs claim the Court must determine whether Pratapshah father of the plaintiffs was the nearest female male relative of Amarsh. The contest between them had to be adjudged in the light of the rules of lineal primogeniture governing an impartible estate which are well established : Succession is governed by the rules which govern succession to partible property subject to such modifications only as flow from the character of the impartible Estate; the only modification which impartibility suggests in regard to the right of succession is the existence of a special rule for the selection of a single heir when there are several heirs of the same class who would be entitled to succeed to the property if it were partible under the general Hindu law; and in the absence of a Special custom, the rule of primogen incum bility furnishes a ground of preference.

The appellant landlord by notice dated 14 November 1966 terminated the said tenancy and filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises. The Trial Court held that the contractual rent was excessive and excessive. The appellants ' appeal to the High Court failed. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained therein deal with orders which may be passed consequent upon dispute as regards standard rent. It is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I to section 12 that the provision in sub section (3), and (4) of section 11 are attracted. The High Court held that in view of the powers conferred by article 90 of the Constitution it was not necessary for the respondent to have "a controlling interest" in the respondent Company and that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8 per cent per annum. G., Bash and not as they subject directly or indirectly to his will and ordering, and therefore, he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above.

[508C D] 2. The High Court found that the later resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the 8th ground that the subsequent Resolution did not make any reference to the allottees at all. Relying on the words "the passing of the S .A. Examination for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be insisted" the Court found, that it wouldmean that where the passing of S. A.S., examination was insisted prior to that Resolution in the same shall continue to be insisted in future also and if passing of that S.As.

The petitioner 's son was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Outpost Jeraikela, Police Station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in Orissa. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behera died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police detention. The petitioner ' s mother, the petitioner and grand mother went to the Police Out Post at about 8 p.m. with food for Suman Behrahera which he ate and thereafter these women came away while Suman Behara continued to remain in police force and Police Constable Chhabil Das of Police Station, Bisra were arrested and detained at the Police outpost. The respondents filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of the deceased for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The State of Orissa and its police officers including Sarat Chander Barik Assistant Sub Inspectors of Police and Constable Nos. 127, Ch Commodhabil Kissujur, Assistant sub Inspector of police and Constable NO.127 filed their respective affidavits in support of their defence. The defence of the respondents is that Suman Beeta managed to escape from police custody at about 3 a.m on the night between 1st and 2nd December 1987 and it was likely that he was run over by a passing train after he had escaped from police possession. In short, on this basis the allegation of custodial deaths was denied and consequently the respondents ' responsibility for unnatural death of Suman Be Dhara. The Additional Solicitor General contended that the evidence adduced during the inquiry does not support the defence of respondents and there is no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that Suman be died in police possession as a consequence of injuries inflicted on him. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The claim in public law for compensation ' for contravention Of human rights and fundamental freedoms, the protection of which is guaranteed in the Constitution, is an acknowledged remedy for enforcement and protection of such rights, and such a claim based on strict liability made by resorting to a constitutional remedy provided for the enforcement of a fundamental right is 'distinct from, and in addition to, the remedy in private law for damages for the tort resulting from the contravention of fundamental right. [503B] 1.2 The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages ' awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public duty, not protecting the fundamental rights of the citizen. The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law, for the wrong done due to breach of public duty.

The petitioner, a prisoner under the sentence of death, sought to be commuted of the sentence by an order dated January 21, 1973. The petition was dismissed by the Chief Reporter on January 21. 1973. In the meantime, the petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court for issue of a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ or direction directing the respondents particularly the Delhi Administration and the Superintendent of Jail to allow her to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of imprisonment. The petitions were dismissed by an interim order dated March 21, 1974. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that if the petitioner were allowed to interview the prisoners, the interviews could be permitted only subject to the rules and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. [1186C] (2) Rule 549(4) of Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentenced sentence of life shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. [1108D E] (3) The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview her prisoners right since the President of India rejected the petitions filed by them for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life. No such right can be claimed by the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to he interviewed is willing to be interviewed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the Bank instituted mortgage suit against the respondent on the original side of the Tripura High Court for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. The appellant contended that the bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the District Judge, but that the surety bond was executed both by the Receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District judge of Agartala his successors, successors in office and assigns". Held, that under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety bond executed both be the Receiver 'and the appellant. In order that the security bond should be enforceable at the hands of the presiding officer of the court, it must be held that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea garden. He was put in possession of the Tea garden in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea gardens were managed by the receiver economically and efficiently. The bond would therefore cover the loss occasioned to the tea plantation due to the Receiver. Held, further, that the order for recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself liable under the terms of the bond.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. On that day, however, an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 stipulates that in every case where a detention order has been made under section 11, the State Government shall, within three weeks from the date of detention of the person under the order, place before the Advisory board the grounds on which the order has be made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purposes of this case is that section 11 stipulates that no Law providing for detention shall authorize the detention Of a person For a longer term than three years unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of 3 months that it is in Its opinion sufficient Cause for such deten tion. Section 15(2) of Gujarat Prevention Of Anti Social Activi ties Act,1985 provides for the constitution of an Advisory board, section 11 provides for reference to the Advisory Boards and section 12 prescribes the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Committee. What was important for this purpose is that sec. 11 stipulates a time limit within which the detaining authority can on its own satisfaction detain a person is three months. The period of two weeks stipulated by section 11 of the Act expired on July 14, 1986, and the petitioner was entitled to be released on July 19, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Board within the said date. On August 7, 1986 he was not so released. This state of affairs continued till August 7. 1986 when the order of detention dated June 23. 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was passed on the same facts on the basis that there was no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under Section 11 of Act against the same person, subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of a period of 12 months from the day of detention under the earlier detention order. The appellant was therefore entitled to he set at liberty. Allowing the appeal and quashing the order dated August 7 1986, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 15 of the Bombay Prevention of anti Social Activities (Act, 1985) provides for preventive deten tion with disfavour and has permitted it only for a limited period of one months without the intervention of an independent body with persons on it of judicial qualifications of a high order. [209E] 2.2 The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authori ty. The procedural requirement is that there fore, to be strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory Boards is to he made within three months, it is no answer to say that the reference though not made within 3 weeks, was made before the hearing of the case.

The petitioner, father of respondent, was awarded a decree in terms of the award. The award was signed by both the parties. Accordingly, he made the award on 18th January 1977. Below the award, both the respondents and the arbitrator had signed. The endorsement reads, when translated in English, as found by the High Court that the award is agreed to and binding upon both the sides and that the whole responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on Shri Kantibhai Vaidya and that he has taken the responsibility. Thereafter followed a spell of litigation. The respondent applied for filing the award and sought the judgment in terms thereof under section 17 of the (1) of the Act. A notice consequent upon the filing of the Award was issued to the petitioner. The application was converted into Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. It was stated in the application that the petitioner had torn off the award as and, therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely on a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1 ) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (3) the award was not set aside under section 30 and (4) that the Award is not remitted under section 16(5) of Act. The High Court dismissed the civil revision application. In this petition, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction; (2 ) the previous proceeding were without Jurisdiction; (3 ) the time taken for making the application to setting aside the Award had expired, and ( 4) the period for making such an application had expired. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award could be said that the parties had agreed not to refer the dispute to arbitration of the named arbitrator and that they made an award.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu family and a severance of the Joint status between the appellant and his sons. In 1954 his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dis missed the appellant 's suit. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) The transfers under exhibit A1 and exhibit A 2 were not hit by section 6(h) of the . [45 D] (ii) The properties gifted under exhibit B 1 andA2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which Venkatacharyulu was governed, he had no power to make a gift of his divided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concumine. The gifts were not saved by section 2(d) of ' the . But the properties gifted were not invalid by the disruption of joint family in 1947. After the disruption, the Joint Hindu Family was free to make gift of her own property to the appellant but he did not make any such gift. [45 F] (iii) The gifts under exhibit R 1 and R 2 were invalid.
