The appellant was the Chief Justice of a High Court. The respondent filed an application for special leave to appeal against the order of the Election Tribunal under section 116A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 on the ground that the appeal presented to him by the respondent was within time if computed after making the deductions permitted by section 12 of the Limitation Act. The appellant contended that the expression "appeal" in article 156(2) of the Constitution meant an appeal governed by the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore the appeal should be dismissed. Held, that the provisions of section 29(2)(a) of Indian Limitation Act were not applicable to an appeal under the Representation Of the People (Amendment) Act, 1950. The expression "appellate jurisdiction" in the first limb of sub section (2)of section 29 of the Indian Limitation Acts means an appeal which is governed by a Code of civil procedure and does not ordinarily deal with substantive rights. The word "appeal " in article 157(1) of Schedule 11 of the Act means an order governed by that Code of Criminal Procedure, whereas the period of limitation is that prescribed for an appeal against an order made by a civil court under section 476 of the Code. It will be noticed that no argument was raised before the High Court that the appellant 's appeal was governed by article 156 of the First Schedule to the Limitation (Amendment). The provisions of 0. XLI, of the Civil Procedure Act were applicable to appeals against orders of tribunals and reliance is placed on the proviso to sub section(3) of that section which provides for an application of a period of 30 days in respect of a suit or appeal governed under the Code, whereas in the present case the First schedule had not prescribed any period of Limitation for an Appeal.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 703 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage operators in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the said order. The High Court held that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand andhalting places '. It was further of the view that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave against the said decision of the High court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 76 of tho Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 which is in Chapter IV of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 which authorises the District Magistrates to specify places within the limits of any municipality notified area, town area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where alone public service vehicles or any specified class or classes of public services vehicles and/or goods may stand indefinite or for such period as may be specified or public service Vehicles may stop for a longer time than is necessary for the taking up and setting down passengers. [717B] T.P Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; , followed. 1.2 The District Magi trate fixed the area as a Bus stand. Regarding the authority which had the power to notify an area as bus stand, there are at least three decisions of this Court. In T. P. Ibrahim vs State Regional Transport Author ity, T.B. Ibrahim & Anr., ; , referred to. 1:3 The Town Area Committee can derive any assistance from this rule. It only authorises the district Magistrate to exercise the powers under section76 of the Uttar Pradesh Act which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Transport author ity as held by this Court in T. B. Ibrahim 's case. [1817D] 2:4 The Town Areas Committee can derived any assistancefrom this rule, and it only authorises tho District Magistrate to do so. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by Regional Transport authority, Mathura to determine the area in question as a vehicle stand and the Dis trict Magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the , for contravention of certain property used in the commission of the offence. The trial court convicted all the accused ' but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence of the two appellants. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) There was no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the . [666 D] (ii) The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission. On the other hand, an attempt to commit the offence is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attemptto commit 'a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit it. [666 H] (iii) The appellants should have been warned that they had no licence to carry the paddy and they might have changed their mind at any place between Samalkha Barrier and the Delhi Punjab boundary and not have proceeded further in their journey. Section 8 of the states that "any person who attempts to contravene, or abets a contravention of any order made under section3 shall be deemed to have contravened that order". But there is no provision which makes preparation to committing an offence under section 6 of the Act. [667 A B] (iv) The conviction and sentences of the appellants under section 8 of 'the , are set aside.

The Sassoons agreed to transfer their Managing Agency of the said companies to Messrs Agarwal and Company, Chidambaram Mulraj and Company Ltd., and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd. by letters dated March 3, 1943, 16th April, 1943 and 27th April 1943 respectively. The Sassoon agreed to transferred their Managing Agencies of the aforesaid companies to the respective transferees with effect from December 1, 1943. The agreement was duly obtained and the Managing Agency was ultimately transferred to the various transferees with retrospective effect from January 1, 1944. The shares were transferred by the Sassoff to the transferees with a view to avoid payment of the remuneration or commission for the broken periods. The transfer of the Sassoon and Company were in favour of Messrs Agarwals and Company. The said commission was under clause 2(d) to be due to them yearly on the 31st December, 1943 in each and every year during the continuance of the Agreement and was to be payable and to be paid immediately after the annual accounts of the company had been passed by the shareholders. The Income tax Officer included the Sascoons ' share of the profits of the Company as income from the total receipts for the years 1943 1943 1943, 1943 1943 and 1943. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but on further appeal the Tribunal held that the Sas Soons became entitled on the very date of the respective assignments to a proportionate share of year 's remuneration for the Managing Agents and that therefore the Sasifons were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The High Court also held that as the Sasiffons had not earned any income for the break periods they could not have assigned it to the transferees with the result that when the transferees were paid the commission under the terms of the Managing agency Agreements, the transferees received the same in their own right even though they had not rendered the services to the Company for the whole of the calendar year 1943. Held, that the managing Agency Agreement was an indivisible contract for a whole year ' and was not a part of the consideration paid by the transferees to the Sashions as remuneration for purposes of convenience, the true nature of the functioning of a Managing Agent, where it is, a firm or a Company which so functions, has been recently held by this Court in Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son, Ltd. vs The Government of Hyderabad, ; , followed.

The appellant was a resident of the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased and the accused 's second son were living with his father. It is said that Sunderpatti developed illicit intimacy with Sahoo; but there were incessant quarrels between them. On August 12, 1963, at about 6 a.m. on the morning of August 13, 1963 the appellant brought her buck and after some wordy altercation between them they slept in the only room of their house. The only other inmate of the house was the appellant 's first son, Kirpa Shankar (P.W. 17), sleep in the room inside the house; and on the early morning of the next day, P.Ws. 9, 11, 13 88 and 15 saw the accused going out of the said house at about six a. m. On the morning when Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the rooms of the appellant, his daughter in law, and thereby finished the daily quarrels. This Court in a series of decisions has reiterated the following well settled rule of "circumstantial evidence". The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be in the first instance fully established. "All the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. Under the Act, the services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under Section 16(1) in Chapter V provides that if the Central Govt. is of the opinion that for the more efficient carrying on of General Insurance business, it is necessary to do so, it may by notification frame one or more schemes providing for all or any of the following matters; (e) the rationalisation or revision of pay scales and other terms and conditions of service of officers and other employees wherever necessary. Pursuant thereto, the central Govt. framed the New India Assurance Co operative Society Ltd. Merger Scheme 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. The appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The appel lant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance Business, immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. in which the undertaking of the insurer to which the service of the officer relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and condi tions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such vesting and shall continue to do thereof unless and until his appointment is terminated. Section 16 (1) provides that where the Central government is of opinion that it for the purpose of efficient carrying out General Insurance Policy, it was necessary to make so, the Board may by a notification frame two or more Schemes providing for every or any other matter; (ee) the principles of service conditions of officers & other employees where necessary. The respondent contended that Rule 5 is ultra vires of Article 14 of the Constitution and that Rule is ultra legis ly of Article 19 of the Constitu tion. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service. [225B] 1.2 The Board did not abolishing the post. It put an rest to the appellant. Obviously due to loss of confidence as his honesty and integrity became suspicious and his continuance in service was felt inexpedient and not in the interest of the business of the respondents. But Rule 8 was available for taking action for misconduct but was not availed. Therefore, the impugned order terminating the services is illegal. [226F] 1:3 The Board had no abolished the post, but put a end to it. It was not necessary to go into the grounds taken in the High Court assailing the invalidity of the termination order as they are not pressed before this Court. [227G H; 228A] D.T.C. vs D. T.C., Mazdoor Congress & Ors., 225 Judgment today today, referred to.

The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice on February 3, 1970 by which he invited tenders for the grant of li cences for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops, in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the register. The entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. Aj Ayodhya Prasad Shah deposited Rs. 329 of 1970 in the High Court with the allegation that the Collector was not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to. issue the licenses. The State Government and the other respondents traversed the claim in Ajodhya Prashad Shah 's writ petition and pleaded, inter alia, that the bids at the auction were not satis fied and, in the interest of the State revenue, the State Govern ment had passed the orders for not accepting Ajodhya P 's bids. The High Court held that section 6(a) of the Amending Ordinance was valid and the grant was invalid as the authorities for fixing the procedure under the amended section 29(2)(b) had not been specified, the Government had "appropriated for itself absolute and naked and arbitrary power" to accept any tender or reject any tender for any reason whatsoever or without any rhyme or reason. The order of the High court was set aside and the writ petition No. 2071 of 1972 was allowed. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector is not for the granting of an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor and that the Act did not empower it to part with that right on payment; (ii) the State had the authority to direct withholding and reauc tioning of the licenses, and (iii) the Act does not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and unfettered power in determining the sum of money" as was sought to be done by the order dated August 19, 1970. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(i) The High Courts have held that although the license fee collected by the State was illegal, the petitioner had already enjoyed the benefit under the licence and had volun tarily participated in the auction, and was not entitled to an order for its refund. [823B] (ii). Section 29(1) provides that a grantee of such a privilege shall not exercise it "unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or the Excise Commissioner. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 (2) (a) does not empower the State to part tain that right, on payment of consideration, with such conditions and restrictions for its regulation as may be necessary in the public interest. [889E F] 2(i). The power of the 'State Government under sub section (1) to grant the exclusive privilege within any specified area, sub section(2) provides, that no grantee of a privilege shah not exercise the same "unless and until he had received a licence in that respect from the collector or the excise Commissioner. [879B] 2.(ii). The State has the exclusive right or privilege to establish, store and sell country liquor and to grant that right to its license holders on payment Of consideration, subject to such conditions as it may think fit, the exclusive privileges" in question.

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with an approver. The prosecution case was that the deceased and his wife were friends and that the appellant had a common intention to kill him, but the appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence. HELD : (i) The evidence showed that the crime was committed by the appellant. [620 E] (ii)The circumstantial evidence did not support the prosecution case. The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that there were no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder and the theft formed the same transaction and were committed by it the same persons. [625 F G] Lachi Ram 's case, followed. (iii)The conviction was bad as there was evidence to connect accused No 3 with the crime. The circumstantial evidence showed the connection of accused No 2 with the murder. [613 A B] (iv)The evidence showed recovery of the chain which Narendra wore a chain similar to the one that was shown. There were civil and criminal proceedings between him and the appellant, and the conviction was not challenged in cross examination. The evidence of the tailor was that he had given some articles from silver idols and other silver articles and wanted money by disposing of the same. [521 C] Lachmi Ram ' s case, referred to. (v)The fact that there is a capital sentence of accused 2 and three others cannot be lost sight of. The law with regard to appreciation of approver 's evidence is based on the effect of sections 133 and 114 illustration (b). [622 A B].

The appellant was the lessee of a Town Planning Scheme, Surat. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. and not Rs. 50 p. by his order dated November 4, 1971. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town Planning officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in case the High Court held that the appeal preferred by his client before the board of Appeal was maintainable he would not press the grounds questioning the constitutional validity of the Act at this stage and the matter should then go back to the Board for a decision on the adequacy of the compensation; if however, it found that the Board 's appeal was right in holding that the Appeal was not maintainable he could urge the grounds challenging the constitutional vires of the impugned Act. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that in cases where the Town planning Officer determined the amount of compensation payable to the appellants the appellant would not raise the grounds assailing the constitutional legality of the act at this late stage and that the matter be remanded back to Board of appeal for a determination on the sufficiency of the Compensation; if, however, the Board found that it was right to hold that the appellant 's claim was not tenable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right. [92 D] 2. Under section 64(1) of the Land Acquisition Act compensation is determined on the basis of "market value" of the land on the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. Section 65 increment means the amount by which the total value of the plots included in the final scheme estimated on the assumption that the scheme has been completed would exceed the same date the market value of that plot when taken into account without the improvements. The increment is thus the difference in the market price of the same final plot with the improvements and without the improvement on the aforesaid date. [94 E F] Shantilal 's case at page 357 of the report, referred to.

The testator appointed his brother Seetharama Iyer as the guardian of his minor daughters as well as of his foster son. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor children attained majority he should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seethara shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to the testator immediately after he attained majority. It was also provided in the will that Seetharams should pay to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the testator. The appellant who was a third son of Seetharamamma, died in 1934 and his brother, Seetharana Iyer, was treated as a foster son (abhimanputra) by Viswanatha and was also minor at the time of his death. He made a will on October 4, 1927. By this will he appointed his second brother Seethama Iyer a guardian of their minor daughters and provided for that as long as his three children attained minority, he should deliver possession to them immediately after attaining majority. The two daughters claimed possession of their lands and their claim was that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one vehi of anja land and another veli land from out of the land in Vattam 149. The suit was resisted by the appellant who contended that the testator had no male issue but left two daughters surviving him who were minors at the date of his dying. Held, that on a fair and reasonable construction of the Will it could not be inferred that the will was bequeathing any particular one of the properties to them. It is only when the uncertainty is so great that there is no way of resolving it and finding out the intention of the executant that section 89 comes into play. But where the uncertainty in the testator 's mind is of a less degree and the intention is clear, though there may be some difficulty because there is more property of that kind than actually bequeathed, that (1) (1860) 5 N. 125 980 980 the benevolent rule should be applied to carry out the intentions of the deceased testator which is otherwise clear. The words in the Will mean the same. Therefore the direction of the appellant was that as far as Seetharamana was nominated by the testator to make the selection and give the devised land to the two daughters must now be partitioned in the ordinary course.

The appellant, a co bhumidar, was the widow of one of his brothers. The respondents filed a suit for joint possession over the share in dispute. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the District Judge decreed the suit for possession in respect of the share. In second appeal the High Court held that there was no evidence to prove that the appellant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the respondents assured the plaintiff that her name shall be entered in the record during the consolidation proceedings. The High Court also found that the name of the appellant as a co sharer with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The possession of the defendants apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. [867F] 1.2 The High court erred in law in holding that the present suit was not barred by Section 49 of U. P.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was appointed as Deputy Prime Ministers of India. The oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Prime Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. Relying on a bench decision of this Court in Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , this Court held that the requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India and that the words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Ministers but the description of him as Deputy Cabinet Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister, along with his other submis sions, this Court, HELD: The words which preced this portion were merely descriptive and forall purposes he was a Minister. [312C] Virjiram Ram Sutari vs Natulal Premnani & Ors. , referred to.

The respondent, a carding and spinning department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work some at 4 p.m., some at 5 p. m. The stoppage ended in both the departments. By 10 p.M. the strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st November, 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ending completely. was a strike and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The respondent contended that the stoppage of work on 1st Nov., 1948 amounted to an illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an unlawful strike and consequently an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 49B. Held, that the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal on this point was correct. The conclusion reached by the adjudicator was clearly right and the conclusion could not be avoided that the workers were acting in concert. That being so, the action of the respondent on the night of 1st 11, 1948, fell within the definition of the expression "strike" in section 2(q) of .

The appellant, a producer, was prosecuted under section 292 I.P.C. on the allegation that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled the guileless into degeneracy. The complaint alleged that the Fascining title was incorrect inasmuch as it had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. The Magistrate, after examining some witnesses took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereupon, the producer moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C., on the score that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censorors, and finding that in the Prosecution nothing frivolous nor vexatious nor vexatious or any material whatsoever to quash proceedings. On appeal, the High court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that the film had been granted 'A certificate by Central Board. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [517 A] (1) Section 79 makes an offence a non offence. When ? Only when the offending act is actually justified by law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution. The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. [ 515 A] K. A. Abbas vs Maybe, art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department more so in cinema pictures. So it is that a special legislation viz. the Act of 1952 sets up a Board of censors of high calibre and expertise, provides hearings, appeals and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional exhibitions and wealth of other policing strategies.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as the sole representative of the Government Pleader for the Patna District, authorised to represent 'Government in all civil cases. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to the Government: "I am, therefore, unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case". The chemistry of Article 226 was governed by severe rules, and the High Court declined to dispense the magic remedy. So he has sought special leave from this Court but Article 136 has its own conditions and limitations. Sans substantial question of law of public importance which deserves to be decided by the Supreme Court or at least flaw in law which is fraught with manifest injustice, there is no other open sea for this House of Justice. That password has not been uttered here despite exercise in professional martyrdom the petitioner claims to have suffered and so he has prayed special leave. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in ordering about a Government pleader is obnoxious but nothing savouring of such conduct is made out although we must enter a caveat that Governments under our Constitution shall not play with law Offices on political or other impertinent considerations as it may affect the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law itself. [766C D] 2. The Court must state that the conclusion that the office is a public office is irresistible. In this view, ordering about the Government pleader was obnoxious but something savouring by such conduct was made out though we must entering a caveat. [764D E] 3. The legal position is plain. As explained earlier, a bunch Of Government pleaders is perfectly permissible consistently with Section 2(7) and Order 27 Rule 4 Civil Procedure Code. Nor do the Bihar rules regarding government pleader help. They are purely administrative prescriptions and serve as guidelines and cannot found a legal right apart from the fact that they do not contradict Government 's power to appoint more than one Government Pleader. Allocation of work or control inter se is an internal arrangement and we see no error even in that behaviour. Not to have provided more government counsel when the volume of litigation demanded it, would have clogged the dockets in Court and helped one pleader to corner all the briefs without reference to expeditious or efficient disposals. [774E F] 4. The State is expected to fight and win its cases and sheer patronage is misuse of power. One effective method of achieving this object is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleaders. When there were several thousand cases in the Patna courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality, it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of lawyers on its behalf, for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single Government Pleader.[766E F; 763A] 5. The law of medicine, and tho industrious litigation is vital for any State if resources are to be husbanded to reduce rather than increase its involvement in court proceedings. It is lamentable that despite a national litigation policy for the States having been evolved at an all India Law Ministers ' Conference way back in 1957 and despite the recommendations of the Central Law Commission to promote settlement of disputes where Government is a party, what we find in actual practice is a proliferation of government cases in courts uninformed by any such policy.

The appellants held 570 out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 and the shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The Mills as the holder of 5,000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of that Bank at the rate of Rs 100 per share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.,000 ordinary shares in the capital of the Bank of India Ltd. having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,676662 more ordinary shares on payment of Rs 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said bank. The Managing Agents may take steps to intimate the shareholders to exercise the right if they like to do so. " Accordingly, the Mills exercised the right to take over only 66 shares out of the shares offered and resolved that the right of the remaining 1,600 shares be distributed amongst its share holders. The seven appellants as holders of 570 shares of a Mills became entitled under section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, to receive Rs.100 for each additional share. Held, that the distribution of the right in favour of the shareholders amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income tax Act and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The High Court was right in holding that the sale of the rights to apply for and obtain two shares of Bank of Indian India amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the ambit of section2(6 A).

The appellant, who was one of the candidates for election to Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency, challenged the election of the 1st respondent to Haryana legislative Assembly from the Jind Assembly Constituency. The returned candidate as well as all other candidates who lost the election were impleaded as parties. In the election petition charges of corrupt practice and irregularities in the conduct of election were made. The appellant contested the petition. After going through the pleadings of the parties, the Court ascertained the points on which parties were at variance and framed appropriate issues. The Election Petition reached the stage of recording evidence. It appears an application was filed by the appellant seeking permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the application. It was averred in the petition that the names of the witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election peti tion and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The Court after hearing the parties made an order upholding the objection raised by the returned candidate that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in his list and therefore, the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in that list of witnesses submitted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High Court. The order was challenged in this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Rule 1A of Order XVI casts an obligation on every party to a proceeding to present a list of witness whom it proposes to call either to give evidence or to produce documents and obtain summonses to such persons for their attendance in Court. Sub rule (2) requires that the parties seeking the assistance of the court for procuring the attendence of a witness must make an application stating therein the purpose of procure the attendance of any witness against whom process has not previously issued, or to producing documents and obtaining summonses. Rule 1 A of Order XVIII casts an obligatory obligation on the party to mention the name of such witness in the list. [532C D] 2.1 The provisions of Order XVII Rules 1 and 1A have been drastically amended by the Amending Act 1976 which came into force on February 1, 1977. Rule 22 of the High Courts Rules would not derogate from such scheme. The scheme is that after the Court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list Of witnesses with the gist of evidence of each witness in court within the time prescribed by sub rule (1). This advance filing of list is necessary because summoning the witnesses by the Court is a time consuming process and to avoid the avoidable delay an obligation is cast on the parties. [540E F] 2:2 The scheme of Rules 1, 1A and 22 of Order XV clearly envisaged filing of a list only in respect of witnesses whom the parties desire to examine and procure presence with the assistance by the court. When a summons is issued by the Judge for procuring presence of a person who has been summoned through the Court, it has certain consequences in law. If the summons is served and the person served fails to comply with the same, certain consequences would ensue as provided in Rule 10 of order XVI.

The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal. Pursuant to this decision of the Selection Committee, the Manager of the College issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager and take over charge within 10 days of the receipt of the order failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter, the appellant wrote to the Manager that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post Principal and he has convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers room. The Management did not pay any salary to the Appellant though he functioned as the Principal and ultimately the appellant approached the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ of mandamus directing the 5th respondent, the Committee, of Management of the college not to interfere with the work of the appellant discharging his duties as Principal of the institution and also to pay salary. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the day i.e. May 1, 1981 on which appointment of the Appellant was made as Principal had the power to make the necessary appointment and the order contained in the radiogram had no effect on the validity of appointment; that assuming such a power to issue radiograms was available to the State Government, if the appointment was made without the knowledge of the Order contained in radiog Ram, the appointment could not be invalidated, and therefore it may be declared that the appellant continues to hold the post. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated May 1. 1981 which has been extracted hereinbefore clearly shows that on April 7, 1981 the Institution had received the order that the power of appointment of Principal has been withdrawn or suspended.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric was supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and fell under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954. The petitioners state that the manufacturers of goods to whom they fabric is supplied "mpregnating the fabric" with rubber fall under Entry 18 of Schedule of that Act. The respondents contended that from year 1966 to 1969, the respondent Commercial Tax officer was not subjecting the goods of this description to sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from taxation. The High Court did not find any error "apparent upon the face of the record" and allowed the writ petitions against the assessment order dated 26th March 1971. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product" but the "tyre cord fabric" manufactured by it is woven by its purchasers "into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner; and (2) the essential question to determine is the stage at which the goods under consideration become a 'textile fabric". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "textiles" given in the Oxford Dictionary is wide enough to include "textile fabrics". [501 B] 2.1 The term "fabric" has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in Webster English Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". The first example of such a product is that "an edifice, a building." The fourth example of the first meaning is: 'a manufactured material; now only a 'Textile fabric ', a woven fabric". [500 C] 2:2.1 In the technical and commercial parlance, there is no sufficient reason for overriding and discarding the High Court 's view that on what appeared to the High court to be a question of fact, it should not decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. There was no appeal by the State of Rajasthan.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is transferred to Labour court, Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Appellate Court, Patna, which order was upheld by the High Court in appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government was misled by the representation of the workman. [295C] 1.2 In the instant case, the key question for consideration is whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workmen and transferring the case from the Labour court Dhanbad to Labour Courts, Patna should have given an opportunity to t he management? The validity of the reasons given by the Govern ment for transferring the ease is another question to be considered. [296D] 1:3 In the facts and circumstances of the instant appeal, the State has withdrawn the pending refe rence from the labour court, Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna on the representation af fic tion of workman, without getting it veri fied from the management, without having got it verified from the Management. The State in fairness ought to have got it examined by giving an opportunity t he Management? [296E F] 1 :4 In the circumstances of this case, it is not possible to appreciate how under such circum stances, the Government could be called upon to give a notice to t the parties before transferring his case from one Income Tax Officer to another without hearing the respond ent. Denial of that opportunity is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Govern ing authority.

The appellant was the manager of a hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The main contesting respondent was that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and (2) the reference in this form was incompetent. Held, that the appeal must fail. The fact that more than three years have passed since the reference is made, does not make the reference incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed. State Of Madras vs M. C.P. Sarthy, [1954] S,.C. R. 334 and State of Bombay vs C., Bombay, ; , referred to. State vs C, P.Sarathy, (1953) S. C R. 335, distinguished. State o Madras vs G. section P. Devarathnam, A.I.R., 1953 S.T.C., followed. The present reference as compared to the award in that case cannot be called vague at all. The dispute was about workmen to whom notice of dismissal had been given and in that connection the names of the workmen concerned were mentioned in the order of reference. It was not necessary for the purpose of section 10 where the dispute is of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names thereof as represented by the union that it may be desirable to mention them in the award.

According to the Appellate Tribunal, the bushments and bearions are the same and as the bearings come under Heading No. 84.06. In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect thereof of parts of the engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, it is difficult to uphold the contention that they are parts of an internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading 84.6. The Appellate Tribunal held that the busiings and the bearions fall under the Heading No 84.05. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification exempts also parts of engines mentioned in paragraph 2 of column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification, in order to avail of the benefit of the exemption granted by the Notification. It has to be proved that the parts in respect to which the exemption is claimed are parts parts of such engines. [226B] 1.2 The Notification does not only intends to grant exemption to internal combustion Piston engine but also to 'part 's thereof. The intention of the notification is clear enough to provide that the Parts of the motors mentioned under Heading Nos.

The appellants and their counsel were the contesting candidates for the post of Mujawar of the Dargah in Madras. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents on the ground that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah in the Madras for a period of 27 days in all the months of February, March, June, July, October & November each year and to restrain the defendants from interfering with the appellants ' right and management in the Dargah. The respondents pleaded that they had been paying such share to their sisterunnissa (lOth de fendant) in the Hundial collection of the Wakf and even if she had got any right, the same was lost as she did not claim any right till her death. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiffs were entitled ted to manage the Dargah for 27 days. In appeal by the respondents, the High Court allowed the second appeals and set aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below dismissing the suit filed by the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a serious error in reversing the above finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in Suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the grounds that Fathima Bee had not made a demand or asked for her share of the hundial collections at any point of time till her deceased death in 1957.

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. At that time his wages were Rs. 18 per month plus dearness allowance. With effect from the 1st November 1947, the Railway Board under the Ministry of Railways introduced a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance and house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December 1947. The scheme was modified by the Railway Boards letter No. F 47 CPC/ 14 dated 1 12 1947, by which certain railway employees stationed at specified headquarters were eligible for the allowance aforesaid at certain specified rates. The first respondent put in his claim before the Authority and by his written statement contested the claim on the ground that the house rent allowances which was the subject matter of the claim was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. Held, that the rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled. The house rent was admissible only so long as an employee is stationed at one of the notified places and has not been offered Government quarter. The rules distinctly provide that the allowance will not be ad raissible to those who occupy government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused to take advantage of the offer.

The detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435 of 1980, the detenu was alleged to have made a written request to the detaining authority on February 18, 1980 for supply of copies of the necessary documents. The detenu had also sent a petition through the Central Government complaining of the non supply of the copies of certain statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention. On March 25, 1980, an order of detention was passed by the detaining Authority purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short called COFEPOSA) by the State Government was served on the detenus alongwith the order of his detention on February 16, 1980. The grounds of Detention were also served on them along with the order dated March 25. On February 18. 1980, they were actually received by the detenus on April 3, 1980 and were produced before a Magistrate. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs Officers and cooperate in the investigation. The detention was challenged mainly on the ground that the order purported to have signed by Shri Salvi, Secretary in the Home Department to the Government of Maharashtra, is void because the concerned Minister of the State had never passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166 of the Constitution, Shri Salvvi had no authority to pass the order. The detaining authority, however, calledously and deliberately refused to supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated February 14, 1980 which was received by him on March 25; 1980. On April 3. 1980 the detenu also made a representation to the State Govt. requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the Detaining Authority in the ground of detention, but the same was rejected on April 8, 1980 on the view that the disclosure of that information was, in the opinion of the Government not in the public interest. The Central Government, however advised the State Gov ernment to supply copies of all the documents. On May 3,1980, the detenus moved this Court by petitions under Article 32 of the Consti tution for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus. On the question: whether the order was void because (1) The detaining authori ty had not applied its mind to the earlier statements of four persons from whom the detenus claimed to have acquired the gems in question, and (2) there was no evidence of smuggling in this case at all and the detaining author ity committed illegality inasmuch as it relied on presumption under section 123 of the Customs Act. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of deten tion dated March 11, 1980 passed by Shri S.S. Das, Secretary to the Govt. Home Department is void as the concerned minister had never, in fact, passed any order such as rejection of that representation. [350B] 2. The mere fact that the grounds were couched elaborate does not absolve the detaining au thority from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied upon In the grounds for detaining the aforesaid accused at this stage would not be in public interest, because, the detention order is vitiated. [351F G] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , followed.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to SS 258, 410 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Bombay High Court as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The High Court also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. The question which arose for determination was whether, several accused person jointly tried have been acquitted by the trial court, the state can prefer one appeal against the acquittal of all them. The appellant contended that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Act was inconsistent with section 419 and therefore not legally prohibited. Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding the joint appeal not to be maintainable and in summarily rejecting the same. The Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High court was correct and did not militate against the validity of a Joint appeal by a State against acquittal of several persons acquitted at a joint trial. There being no legal bar (at least) on the basis of which the judgment of the High court mainly proceeds merely, merely lays down that the Appellate Court hearing an appeal cannot admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits. The decision in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case was not inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. The view taken by the High Courts on the construction of this section is clearly unacceptable and does not militate from the maintainability or of a separate appeal by State against a common order acquitting some persons acquitted in a case. Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal, [1960]3 S.C.R. 78, referred to.

The appellant was a firm carrying on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on money lent business in the latter Federated malaya States. In the course of assessment for the year 1939 40 it was claimed by the appellant that having regard to the severance of joint family status, the income of the family from April 13, 1938 to June 2, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by virtue of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the families. but rejected the contention that the family was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) of the 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of 1922 Act and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. In reference to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that the foreign business of the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of the 1918 Act because the assessee was only taxed on remittances received from and out of the profits of the foreign income, and there was therefore no tax on the foreign trade. HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the assessee 's foreign business was not charged under section 3 of the 1920 Act. [908 F] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar & Others, ; , referred to.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department. The Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax held that the supplies of bricks were sales. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the manufacture and sale of kiln burning bricks to that department and the supply of bricks to it in terms of their running Bill No. XI dated 28th October 1967 is a sale or a works contract ? The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works Contract. In coming to this conclusion, the High court held as follows: (1) The transaction envisaged in the contract was a work contract; (2) The contract in that case though prima facie word word cd as regards the relevant clauses in similar fashion as the contract in the instant case is in fact cast in a different mould and it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contract with which we are concerned. (3) The question will depend upon the intention of the parties executing the contract. As the question was not always easy and has for all time vexed jurists all over, the Court held that as per the decision of this Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain 's case it would completely govern the facts of this case. In the present case the property in the bricks was entirely of the assesee. He had not only to manufacture that but also to stack them for facilitating delivery. The essence of the Contract was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture. (4) The High court was right in answering the question against the assessee.

The petitioner, an assessee under the Income tax Act and Wealth Tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77 was liable to pay income tax and Wealth tax in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act, 1976 which was passed by the Lok Sabha during its extended period which was extended under the provisions of the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act,1976 after the expiry of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting. The petitioner contended that the duration of the house of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House was passed, the House had no effect and consequently all Acts passed by both Houses of Parliament during the extended period including the Finance Bill, 1976 were ultra vires. The Union of India contended that (1) the two Proclamation of emergency dated 3 12 1971 and the proclamation of Emergency issued under clause (1), of Article 352 of the Constitu tion could be revoked by a subsequent Proclamation; (2)(a) the House which was also passed on February 16, 1976 had ceased not to be In operation on April 26, 1975; (b) the Houses of the Parliament approving the two resolutions had been approved by the resolutions passed by either the Houses and approved by resolutions of both the Houses; (c) the proclamation dated March 3rd Decem ber 1971 had ceased in operation on March 3, 1972; and (d) the Proclamation of the Emergency dated March 25, 1976 having ceased to operate on March 31, 1972. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Pro Clamations dated March 23, 1977 and March 25 of 1978 were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions of the Houses passed by Parliament until they were duly revoked by the two Houses of parliament. [439C D] 2.1 The production of the Lok Assembly Debates and of the Rajya Sabha containing the proceedings of the two House of Parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the three Houses of India and the time before when the resolution was duly adopted amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [441D] 2:2 The production and production of copies of the journals or the reports containing proceedings of two Houses Parliament relating thereto relating to period between April 26 and March 31st, 1972 are not in dispute by the petitioner. The fact that the two proclamation had been approval by the resolution passed by Houses of both Parliament as set out earlier in the course of this judgment is not disputed by the respondent. [442E] 2 :3 The two Proclamation dated March 27, 1977 were kept In force by the President 's Government on April 1, 1974 and they were published in the official reports of the respective Houses of States which are printed and published by them. The Court has to take judicial notice of the proceedings under section 57 of the . [442G H] 2(a) The two pro Clamions of Emergency were kept at force by reason of the resolution dated March 31.7.1975 passed by two Houses, Parliament approving each of them had not been published in their official reports. The reports of proceedings of Parliament and the State Legislatures are widely circulated. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament or the Legislatures of States.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High Court. He was therefore entitled to contend at the time of the leave application that the property in dispute was of the value of not less than Rs. 20,000/ . Held, that the appellant 's case was accepted by the Trial Court but was rejected by the High court and the High Courts were right in holding that the properties in question constituted a temple. The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the aforesaid assumption. [157 A] In the instant case the property was the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the High 'Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property belonged to and was an alienable private property. [158 B C] The appellant ' claim that the premises belonged to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the family was accepted. The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 37 of 1950 under section 84(2) of Madras Act 11 of 1927. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on valuation made by him therefor. The refusal of the appellant to grant leave by the Court under either of the clauses (a) and (b) of article 133(1) was based on the observation that whether the property is a private or a public temple, it was incapable of valuation.

The appellant company, which had given rise to the present appeal centered round two items of claim made by the respondents. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day on all working days in lieu of tiffin arrangements which were at present made by it. In regard to the second claim, the Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiff in lieu thereof. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant. The result is that the question posed by the respondent 's demand must be considered. The fact that a retired person has made an application for employment under the Factories Act cannot be ignored. [574 F] Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Union of India, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the appellant had throughout been making provision for t heiffin of its employees and, in fact, when after the award was pronounced in 1956 and this question was taken up for further negotiations between the parties, the appel lant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make a suitable provision in that behalf. [575 F] The history of the relations between the appellant coupled with the prevailing practice in comparable concerns in the region strongly supports the view taken by the Tribunal that in the appellant 's concern it was an implied condition of service that in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for payment for tafiffin was an amenity to which the employees were entitled.

The respondent, an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He applied for and obtained an order for attachment of the money lying in the executing court. The Union of India then applied to the High Court of Calcutta in revision. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The money in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India had ceased to be provident fund money and was liable to be attached. [32 F] (ii) Section 50 of the Indian Contract Act provides that a compulsory deposit in any Government or Railway Provident Funds shall not in any way be capable of being assigned or charged and shall not be liable to attachment under any decree or order of any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court in respect of any debt or liability incurred by the subscriber or depositor. [33 F] In the instant case, the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal of attachment. The order of attachment of amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway Administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . [34 C D] (iii) Section 5 of the , provides that "The performance of any promise may be made in any manner, or at any time which the promise prescribes or sanction sanctions. Browne had not authorised the Reserve bank to receive payment of the amount on his behalf nor had he sanctioned payment to the ReserveBank in discharge of the liability of the Railway Administra tration. The Bank was therefore in respect for the provident fund moneys in the position of a trustee for Browne and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and to remit it to Browne.

The appellant, a permanent employee of the respondent company, was terminated by the management on the ground that he had lost confidence in the employee. The employer challenged the termination as 'wrongful ' and mala fide. The Labour Court held that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that even where a management had the power to terminate the services of its employee without reasons but with notice pay only, the colourable exercise of that power invalidated it, and that the order did not amount to one of dismissal as and by way of punishment. HELD : (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Labour Court on this point is not conclusive and the Tribunal can go behind the form of the order, look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter, if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct 'as a colourable exercise Of power by the Management. [490 E F] (ii) The management had not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968. Further after 1968, the appellant was given two extra increments in addition to his normal increments as stated earlier, in appreciation of his hard work. It was manifest therefore that the impugned action was not bona fide. [448 F] Murugan Mills Case (supra) approved. (iii) The Management had not discharged the grounds on which this inference could be drawn. There is only the ipse dixit of the employer that he was suspecting since 1968 that the appellant, was divulging secrets relating to his business. The management could well have disclosed their suspicion in reply and told the Union and the workman that they resorted to an innocuous discharge to avoid punitive trauma. [49 E F; G] (iv) The loss of confidence is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. In the light of what we have indicated, it is clear that loss of faith is often one subjective feeling and individual reaction or to an object set facts & motivations.[49 E] (v) The Court has the power land, indeed, the duty to X ray the order and discover its true nature if,he object and effect, if the attendant circumstances and the ulterior purpose be to dismiss the employee because he is an evil to be eliminated. But if the management, to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of termination simpliciter such action is bad and is liable to be set aside. Loss of confidence may be evidentiary of good faith of the employers.

The petitioners, who were the State of U.P., and the Lions Club of Pottery Town at Khurja in Uttar Pradesh arranged for the promotion of eye care through 'eye camps ' organised by social and voluntary organ was con tended to extend facilities of expert Ophthal mic surgical services to the residents of the town. The club invited Dr. R.M. Sahay, a team of doctors to offer the surgical services. The Camp was arranged in 'Aggarwal Dharamshala ' at Novelty Road, Khurja. Dr. Sahay returned on the 24th April and undertook himself some ameliorative treatment. But the operated eyes had been damaged completely. Similar mishap, but on lesser scale affecting some patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. Some of the victims were later sent to and treated at Dr. P. Sahay 's Hospital at Jaipur. But their condition did not improve. It is now undisputed that this terrible medical misha p was due to common contaminating source. The suggestion in the Report of the 245 enquiries that ensued is that, in all probability, the source of the infection, referred to as E coli cation of the intra ocular cavity, was the "normal saline" used on the eyes at the time of surgery. Dr R. M. Sahay and his team of doctor and para medical staff, who arrived in Khurja on 21st April, 1986 under Invoice No. 1533. Originally, the four respondents were the state of U .P., Dr.R.M., Sahay, the Chief Medical Officer, Buland Sahar District (U.P.) and the 'Lions Club, of Potteries Town, Bulandshahar. However this Court by its order dated 26th September, 1986 directed the Indian Medical Council and the Union of India to be impleaded as parties to the proceedings. In the Writ Petition, the petitioners have made serious allegations about the very bona fides of, and the intention behind, the sponsoring of the iII fated 'eya camp ' and have alleged that motives of monetary gains by way of State and International subsidies were causing serious mishappery for the patients. The prayers in the writ petition are that the victims of this medical mishp be given expert rehabilitatory treatment and appro priate compensation; that Government do conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and that appropriate legal action be instituted against Dr. M/s Mehtaad Company, Jaipur on 22nd April,1986 under Invoices No.1533. The prayer in the Writ petition is that the respondents victims of the medical misho cation be given specialist rehabilit ary treatment and re instate compensation and appropotism; that the Government do conducting a thorough inquiry as to whether to undertake the case, a duty of care in deciding what treatment to give or a dutyof care in the administration of that treatment. The petitioners have also made serious allegation about the alleged mala fides of the sponsoring authority, and have con tained alleged that motive of monetary gain by way o State and international subsidy. Allowing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The findings on the conduct of Dr. S.M./S. Mehta are not mere cases of eye sight of the patients not having been restored in the sense that the surgical operations conducted on them did not yield the desired result; or that no positive bene fit was derived by them from the surgery. [249B] 1.2 The findings of the Court on the basis of the report and recommendations of the expert sub committee of the Indian medical Council may be consid ered by the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9th February, 1988.

The petitioner, a registered society under the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984, was constituted by the State Government in 1948. The Society had its registered office at Gauhati. It was established in Madras City in the name of Dakshin Bharat Hindi Prachar Samchar Samiti with its head Office at Gauhati, which it is a literary body and under Section 4 of the Bidban the objects of the Samiti have been stated thus: (a) To propogate and promote Hindi as a na tional language in Assam Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Manipur Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh as provided in Article 351 of the Constitution of India; (b) To expel Hindi as na tural language in India Meghalaya, Meghalaya, Nagaland; Manipur, Tripura and 10 other holders of office of the Assam Rashtraba Prachar Board at Gauhati; (c) To impris on the religious faith of the people of Assam and to promote Hindias a na Tional language; (d) To confer upon the members of the Society their rights under Article 19(1)(c) for all times to come. It is also alleged that after the passing of this Act, the notification under Section 3 was issued which was EPG 57/34/75 dated 1.10.84 by which the Rashtra bhasha Samchar Board was constituted with effect from 12.8.1984 and Section 1 sub clause (ii) of this Ordinance provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asam Rashtradhasha Parcha Sewak Sangh had its jurisdiction immediately before the commence ment of the Ordinance by a Notification No. 3 the Governor of Assam fixed Ist of October, 1984 as the appointed day on which the aforesaid Ordinance came into force and Section 3 of the said Ordinance provided for temporary transfer of the management and control of the affairs of the A.R.B.P.S. from the Board constituted under Section 5 of the Act. The petitioner challenged the action taken by the respondent State Government under the asom Raka bhaskha Prachar Sangha Pra char Samiti (taking over of management and Control), Act,1984 on the ground that it was mala fide action motivated with selfish political motivation; that the provisions of Section 3 were not applicable to the case. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioner had failed to establish that the institution was a public body constituted by its members having elected Byabasthapika Sabha and the Karyapalika of the Board with immediate effect and also constituted an ad hoc body with himself as Chairman and five others as members to manage the affairs. The Court, however, held that the Act itself was ultra vires of the Constitu tion inasmuch as it infringed the fundamental rights of the members who consti tute the Samiti their rights thereunder under Article 14(1) (c). In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the procedure stated in this Section of the constitution was followed and as only one person opposed the Constitution amendment was passed, the Chief Minister ceased to be the Ex officio President; and since then according to the petitioner he had nothing to do with the Samiti or its ideals and who were not even the members o f the Samiti had been nominated as the members. Allowing the Writ Petitions, HELD: 1. The Act of 1984 and a notification appointing a Board was issued by the Government under Section 2(2) of the Raka Samity (Taking Over of Management & Control) Ordinance, 1984.

The appellants were the reversioners of a Hindu widow. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940, executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proper finding should have been that Sumitra Devi made a "sankalpa" of the gift of four houses at Asansol in pursuance and fulfilment of an ante nuptial agreement, even though the gift was made some two years after the marriage; furthermore, a reference was made to section 14 of the , which lays down that for the purpose of making a gift of immoveable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses.
