Held: (i) The finding of the courts below that there was an "samotably" made a 'sankadhi ' of the four houses in question after the Sampradan ceremony on the occasion of the marriage of Kamala Devi and that such a gift was again confirmed at the Gowna ceremony. (ii) The evidence of Sumitra ' with regard to the promise made regarding the gift by her and that the acceptance of such a gifts by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala 's wife did not make it absolutely clear or specific that the promise related to the four particular houses which were the subject matter of the subsequent gift. (iii) The findings of the final court of fact as correct, the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram Kishori Lal Sao and in pursuance fulfilment of the solemn agreement made by her, was for spiritual benefit of the appellants and valid in Hindu law.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) filed an election petition in the Punjab and Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices detailed in the petition. The respondent denied having indulged in any corrupt practice as alleged by Avtar Singh. It was not necessary for the appellant to go into further details because, in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh would have gone to the appellant (Azad Singh). The High Court held that the allegations of corrupt practices were proved. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent (Tej. Singh), which has been fully proved, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. [419D E] 2.1 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing by Tej Singh has been clearly admitted by him as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view Of the very wide margin of vote (123), between Tejinder Singh and the returned candidates, a firm presumption and possibilities that the voters polled in his favour would have went to the appel lant (Activity Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, he got an Ordinance promulgated by the Governor. The Ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board shall be with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. It was alleged by the appellant that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent, Bhajan Lal called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant thereto eleven officers withdrew from the petition. It is alleged by him that after being unsuccessful to threaten the writ petitioners he called him again to his office on July 27, 1983 by the Acting chief Conservator of Forest and criminalally intimidating him to withdrawing the writ Petition. Thereafter, the appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the petitioner. The Single Judge of the High court after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule niisi. It also held that there was no need for interference by this Court. The appellant filed a writ petition in the Punjab High Court challenging the order of assessment on the ground that the authority concerned had erroneously exercised its jurisdiction by not granting exemption to the petitioner and that the appeal is incompetent.

The respondent, who was the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff, had two inam lands at Mundhava which were then numbered Pratibhandi Nos. 71 and 72. On 1st July 1863, taluqdar sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7,999. The sale deed provided that in default of payment of rent the tenant 's rights would come to an end. On 18th August, 1870, Ladha Ibrahim sold his lease hold lands to one Ladharaj Sheth for Rs,7999. On the same day the purchaser passed a rent note in favour of Bhonriram. The rent note provided for the payment of the agreed rent in the month of Pousb every year and stated that in case of default the tenant or his heirs would have no right over the land. On this date Ladha, Ibrahim sold the tenancy rights of one Girdharilal for Rs 7,000 to one M. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenants rights had ceased by forfeiture for non payment of rents. The trial court rejected the claim but the High Court in second appeal confirmed the decree of the trial court granting possession against forfeiture but observed that the defendants having obtained relief against forfeiture thrice before should not expect to get it for a fourth time if they again make default in the payment. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The rule laid down in section 111(g) of the , is that a tenant cannot by his unilateral act and by his own wrong determine the lease unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach. In the present case the tenant was a recalcitrant tenant and was a habitual defaulter. Rent has been in arrears at times for six years, at other times for three years and at other occasions for four years and so on, and every time the landlord had to file a suit in ejectment which was always resisted on false defences. No rule of equity is a tenant entitled to a notice in writing telling him that the lease has been determined. The right and obligations under those leases have to be determined according to the rules of law prevailing at the time and the only rule applicable seems to be that a person cannot by unilateral act or by his wrong determine a lease unless he gives an express indication by any unequivocal expression on his behalf that the lessee has been deter mined. The rule is that if at the date relief is asked for the position has been altered so that relief cannot be given without causing injury to third parties relief will be refused, but if that position is not altered so it can no injustice be done there is no real discretion and the court should make the order and give the relief. The Court is to consider all the circumstances and the conduct of the parties. If the purpose of the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the leased lease and to avail himself of the tenant, ' breach of covenant it could as effectively be achieved by an oral intimation as by a written one without in any way disturbing the mind of a chancery judge. That it is not so apparent from the circumstance that the requirement of a notice is merely statutory and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based on any well established principles of equity. The English law on the subject is not the same and it cannot be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of equity, equity and good conscience. (ii)The High Court was right in holding that the provision in section III(g), as amended in 1929 embodied a principle of justice, equity, and good justice and fair conscience and according to it the institution of a suit for ejectment would be sufficient indication on the part of the landlord for determination of the lease and a notice under writing as required by the amended section would not be a prerequisite for institution of such a suit.

The Associated Cement Companies Limited (the Appellant) has quarries worked by its department called Kymore & Bamangaon Lime stone Mines at Ky More, District Jabalpur M.P. Workers employed in the said quarries have a union called Koymore Quarry Karamchari Sangh and the four concerned workmen Rama Shankar Barmapradhan, Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf (fourth charge) were at the material time the office bearers in the union. In connection with implementation of the Recommendations of Second Central Wage Board for cement industry, after serving a strike notice on the management of the Appellant on 13th September 1968, the Karamchari Sangh served Charge sheets dated 3rd October 1968 on the Respondents in which four common charges were levelled against all of them; in addition a fifth charge was levelled against two of them Emmanianual and Md. Rahaf (second charge) being held not to have been proved. The Enquiry Report was forwarded to the General Manager who after considering the same and after taking into account the previous service record of the Respondents by his order dated 31st December, 1968 dismissed the Respondents from service. That order was served on the respondents 30th January 1969. 365 A dispute having been raised with regard to their dismissal, by common consent, the same was referred to the arbitration of Shri T.C. 10 A of the on 14th April 1969. The Arbitrator gave his Award on 9th February 1970 whereby he came to the conclusion that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the Respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17; he further held that though before him the Management had by leading evidence proved their mis conduct by establishing the first three charges against all, the fifth charge against Emman oral and Mohd., Rauff (fourth Charge being held to have not been proved) the punishment of dismissal in respect of Emmanulual and M.C., could be confirmed but set aside the dismissal order in respect thereof. The Appellant challenged the Award in the High Court by means of a Writ Petition (Misc. Petition No. 129 of 1970) contending that the Arbitrator had misconstrued Standing Order 17 and that no second notice was required to be given to them; that in the alternative the interference with the punishment was erroneous while another writ petition ( Misc. Petition (C.) No. 365/1970) was filed by the Respondents against the punishments that were awarded to each one of them the High court by its judgment dated 27th July, 1972 confirmed the Award of the Arbitrator by dismissing both the Writ Petitions. The appellant contended that the learned Arbitrator as well as the High Courts have erroneously construed the certified Standing Order no. 17 and therefore the finding that the inquiry was vitiated deserved to be set aside and according to him if the enquiry was valid and not vitiated the punishment imposed on Rama Shankar and Barma Pradhan could not be interfered with. On behalf of the Management it was urged that since the Arbitrator has power to interfere with the dismissal in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the order of dismissal of Rama Shanker and Barmaspradan and that the concept of second opportunity being given to a delinquent which obtained under section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 or article 311 of the Constitution prior to the insertion of the proviso to Article 311 (2) could not he invoked or applied to the instant ease nor was such second opportunity any requirement of the ordinary law of the land or of Industrial Law and in this behalf reliance was placed on two decisions of this Court in Hamdard Dawakhana case and in Saharanpur Light Rly, case.

The appellant was the owner of certain lands under leases granted by incompetent persons to be deemed tenants. The appellant claimed that he was himself the owner and that he had come into possession of the lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he being himself the owners of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969 provides for a conjoint study of the provisions con tained in section 7A to 7C and sections 8 and 9 of the Act which immediately precede and succeed section 7D. Those sections are in the following terms: "7A. Certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to bedeemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law, or in any contract, custom or usage, or In any judgment, decree or order of court, any person who is in occupation of the land of another at the commencement of the Karnataka Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation thereof for not more than two years within a period of twelve years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1957. Explanation I In computing the period of occupation of a person for the purpose of clause (c), the period during which the predecessor ininterest or predecessors in interest of such person was or were in occupation shall also be taken into account. Explanation II For the purpose Of this section, a person shall be con deemed to have been in continuous occupation notwithstanding any order of Court for delivery of possession to another person or any court record of dispos session. [113F H] 1.2 The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to persons whose posses sion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come to possess with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the Legisla tion to confer the benefit of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 2D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". [113A B] 1:3 In computing, the period for which a person is deemed to he in continuous possession of any land at the commence ment of the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1970, the periods during which predecessor in interests or predecessorsin interest of the person was/were in occupation would also be take into account; and Explanation II to section 7C must be interpreted as meaning 'in lawful posi ture. [114B] 2:1 The intention is to grant relief only to those persons whose occupa tion had a subsisting origin in that sense that he has either bona fides believed the land to be Govern ment 's Lands of which he could later obtain assignment or have taken the land on lease by persons who were not competent to lease the land.

The appellant was convicted under section 135(b)(ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant contended that he had been in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967, and that the goods were also as a necessary consequence, that the appellant had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellant under section135(1)(ii). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. Section 123 of the Act only lay down a procedural rule, they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 30 10 1968. It is immaterial that the appel lant was found in possession on 21 5 1967. There is also another objection to the applicability of section 123(1) of Act. [541 F] 2. Section 106 read with section 114 of the Evidence Act, was sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the Court to presume that the person knew that the he must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. The admissibility and sufficiency of (1) [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 364, referred to. 3. Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act only lays down a substantive rule, that they could apply when the ease came up on trial before Magistrate who ultimately decided it. Indeed the complaint was filed in December 1968. The complaint itself is filed on June 30, 1968. [542 A] 4. Section 108 read with Section 114 of Evidence Act provides that the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession the goods are seized. It would also follow that the customs authorities could have applied to the appellant 's case rested on his bare assertions in a written statement. Of course, no one had come forward to state or allege that the appellants were illegally imported or smuggled into the country without payment of duty. [543 B] 5. The onus of proving the innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant was on the prosecution. [544 D E] 6. Section 112 read with s 114 of Indian Evidence is not sufficient to entitle the prosecution for proving that the accused knew that he knew that they must have had been smuggled and imported in violation of the laws. The burden of proof of innocent possession is on the accused. [545 F G] 7. Section 118 of the Customs Act, provides that it would apply only to goods seized under the Act. It was not necessary for the prosecution in proving that he was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods.

The appellants, who were members of an unlawful association formed themselves into an Association to collect the quota of cloth to be allotted to them and sell it on profit wholesale and retail. The Association at Budhar, consisted of 25 members who made contributions to the initial capital of the association which was one lac of rupees. No formal Articles of Association were written; nor Seled. The appellants filed a suit for accounts of the Cloth Association. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and came to the conclusion that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of the Gwalior cloth and inasmuch as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for account must fail. Held, that the preliminary objection must succeed. The provisions of a public statute which no court can exclude from its consideration are those referred to in the following passage at p. 145 of Lindley on Partnership (11th edition): " The most important consequence, however, of illegality in a contract of partnership is that the members of a partnership have no remedy against each other for contribution or apportionment in respect of the partnership dealings and transactions. However ungracious and morally reprehensible it may be for a person who has been engaged with another in various dealings and dealings to set up their illegality as a defence to a claim by that other for an account and payment of his share of profits made thereby, such a defence must be allowed to prevail in a court of justice. The analogy does not really apply. For the reasons given above, it is clear that the suit before the High Courts was not one for accounts or for accounts lay at the instance of the plaintiffs appellants who were also members of unlawful Association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked.

The respondents, who were accused in a complaint filed under section 51 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972 against two other accused, namely, (1) the appellant and two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 13 of Kundurugutu Range Forest and removed the ivory tusks of the elephant; (2) the third accused was convicted under section 9(1) read with section 51 and 379 IPC read with Section 54 and 39 of the wild Life Protection act, 1972 and (3) the Magistrate took cognisance of this offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. or quashing of the order of the Magistrate taking cognizance against them. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the respondents. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the learned Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of Section 210(1), Cr.P.C., 1973 and that as an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence the learned Magis trate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of summons against the accused, and that since the investigation by Police was not in progress, it could not be said that he acted contrary thereto. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy and object of the Bird Life Protection (Amendment) Act, 1986 has a long history and are the result of an increasing awareness of the compelling need to restore the serious ecological imbalances introduced by the depradations inflicted on nature by man. The preservation of the fauna and flora, some species of which are getting extinct at an alarming rate has been a great and urgent necessity for the survival of humanity and these laws reflect a last ditch battle for the restoration, in part at least, a grave situation emerging from a long period of callous insensitiveness to the enormity of the risks m mankind that go with the deterioration of environment. In his foreward to 'International Wild Life Law ', H.R. Prince Philip, The Duke of Edinburghgh said: "Many people seem to think that the conservation of nature is simply a matter of being kind to animals and enjoying walks in the countryside. " Environmentalists ' conception of the ecological balance in nature is based on the fundamental concept that nature is "a series of complex biotic communities of which a man is an inter dependant part" and that it should not be given to a part to tresspass and diminish the whole. [467C D] 1.2 The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act ' in section 56 of the Act, merely imports the idea tat the same act or omissions might constitute an offence under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. [468E F] 1:3 In the context of what is meant by "same offence" in section 856 of the , merely imports that the idea that the same acts or omission may constitute an offences under two or more enactments, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable for punishment twice for the same offences. [470G H] 1 :4 The expression 'any act ' or omission constitutes an offence u/s 9(i) readwith section 50(1 ) of the .

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 3(1) of the . The Magistrate ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs. 10,000 be produced which in actual impact was a double denial of bail benefit. The direction of this Court did not spell out the details of the bail and so the magistrate ordered that the surety h ll a certain sum of money be produced. The petitioner moved this Court again to modify the original order "to the extent that he be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs 2,000/ or on executing a personal bond or pass any other order or direction as this Hon 'ble Court may deem fit and proper". From this factual matrix three legal issues arise (1) Can the court, under the Code of Criminal Procedure enlarge, on his own bond without sureties, a person undergoing incarceration for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict who has appealed or sought special leave ? (2) If the Court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and (3) Is it within the power of the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? This formulation turns the focus on an aspect of liberty bearing on bail jurisprudence. The victims when suretyship is insisted on on or heavy sums are demanded by way of bail or local bailors alone are presona grata, may well be the weaker segments of society like the proletariat, the linguistic and other minorities and distant denizens from the far corners or our country with its vast diversity. In fact the grant of bail can be stultified or made unreasonally inconvenient and expensive if the court is powerless to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district borders as good or the sum is so excessive that to procure a wealthy surety may be both exasperating and expensive. The problem is plainly one of the human rights, especially freedom vis a vis the lowly. This poignant import of the problem persuaded the Chamber Judge to invite the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Citizens for Democracy to assist the court in decoding the Code and its provisions regarding bail. There is already a direction for grant of the pre trial release which has now been developed in socially advanced countries and particularly the United States, since then, the bondsman emerged as a commercial adjunct to the processes of criminal justice, which, in turn, bred abuses and led to reform movements like the Manhattan Bail Project. This research project spurred the National Bail Conference held in 1964 which in its crucial chain reaction provided the major impetus to a reform of bail law across the United State. Indeed, this legislative scenario has a lesson for India where a much later Criminal Procedure Code 1973 has largely left untouched ancient provisions on this subject, incongruous with the Preamble to the Constitution. The American Act of 1966 has stipulated, inter alia, that release should be granted in non capital cases where there is reasonable assurance that the individual will reappear when required; that the Courts should make use of a variety of release options depending on the circumstances; that information should be developed about the individual on which intelligent selection, of alternatives should be based. The Manhathan Bail Project conducted by the Vera Foundation and the Institute of Judicial Administration at New York University School of Law found that about sixty five percent of all felony defendants interviewed could be recommended for release without bail. In short, risk of financial loss is all insubstantial deterrent to flight for a large number of defendants whose ties with the community are sufficient to bring them to court. The jailed defendant loses his job is he has one and is prevented from contributing to the preparation of his defence.

The assessee, a newly established undertaking, had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills, Amritsar, and sought to include in the computation of capital so employed Rs. 2,21.460 advanced to 'Castle ' as a newlyestablished undertaking and sought exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as an industrial undertaking. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Under section 66(2) invests the High Court with jurisdiction to require the Appellate tribunal to state a case and refer it if the Appellate Tribu nal has refused to state the case on the ground that no question of law arises. The refusal of the Tribunal to state 'the case for the opinion of the High court on the view that a question of fact does not arise out of the order is not conclusive. [431 D] (ii) Non inclusion of the income of 'Cartle ' in the assessment of the assessee may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assistant Commissioner relied. [ 430 E F] (iii) The conclusion of the Income tax Tribunal that the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate 'Tribunal in coming to the conclusion, it did 'not ' consider the other questions whether the constitution and ownership of the two businesses 'were the same.

The Minister concerned, in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party. The Minister was also directed to file his personal affidavit. In the writ petition filed by him, Duggal respondent challenged the validity of the later order dated February 18, 1975. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and directed that the Minister be impleaded as party. Allowing the appeal partly, HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a Party was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not inclined to interfere with the order of the High court adding the Minister to the writ petitioner. [972B] The direction of the high Court for impleading the Minister was given with a direction that the Secretary should file his affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. [983C D] In the instant case, the High Courts were in error in directing that the Chief Minister be impleading as a respondent. The other part of the order whereby the Minister con cerned was directed to be filed his personal affidavits is set aside. [992E F] The High Courts are, however, in error, in direct ing that the Ministers concerned should file their affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge, Ambala contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rents due under a lease 343 under section259 of the Cantonment Act and in any case that could not be done without taking into account the objections of the respondents. The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Magistrate and held that the rent under a leases could not, therefore, be recovered under section 260 of the . On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) Section 259 of ' the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937, which expressly authorised the Board to recover all arrears of land revenue and "other payments" under the Rules by resorting to section 259 was not intended to be included in that expression in section. [344 D] (ii) The words "rent on land and buildings" used in section 259 must be claimable by the Board under the Act or the rules framed thereunder. Therefore, the action for recovery can be taken under section 258 with respect to rent on land & buildings only if such rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Cantonment Property Rules or the Land Administration Rule. [345 E] (iii) The section does not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and building to take action for recover rent thereof by suit under the general law of the land. Further, by providing for recovery of rent of the kind mentioned in section 258 no other provision has come to the notice which can support the view that the section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilt not be possible for the Board either to recover rent from a tenant who was liable under an express provision of the Rent Acts or the Rules.

The appellant was employed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. Section salesmen and local salesmen are appointed for certain number of districts and in the area of each section salesmen, a number of local salesman, local sales men and local travelling salesmen were appointed. The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman and he was paid Rs.4,000 per month as salesmen. The respondent company controls this through the territory office at Delhi. Neither the section sales man nor the local sales ary or local sales officers are employed in the shop of wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the products of the company and to collect the amount of sale. The section sales men & local salescers and local trav elling salesmen appointed in the areas of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promotion in the Area of his opera tion. The Labour Court held that the appellant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In appeal by the appellant, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. It is seen from the facts found that the appel lant was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study in the market condition. He was also required to suggest about the publicity in markets and melas, advertise ments including the need for posters, holders and cinema slides. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. The supervising work of the other local sales man was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental tO to his primary work of canvassing, and promotion In the light of the finding of Tribu al on the question whether the appellant is a workman, it is not applicable to him and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [418C D] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmah Colliery Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J.M. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others; , referred to. 1.2 The appellant is required to send reports about the publication and advertisement of placing posters, holder cinema slide and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the document relate to matters of publicity in melas and some relate to the existing position of the stock of the goods of the Company in the locality and action taken to ameliorate stocks. It was not the duty of the appellant to procure orders for the Company. None of the salesmen who were employed to sell them would come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Section salesman & local Salesmen and the local Sales men and Local Trav elinglling salesman were employed by the company in order to canvass and promote the sales of the companies. From 475 perusal of the records produced before it, the Tribunal further observed that the termination of the appe lant from service was illegal but dismissed the application only on the ground that the was not applica ble. [474B C] Burmahs Shell Oil storage & Distribution Co. vs Burmath Shell Management and staff; , , ; Burmah Mahan Storage and Distribution Company V.

The respondent Nos. 1,2 and 4 are shareholders of the third respondent. The High Court by its order dated 30.6.1964 held that the land in question was not a `pakka ' tenant ' and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The Company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court confirmed the order of the trial court and dismissing the company 's appeal, holding that the Company was not an `pukka ' tenants ' under section 185 of the Code as it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act No. 66 of 1950. The State appealed to this Court by special leave against the High Courts ' order. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 182 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code is attracted. That section reads: "182. Government Lessees (1) Every person who holds land from the State Government or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by the State Govern ment or the Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as a Bhumiswami shall be called a Government lessee in respect of such land". The term `Pukka tenant ' included Istmurardar tenants, Malikana Haq holder tenants Hakkiyat Mutrikat Sharahyana Muayana and Sakitul Mikiyat tenants. An "ordinary tenant" is defined by Act No 66 of 1951 as a person holding land from State Government under section 181, Section 181 of the code reads: "(1) A Government lessee may be ejected from his land by order of a Revenue Officer on one or more of the following grounds, namely: (i) that he has failed to pay the rent for a period of three months from the date on which it became due; or (ii) that the term of his lease has expired or (iv) thathe has contravened any of the terms and conditions of the grant: Provided that no order for ejectment of a Government lessees under this sub section shall be passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence". [179E F] 2. The finding of the Additional Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for a long period far in excess of three month from the dates on which they became due. In the circumstances, the Additional collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of Act.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of which were brought into force were brought in the principal Acts : "ceiling area" and "privileged raiyat" were defined by clauses (5) & 24 of section 24 and the expression "classes of land" was defined in section 2(5a). The original Chs. III and IV of the Orissa Land Reform Act 16 Of 1960 and the amending Act 13 of 1965 were both Acts enacted for ensuring agrarian reform, and the lands held by the petitioners were "estates" within the meaning of article 31 A of the Constitution. By virtue of section 1 (3) the rights of the land holders were sought to be extinguished or modified. But to the operative part of article 32A by section 2 of the Constitu tion (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, the second proviso was added. The State Legislature amended the principal act by Act 13 Of 1965 and by Act 15 of 1965 amendments were made in the Principal Acts : Held, that the law relating to the ceiling limit viz. IV of tho principal Act was never made operative by a notification and was repealed by Act 16of 1965. The decision of this Court A. Thangal Kunju Mudaliar vs M. Venkatachalam Potti and Anr. ; , followed.

The widow, who had acquired title by adverse possession, applied for a decree of the suit in the Civil Court. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that there was a severance of joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the Suit on the view that a suit of this character was not maintainable in law. On appeal to the High Court, Held, that the widow 's self may be incapable of invoking the provisions of section 32(1) of the Indian , for the proposition that in case of alienation by a Hindu widow of her husband 's property without any justifying necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by an adverse possession against her the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. Sulaiman J. in the Allahabad High Court had clearly held that the decision of the High court was right and this appeal must fail. The law of limitation has no application where there is no necessity for alienation, the interest which she herself holds and which she can convey to others, is not an indefeasible life estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu law cause extinction of the widows estate. In deciding this case the learned judges agreed with Boys J., in the conclusion arrived at by the latter principally on the grounds that it would not work any hardship if the reversioner, in whose favour the surrender is making, were to take the property subject to the transfers made by the widows so as to allow the transfers to remain valid for her life time or at any rate during the period of her widowhood.

The respondent company was the adopted son of Mangturam Jaipuria. After his adoption Mangtram Jaiprauria got a natural son, Rajaram Jaippore, a natural person, Rajaram, Jaipuri and R.D. Jaiplauria became the Chairman and Managing Director of the newly established Polytex Company in which the Cotton Mills Company had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each. From about 1975 76 on account of a very serious set back in its financial position the Cotton Mill Company could not meet the wage bill, the dues of the U.P. Electricity Board and several other monetary claims against it. There were serious labour troubles in its factory and its work virtually became paralysed. The total liability of the Cotton mills Company was in the order of Rs 2 34 crores in the year 1977. Land Revenue Act, 1901 (Act No. 1 of 1901) appointing a Receiver in respect of the shares in question attached to them and ordering that 3,50,000 shares be pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh against a loan for the purpose of meeting the dues payable to the employees of the cotton Mills Company and he made a further order under section 149 of the Land Revenue (Amendment) Act, 1984 appointing Sitaram Jaipura as a Director of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. The requisitionists of the meeting also asked the Polytex company to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 284(2) and (5) read with section 190 of the Act for appointment of Sitaram Jaimuria as a Special Notice under section 169 of the . The appellants, however, requested the Court to decide the question relating to the right of the respondent company to join as a requisitionist of a meeting under section 170 of the , or to vote at a meeting of the company since it was likely that one or the other member might raise it as an issue at the next meeting. The principal ground urged on behalf of the appellants is that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Textile Mills Company has ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polyester by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur in respect thereof, the attachment of the 9 lakhs shares out of the said 10 lakhs share with the Government was illegal and that the attachment could not be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under Section 169 of Act requisitioning the extraordinary General meeting and without the support of the shareholders of the Company. The appellants contended that since a Receiver had been appointed by the collector in respect Of the shares held by the Cotton Spinning Mills Company, they had also been attached, the shares which belonged to the respondent could not have any effect on them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 137 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 provides that if any person obtains an order for the appointment or of a person to manage, the property of a company, or if any persons appoints such Receiver under any powers contained in any instrument he shall, within thirty days from the date of the passing of the order or of the making of the appoint ment under the said powers give notice of the fact to the Registrar and the Registrar shall, on payment of the prescribed fee, enter the fact in the register of charges maintained under section 130 of the that Act.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the Suit was simply one of title to the suit property, it was not necessary to decide whether the suit Land was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat malli deh, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved by the said finding recorded by the trial court, the Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986. The learned Judge who heard the Revision petition came to the conclusion that the issues involved in this case were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Act and accordingly he held that the Suit filed was not barred by the provisions of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The High Court also found that the plaintiff in that case had only stated in the plaint that the land in question was 'Gali Sheh re aam ' or a throughfare belonging to the Gram Panchayats which was being used by the plaintiff as an approach to his house for about 30 years and had prayed for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with his right. The plaintiffs have preferred this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India praying for grant leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The above decision is clearly distinguishable from the present case since in this Case the Panchayat which had been impleaded as a defendant had raised the plea that the said land was a part of shamlat and that it had been vested in it. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question is shamlat ab initio or not. [835E F] Bhagu & Ors., vs Ram Sarup & Ors, [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366; Bhagu and Ors., v Ram Sarup and Ors. , ; referred to. 1.2 The above decisions are clearly distinguishable on the facts of this case since the Panchayat in which the suit had been impleading as a party had raised an plea that it was a shamlatted deh confer jurisdiction on the civil courts when by virtue Of section 13, the jurisdiction of civil Courts to try such suits had been taken away. [853F] Bha gu & Ors.

The appellant Board issued a notice to the respondent demanding payment of consumption charges for electricity supplied by it. The respondent refused to pay the consumption charges on the ground that the supply was in the nature of an advance payment. The appellant Board filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the demand. The High Court held that the Board had power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the deposit did not contemplate appropriation was not correct because in the absence of guidelines with regard to framing of terms and conditions for the supply of electricity and the conditions on which it was supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply that the respondent Board shall not pay interest on the security deposit had statutory basis and accordingly cannot be struck down as arbitrary on the basis of a commercial transaction governing a bank deposit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The true nature of the transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of electricity estimated for a period of approximately three months. In one sense, the consumption security deposit represents only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer. [278F] 1.2 The Electricity Board 's interest requires that there should be some protection by way of security of advance payments in respect of the consumption of this three months period. The Electricity Act provides for payment of interest at certain rate, in the case of Rajasthan and Orissa the Boards have clearly stipulated that no interest shall be payable on the securities furnished to the appellant. [279F] M/s. Mills, Bharatpurv Assistant Engineer, ; , Bharatpur AIR at 109; M/S. Mills; Bharatpur vs Assistant Engineer (D) R.S.E.B., Bharatpur ; and M/M.P. State Electricity Board AIR 1 990 Andhra Pradesh 58 at pages 68 69 it was observed: "The Board may supply electricity to any person upon such terms and condition as the Board thinks fit". [278C] 1:3 The Electricity Supply Act provides that the requisition for supply of energy by the Board is to be made under proviso (a) after a written contract is duly executed with sufficient security. The payment is in terms of the agreement interpreting the conditions and conditions of the supply. Thus, it will be clear that the true nature and character of the transactions in these case is one which of advance Payment of charges is for consumption estimated for an period of nearly three months; in one sense the consumption is security deposit representing only a portion of the amount which is paid to the Electricity Board on bill being raising against the appellant, and that in such circumstances it is well entitled to require the consumer to co operate by paying their bills regularly. [280F] 2. The Board ' 's interests requires that There should be no security deposit with interest for the consumption or any such violation but should serve as a deterrent on the consumer in discharging his obligations towards the Board. While the terms and Conditions of supply of Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar provide for payment to the consumers of electricity, the Board has clearly stipulated therein that no Interest shall be paid on the stocks furnished to it. [281F] 3. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposited has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus.

The petitioners, a Telecommunication Research Centre, were recruited in four batches in 1965 and 1973. The Class I posts in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre consist of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Adminstrative Grade Level I) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade) 4. Assistant Directors (Senior Class I). The Posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I are filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, (the petitioners belong to this category; (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the union Public Service Commis sioner by written examination followed by an interview, (These officers belong to the Indian Telecommi tation Service Group B) and (c) by transfers of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Telegraph Engineering Service, Group. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belonged were not given any Special Pay in these grades and they were given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It was contended that the petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the Telecommunication research Centre for a limited purpose were not entitled to any Special pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telephone Service Group A and Group B. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: 1(a) The petitioners have filed these petitions demanding payment of Special Pay to them also. [1010 F] (b)(c) The petition ants (direct ent recruits) are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the telecommuni tation Research centre. They do the same job as the transferred officials. The Special Pay is not being paid to the 1012 transferred officials for compensating their displacement or for their qualifications. It is not deputation allowance. It paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the post of Telegraph Officer. [1001 F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (d) The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred official officials and that the transferred employees have to be paid extra amount by way of Special pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same rate as the scale of Pay of direct recruits because the transfer transferred officials had to perform in the instant Telecommunication Project duties which are not in their general line. [ 1010 F G] (e) The Court has no justification to deny the Special Pay at the same rates to the direct recruits working in the Exchange Research Centre. Denial of SpecialPay in the above circumstances to the direc tions amounts to viola tion of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.

The appellant, a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, was employed as a mUnshi in a appellant ' s Bidi data at Bhandara. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty, insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry in respect thereof was held on May 15, after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 and the said respondent filed an application under section 78 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, for reinstatement before the Labour Court under section 79 of the Act on the 5th August. His complaint was that the charge sheet was not proper, that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under Standing Orders, that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court for relief under section 7 8 (1) D. The High Court also held that it had not been necessary for the appellant to make an application tinder section 42 (4) of the Industrial Relations act, 1946 which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Courts and prayed that the order of the Labour Commissioner should be set aside on that ground alone. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an industry there must be compliance with the provisions of that chapter. [737 A] (1)(a) The scheme is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the labour court. [750 D F] (b) In regard to disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A of sub section (1), of section 78, the legislature felt it unnecessary to make any mention of an order under para D in section 84. Paragraph D thereof gives the Labour ' Court the power to try offenses punishable under the Act and cognizance of such offenses .an only be taken under section 82. [751 A B] (2) The Statement of Objects and Reasons amply demonstrates that by introducing paragraph D in Section 78(1) the legislature was 'only seeking to arm the LabourCourt with further and more effective powers to grant relief. Under section 79(1), proceedings before a Labour Court in respect Of disputes falling within clause (c) of para A of the sub section must be commenced on an application made by any of the parties to the dispute etc. and under sub section(2) every application under sub s.(1) has to be made in the prescribed form from and manner.

The respondents, who were the successors in interest of the lessor company, filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had been occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before the Munsif Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the civil court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the application under Section 12 of Act before the Civil Court was not maintainable as the respondents by their notice did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The proceedings arising out of the appellant 's applica tion before the trial court should be treated as a suit and his decision as a decree. It has to be kept in mind that it is the same court before which both a suit under Section 11 and an application Under section 12 are to be filed. [975D] 2. The question of dealing with eviction of tenants under section 11 and extension of period of lease under section 10, the civil Court is the proper forum. In the instant case, it is not necessary to decide the question as to whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the court by an application u/s 12 of tho Act because even on assuming the argument of the respondents to be correct the appellants should succeed. [936E F] 3. The jurisdiction of the Court is concerned. The questions are whether the petition which was filed by the appel lants as an applica tions under section12 should be read as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. With the assistance of learned counsel for the par ties, it has gone through the relevant papers in the case and are satisfied that both the parties dealt with every aspect of the case from their respective angles elaborately, and led their full evidence both oral and documentary and the case was tried by the Munsif in the same manner as the trial of an eviction suit. [946E F; 975A] 4. The respondents filed a regular appeal from the decision before the District Judge, Ranchi designated as Judicial Commissioner, and he also went into the entire controversy thoroughly. The appel late Court, designated as judicial Commissioner, was also one considering every relevant question in the matter. The findings on the disputed issues of fact between the parties were concurrently recorded against the tenants by the first two courts and it was not open to the High court to reverse them under section 100 C.P.C. [947B] 5.

The appellant a registered Society filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appellant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur city where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as Secretary of the society. In support of his claim, he produced certain documents on the basis of which the Trial Court allowed the suit to be withdrawn. According to the case of the appellant, Hari Narain Mahant was not elected as he had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. Since no notice was given of his application for withdrawal of the Suit either to the then Secretary Laxman Das or to the learned advocates Sri Satya Narayan Sharma or Sri Shyam Sunder Agarwal, through whom the suit had been instituted, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later, in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was nominated and when he learnt about the fate of the case, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit on the ground that he had not engaged the lawyer claiming or to be representing him and had not authorised him to compromise the suit and accepted the case. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. While agreeing with the argument of the appel lant that the trial Judge had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary of Society on the relevant date in favour of the respondent, the High Court observed that the mistake could not be corrected in the present situation. It accordingly directed the trial judge to consider the question whether the application filed under section15 1 of C.P.C. for restoration of the plaintiff 's suit under its inherent power and accepted his case of Hari Narain Pandit. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High court by a petition under section 1 15 of the code of Civil Proce dure, which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle was correctly discussed in Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483, pointing out the distinction in cases between fraud practised upon the Court and fraud practised on a party. Let us consider the cases in which consent decrees are challenged. If a party makes an application before the court for setting aside the decree on the grounds that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it is satis fied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the Court was induced to pass the decree. [237F H] 2. The case has to go back to the trial courts for reconsideration of the evidence on this point, but the reality of the consent cannot be so investigated. The principles have been followed in this country for more than a century.

The appellant was charged along with the co accused of having on or about July 11, 1953 transferred by sale High Denomination Bank Notes of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. I,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant contended that Ordinance was not in operation at the date when the offence was alleged to have been committed and that therefore the prosecution was not maintainable. Held, that the Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940 and April 1, 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance in the present case having been passed during the periods between June 28, 1940, and April I, 1946 was perpetual and in its duration with the result that it continues in operation until it is repealed. It was not necessary to refer to the other Ordinances appearing in this compilation but suffice it to say that in respect of all Ordinances which were thus promulgated by the Governor General in exercise of the power conferred upon him under section 72 Of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, the continuance thereof even after April 1 was predicated and the adaptations prescribed in the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950, issued under the Constitution of India were made applicable thereto. The law in the State of Jammu and Kashmir with regard to these High Denominations was not done but for the acceptance of the position that the ordinance in question continued in operation even after the declaration of emergency having come to an end was made on April 1 1946, and was in operation on July 11.

The appellants were convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court upheld the conviction of the appellants but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the death sentence was Parliament 's function, and that the sentence should be enhanced to life. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The determination of public opinion on this difficult an(l complex question was essentially a legislative, not a judicial function. The deliberate extinguishment of human life by the State for an offence of murder, they reasoned on metaphysical theories of punishment, was a denial of human dignity. They concluded by stating that the murder penalty was usually inflicted only on a few, i.e., the poor and down trodden who are outcastes of a society which led to the irresistible inference that the punishment was not fairly applied. This may be a 'progressive ' stance, which is out of place in a judicial pronouncement, which ought to be based on the facts and circumstances of the case and the law applicable. But the professed view does not stem from a firm belief in dignity of human lives for they themselves advocate the death penalty for certain classes of offenders, (I) R. On the facts before them they commuted the sentence of death to a sentence of imprisonment for life, and the decision cannot, therefore, be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi. [1069 H 1070 A] 1.2 The assessment of public, opinion on the difficult an (l complex questions, was essentially one of political expediency and not a Judicial function. [1000 B C] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar ; , applied. Rajendra Prasad 's case ; , referred to.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. The appellant claimed arrears of salary, but he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry held by him, reduced the appellant 's rank from the post of an Income Tax Officer to that of an income tax Inspector, and reduced it to Rs 16,562.29 as arrears of pay. The appeal filed by the appellant was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant is given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [58 D] (2) The plea that the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry. Therefore, the two authorities cited: The State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N. Roy Biswas, and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State, do not help the appellant. [584 E] (3) The High Court had given its judgment eight months after it had heerad argumenst. He urged that the result was that the High court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently been forgotten. The Civil Procedure Code does not provide a time limit for the period between the hearing of arguments and the delivery of a judgment unless explained by exceptional or extraordinary circumstances, is highly undesirable even when written arguments are submitted. It was for the appellant to satisfy the departmental authorities which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he had suffered some injustice which to be set right. He had been given a second opportunity by the punishing authority before it inflicted the punishment of demotion. Nothing further was required by law.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales of manga nese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. were complete within the state of Andhra pradesh. The Sales Tax Authorities held that these contracts were integrally connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with the M/s.M/s Binani Bros. (P) Ltd., and that the contract of sale occasioned the export and that they were not the last purchaser but the M M.T .C. was the last buyer within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. The High Court held that the contracts between the appellants and the MM.M Company were integrly connected with and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that (1) the contracts were different and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts; (2) the High Court erred in holding that all contracts between them and MM Company could not be said on the terms and conditions of the contracts in that case to be exporters of the goods. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1(a) The contracts between M/S.M./s Binini Bros. were different contracts and it was the S.T.,C. which entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. contract with a foreign buyer. This Court in Serajuddin 's case (supra) has laid down that the mere mention of F.0.B price or F.o.B delivery in contract between a merchant and the S .T. C. an F. O.B., which.exports the goods under a separate contract with the foreign buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte grated or the contract between the merchant and S. T.C., an F, contract with A foreign buyer; and (3) the mere mentioning of F0. B price or delivery in the contract would not make these contracts either in inte tent on gruntled or the Contract between the seller and the C.T.; and (4) the decision in National Tractors Hubli vs Commissioner of Commercial Taxes Bangalore, [1975] Supp. S.C R. 169, relied on. F.A. contract is that property in the goods passes only when they are put on board the ship. The loading of the Goods is an unconditional appropriation which passes the property. This is not because of any peculiarity of F .O. B. contracts but because in this type of contract the seller 's duty is to deliver the goods F.F.O.,B. Once they are on board, the seller has delivered them to the buyer and it is natural that they should thereafter be at the buyer 's risk. [444E F] (b) The decision in Serjuddin 'S case was no longer good law. In the National Traits case this Court relied on the decision of this Court in Coffee Board case and Serajiduddin ' s case to the other five contracts. [443F G] (c) The correct law is laid down by this Court. It has to be found out whether the contracts are integrated contracts in the Course of export or they are different.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court, Delhi for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probation was extended upto 8th Sept., 1974 and on the expiration of this extended period of Probation, his service was terminated by letters dated 12st October,1974 and 12th Oct. 1974 as he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and therefore the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination would constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where pre requisite for valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about termination of service is ab initio void. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service of the workman and the workman continues to be in service. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25 F. [532B C] 1.2 The conditions are that commencing the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment the date Of termination of the service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained, move backward to a period of 12 months just preceding the date when the workman had rendered service for a periodof 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively answered in favour of the workmen pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in sub section 2(a) it will have to be assumed that the workman is in continuous Service for a periods of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in section25F. On a pure grammatical construction the contention that even for invoking sub section (2) of section 25B, the workman must be shown to be In continuous service would render sub section(2) otiose and socially beneficial legislation would receive a set back by this impermissible assumption. And in any event, even if there be any such thing in favour, of the construction, it must be negatived on the ground that it would render subsection (2). [533E F] 1:3 The conditions for a valid retrenchment have not been satisfied by the mere fact of the number of working days being not less as 240 days, are fulfilled.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The Deputy Commissioner by order dt March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he be will get one month pay as required by the Rules. The appellant challenged the authority of the Deputy Commis sioner or the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. On the report of the enquiry officer that the chage relating to taluqdari was proved, the Deputy Commi tt Commissioner ordered that he be terminated. The High Court held that the appellant 's appointment was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order of dismissal was at all given and that the order was invalid. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the protection of article 310 (2) of the Constitu tion applies as much to a temporary public servant. The protection of Article 311 (2), therefore, applies as far as a temporary Government servant is concerned, but in principle it will make no difference whether the appellant is a probationer or a temporary employee. State of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , referred to.

The appellant State Government issued a notification on July 25, 1969 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25,1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The appellant challenged the validity of this notification on the grounds that it was not at all attracted in the matters of making promotions in the same service", and its true and correct interpretation would be that "it is applicable only to "making promotions and transfers from one service to another" and that the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu and Kashmir, which had been consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfer from one Service to another, and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order No. 643 HTETE dated July 25 1969 in regard of the appointments of respondents Nos. 3 to 46 and directed that it would be open to the State Govt to make a fresh selection of Professors.
