Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that and is in fact the case of the appellant State, that the Commission was consulted in respect of the principles regarding be followed. [875 E] In the instant case, the State Govern ment had stated in its reply to the writ Petition that for every post of Professor, names of four Lecturers strictly in order of seniority were sent to the Commission "at its direction" and they were interviewed and examined by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Commission. The State Government had also stated in their reply that for each post of Professors, names were sent at its direction. The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits.

(1)(2), and (3), of article 195(3), do not in express terms make that clause subject to those of clauses, the powers privileges and immunity of a House of the Legislature are only those of the House which Parliament is considered in Sankari Prasad Singh Deo vs Union of India ; , referred to. The respondents and two others, namely T.K. Satyanarayanan (No. 9) and V.S.R. Gupta (No . 10) in the list (Annexure 1), were all Readers in the private college each having put in more than eight years of service there as a Lecturer. T. K. Satyanmurty was promoted as Reader on 4 1969 and was drawing Rs.600/ per month on the date of taking over. V. S.R Gupta was promoted to officiate as Reader in the Government College much later than the four of the Respond ents (Nos. 1, 4, 6 and 7) in Annexure I. The respondents and T.M. K Satyanmuddy were confirmed as Lecturers but were promoted as Readers prior to the transfer of the college. The last two Readers in Class II temporarily on ad hoc basis for a period of six months with effect from the forenoon of March 9, 1971 or till the appointment was made in consultation with the Orissa Public Service Commission, whichever is earlier; subject to verification of character and antecedents and production of medical fitness certificate. Appointments were, thus offered to. the respondents under the terms and conditions of take over which have been already extracted. The grievance of the Respondents is that although they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over, their names were not referred to the Public Service Commis sion for consideration of their suitability for appointment as Readers in Government College. It is not disputed that they are otherwise educationally and by experience qualified for the post of Reader. The High Court found that the requirement of eight years ' teaching experience, as mentioned above, which is needed for appoint ment as a Reader is more than amply fulfilled by each of the respondents. The Respondents filed a Civil Miscellaneous Petition No. 4069 of 1976 before this Court on April 30, 1976 to urge this additional ground by such a belated application when the High Court had no opportunity to consider the question. Allowing the appeals and dismissing the Writ Petitions, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of 8 years of teaching experience as mentioned in the circular of March 23, 1971 is arbitrary and discriminatory. This condition has no nexus, what with the object underlying the qualification test in an educational institution having regard to the most essential condition of intrinsic quality and efficiency of the teachers. It was not unknown that private institutions generally have great handicaps in the matter of finance and oftener the teaching staff in a private college has not the same scales of pay and sometimes even has much lower scales than that of the Government colleges. It would be one thing to lay down appropriate educational and intelligibly relevant qualifications for certain posts in a college and also teaching experience of a specified duration but not otherwise qualified, on the sole ground of drawing a particular amount of salary on a particular date cannot be countenanced. TM.K Satyanmagurty (No 9) was promoted by the Government as a lecturer while in the Private College much earlier than the 4 of the respond ent respondents were drawing a little lower pay.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) of the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1948 for plying their vehicles on the route. The U. P. State Government issued a scheme in respect of the route and the date of publication of the approved or modified scheme was published by the Corporation under section68C of Chapter IV A of the . The route in question is an inter regional route and therefore an application for temporary permit for the period intervening between the date when the scheme was prepared and published under section 67C of the Act. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Authority for grant of temporary permits to ply their vehicles. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal upheld both by the State Road transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 68 F (1) C) clearly envisaged a situation where the application for a temporary permit is not made under section 69 F(I A) by the corporation. And there is felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question. [986C D] 1.2 The State transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be will have to examine the application of the present appellants for the remaining 4 vacancies and grant four permits according to law. [984F] 2.1 In interpreting the provisions of Chapter V A it is undoubtedly true that the Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provision of Chapter VI A of it is certainly true that section 68F(1 C) does not admit of such a construction. [983A] 2:2 In construing the provisions Of Chapter VA it is indeed true that in interpreting the relevant provisions of the undoubtedly the competing claims between the Corporation and the other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions contained in the Act, but the overall consideration namely the service is for the benefit of the travelling Public should never be overlooked for a moment. Reverting to the facts of this case if the approach of the High court is accepted it would lead to a startling result.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, inherited the suit properties from his maternal grandfather. On March 22, 1927 he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. Subsequently on April 12, 1929, he sold the equity of redemption to the said mortgagee for Rs 11,000 and in suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appellant in the court of the Sub Judge, Panipat, from which the present appeal arose, the appellant had claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the impugned alienation were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity, but he ordered that the memorandum of appeal should be returned to respondents I 9 to enable them to file an appeal before the High Court. That is how the present case has come up before this Court. Held: (i) The decision of the first Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case must be taken to have been overruled. In the present ease, it was difficult to say that the doctrine of stare decisis really applies because the earlier decisions were not correctly decided. (ii) It is well settled that a decision which has been followed for a long period of time, and has been acted upon by persons in the formation of contracts or in the disposition of their property, or in legal procedure or in other ways, will generally be followed by courts of higher authority than the court establishing the rule, even though the Court before whom the matter arises afterwards might not have given the same decision had the question come before it originally. (iii) The doctrine of law stare decisis is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them was sitting on a Verandah, they attacked him with a dagger while the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebrahim Ali did not prove fatal. The jury returned an unanimous verdict of guilt against all the appellants on both charges. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there could be no conviction under section 446 of the Code unless murder has actually been committed. HELD : (i) There can be no doubt that the words "in order to" have been used to mean "with the purpose of". If the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offence punishable with death, the house breaking is punishable under section 448 of the Penal Code and if it is done "in Order to" the committing of any offence punishable under that section. [982 H] (ii) There is no substance in either of these contentions. Section 449 of the I.P.C. provides that whoever commits house trespass in order to the committing 'of an offence" even though the offence may not be completed.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration of his title as collateral within four degrees of Gurdial, who was a Sarswat Brahmin. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable; (ii)that the parties were governed by Hindu Law and not by custom; (iii) that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. The Subordinate Judge held that the lands in suit being in possession of tenants, the suit was maintainable but the suit dismissed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court modified the decree and directed the parties to bear their own costs. Held: (i)(a) The custom in Rattigan 's Digest of Customary Law is that a daughter excludes the collateral from succession even though they are within the fourth degree. Rattighan 's work has been accepted by the Privy Council as "a book of unquestioned authority in the Punjab". (b) In the present case, the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was initially on him and that being the position no burden was cast on the respondent which she need have discharged by adducing evidence of particular instances. The High Court was right in holding that the instance relied upon by the appellant is wholly insufficient to discharge his onus. (c) In order to enable the appellant to displace the general custom recorded in Ratigan ' s Digest, the respondent must produce a Riwaj i am which is a reliable and trustworthy document. It has been held in Qamar ud Din vs Mt. Fateh Bano, A.I.R. 1935 Lah. 306, that if the Riwazi am produced is a credible and trustworthy evidence, has been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up. (ii). In the last case, however, the collateral 's were beyond the fourth degrees and it was enough for the Court to say that irrespective of whether the properties in dispute were ancestral or self acquired or whether the property left by him were of any substantial value at all as would have made it worth while for the daughter to claim the same in addition to the properties gifted to her by her father during his lifetime. (iii).

The respondent was the Managing Director of a number of companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. He was also a Director of other companies, and had on occasions acted as liquidator of some Commis sioner of various estates. On 4 7 1949 he applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs Douglas Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee, managing agent, liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court of Calcutta. The reference was heard by a Bench consisting of the Chief Justice Das Das, J., and section R. Das Gupta, J. who differed in their opinion. The question for decision in this appeal was whether a separate duty was payable in respect of Government stocks under the provisions of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 over and above what was paid under section 74(1) of Finance Act, 1910 on account of other investments. Held, that the transaction was a single transaction whereby the donor constitutes the donees jointly and individually his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act as managing director, director, managing agents, secretary or liquidator of any company in which he is or may at any time thereafter be in terested in any such capacity as aforesaid and also in his own capacity as managing directors, director or in any capacity whatsoever as occasion shall require. The transaction was one a single sale whereby the respondent constituted the doneees jointly with the power to act on behalf of the donor in his personal capacity and in the other capacities; he was not one individual when he was acting as a trustee of a particular estate and he was therefore not a third individual when it was acting in his capacity as a representative of a company.

The assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of business by the two appellant companies for the year 194950 the Income Tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating the depreciation allowance to which the assessee was entitled in computing the profits or gains of the business, the written down value had to be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, if it had been in force and a claim had been made supported by prescribed particulars. No claim was made or could be made for such allowance, but no depreciation allowance would then be allowed to him. The assessee 's contention that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words which would have been allowed to he if the Indian income tax Act 1922, was in fact in force in the past as in fact no claim was raised or could he made for it for such allowances was rejected by the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that this expression "or which would had been allowed" meant not only that the depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax but also that the interest allowed under the Saurashtra War Profits Act had to he deducted in computing written down values. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in answering the question referred in these cases out of which Civil Appeals Nos. In 1950, Saurashtra became a Part A State of the Union of India; by section 3 of the Indian Finance Act, 1950, the Indian Incometax Act, was extended to it. [226 F] Rajaratna Naranbhai Mills Ltd., vs Commissioner of Income tax, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was a contractor of the respondent State. The contract pertained to the construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at the Raichur Thermal Power Plant at an estimated cost of about Rs. 1.8 crores. The petitioner invited tenders from registered contractors of appropriate class. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" viz., that the intending tenderers should have executed civil and architectural works including insulation in a power plant/industrial complex, preferably in power plant; (2) should have an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding three years. Paragraph V required the intending bidders to furnish the following information "along with the application for issue of blank tender books", namely: (a) Audited Balance Sheet/Certificate from Chartered Ac countant for preceding three year; (b) Latest income tax clearance Certificate; and (c) Latnest income Tax clearance Certificate. The issue of the blank tender book was to be between 23rd January to 27th January, 1989 and the completed tender books had to be submitted by 3.00 p.m. on 6.2.1989. These were scrutinised with reference to the prequalifying requirements and data on experience, work done etc. as furnished by each of them. The respondent rejected the petitioner 's application for con tention that the extensions of time given to M.C.C., to submit the tender with requisite clarifications were not warranted. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the K.P.C.; should not at all have entertained the tender of M. C.C; (ii) the extension of time granted to M;C. to submit tender with necessary clarifications were neither warranted nor arbitrary and therefore its application for tender forms should have been rejected at the outset. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of para I(3) is not fulfilled in the present case. [234F] 1.2 In order to satisfy itself that the requirements of para l(1) and (2), are fulfilled, the KP. C call for the certifi cates mentioned in para V and the fulfilment of the require ment in para I (3) has obviously to be verified by reference to audited balance sheets called for under clause (a). It is clear that apart from para 1, there are some other requirements in the N.I.T. which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply of tender forms. These include, if not all, at least such of those documents referred to in para l.

The appellant was the owner of a house. On October 10, 1947, in pursuance of an oral exchange, the appellant took possession of the Danepur Road House and put in possession of it on October 10. The appellant filed an amended application dated the 14th August 1948, furnishing the required particulars. This application was not disposed of by the Additional Custodian for reasons not clear on the record until the 20th March, 1952. On that date he passed an order confirming the exchange. After the order confirming it was passed by the Custodian on the 20rd March,1952, the appellants filed an application before the Custodian General to show cause why the order of the Additional Deputy Custodian dated the 20nd March, 1953, confirming the transfer and further orders sanctioning mutation and other consequential orders made in connection therewith be not set aside. The Custodian General rejected this application on the ground that the appellant had no power under section 27 of the Act to revise the original orders of the Custodian or Additional Custodian under section 28 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950. On appeal, the Custodian held that the order was final and conclusive and that the revision application filed by the appellants in 1948 was not open to appeal or revision but became final and binding on the Custodian. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the revisional power could be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal was filed against it. Held, that the contention of the appellant that the exercise of revisional powers in this case by the custodian General was without jurisdiction or is illegal must fail. The order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian under s 27 of Central Act XXXIII of 1950 and therefore the order dated 20th April, 1952, was subject to the revisional powers of the Assistant Custodian General under section 8 of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Ordinance, 1949.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of hardware merchants. The respondent company claimed bonus for the relevant four years prior to 1965, when trouble began. The dispute related to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 and the claim for bonus for those years was founded on tradition or custom or condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practices or custom prevalent in the establishment before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. " The appellant company contended that the claim put forward by the appellant before the Tribunal was on the face of it unsustainable on the short ground that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and, therefore fell squarely within the Bonus Act; that the dispute referred by the State Government related to a totally different type of bonus, namely customary bonus or one which was a term of the employment itself. The Tribunal dismissed the appellant 's claim in limine on the score that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (1) the claim made by the workmen before the tribunal was, on the facts of the case, unsustainable on its short ground; (2) the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try the dispute as the demand was not based on profits or the financial results of the employers but was based on custom and service condition not one based on profit; (3) the reference was bad for non disclosure of material facts by the respondent company in the course of conciliation proceedings; and (4) the award was bad because it did not mention the name of a festival as a matter of pleading, did not detract from the claim of customary bonus. HELD: (1)(a) The Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute on the ground that the demands were not based upon profits or financial results. [501 B] (b) The reference was not bad for want of material particulars by the respondents. The Industrial Tribunal had rightly held that the reference did not fall within the provisions Of the Bonus and the award made by it was invalid. [602 D E] (c) The claim in question was not a matter based on any profit. The effect of the award of the Industrial Tribunal 's negation of the profit based on bonus claim in 1965 on custom based bonus for subsequent period is again relevant, if at all, as evidence, which falls outside the consideration at present. [599 A] (2)(a). The reference to the Labour Appellate Tribunal was not valid because it related to any festival by the workers in their pleadings (reference to Diwali as the relevant festival in the statement of the Case in this Court) and so, the decision of the Tribunal on that question did not suffer from any infirmity.

The petitioners who were promotees, were appointed directly from the Bar to Haryana Superior Judicial Service. Some of the more important grievances of the petitioners are that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly and unjustly made to depend upon fortuitous circumstance of the date of confirmation in the Superior Judicial service; that even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation; and that the High Court applied the principle of rotation as between promotees and direct recruits at the time of their confirmation when, in fact, that the relevant rules provide for is the application of a rule of quota at the date on which he completes the period of probation. The petitioners who are promotees, challenged the validity of the Punjab Superior Judicial Services (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976 by filing writ petitions in this Court contending that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and the direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that is to say, not only at the stage of appointment but at the place of confirmation also; that the seniority of the members of the Superior judicial Service was so integral and vital to the control of the High Courts over them, that any erosion thereof would both be violative of Article 235 of the Constitution and equally run counter to the settled concept of independence of judiciary which is now coming to be recognised as the basic feature of the constitution.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed R.P. No. 1615 of 1984 before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Wardamagam, Karimnagar and Adila bad is the criteria. The Adilabad division consisting of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts of the Commercial Taxes Division cannot be treated to be a zone and the divisional seniority prepared by the department is bad in law. The G. O.Ms No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982, issued under Paragraph 3(7) of Andhra Pradesh Public Services (Organisation of Local cadres and Regulation) Order 1975 for the purpose of recruitment, seniority, promotion, transfer etc. of local cadres is co terminus with the zone V of the Presiden tial Order. The appellant was the manager and Karta of a joint Hindu family. The suit was decreed by the trial court against him but in appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether the mortgagor had power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. It is not competent to the mortgagor to grant a lease unusual terms, or to alter the character of the land or to authorise its use in a manner or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. [117 F] (ii) The true position has been stated in the following terms by this Court in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, ; , and Madan Mohan Singha vs Raj Kishore Kumari, ; referred to. (iii)The question of the sufficiency or insufficiency of the security was not really gone into but the court considered that the lease was granted in good faith, was for a limited term and stipulated a fair and reasonable rent and it was therefore operative against the mortgagee. [118 E F] Balmukund vs Motilal, ; and Madanmohan Singh vs Raj Kishor Kumar, A.I.R. , referred to (iv)The true position is that the mortgagor in possession may make a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of administration, for instance he may create a tenancy from year to year in the case of agricultural lands or from month to month in the ease of property consisting of houses and his dealings with the mortgaged properties in the normal course of Management would be operative against mortgagee. The true effect is that section 66 has no application to leases of the mortgaged Property, but it is not open to the lessee to grant such a lease by the mortgagor, in possession.

The petitioner, a contractor, sent bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal, the division bench set aside the order of the learned Single judge and directed the petitioner to rescind the contract of Arbitration. On further appeals, the Division Bench held that it was an exceptional case for interference, the learned single Judge cancelled the arbitration clause 68 of the contract in matter Nos. 1326, 1364 and 1365/90 dated November 23, 1990. In these special leave petitions, on behalf of the petitioner, it was contended that Clause 68 of Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the Respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator; and that Section 5 has no application to the facts of this case. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that Clause 67 of the Contract provides that where any disputes or differences have arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract, the matter shall be referred to arbitration, and that the Court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. Allowing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as they apply to the proceedings in court. Sub section (2) of Section 37 of the Arbitration Act regulates the limitation for the arbitration proceedings. [362C D] 1.2 In all cases it is not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. In given circumstances and the factual background the Court may be justified to exercise the power under Section 5 and12. The question then is under what circumstances such power would be exercised. [363D] 1:3 The provisions Of the Limitation Acts would apply in arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration whilst still relying on the clause as barring the claim. [361E F] M/s Amarch & Lalit Kumar vs Shree Ambica Jute Mills Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The mortgage was an estate within the Act. That property included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The Act came into force after the passing of the aforesaid preliminary decree. The appellants applied under section 14 of the Act and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act, but that objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (1) that the objection in question was barred by the principles of res judicata; and (2) that it was barred because the bar of section 4(d) pleaded was not tenable. The High Court held that the application was barred under the principles Of res judicata. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decision of the majority of the judges in the Full Bench decision in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh is not correct. [912 F] (ii)The decision in Ramnarain vs Basudeo, A.I.R. 1950 Pat. 354, referred to. (iii)In construing section 4 (d), it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the , do not fall within the protection of the section.

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 206/89 and connected batch of Civil Appeals were candidates for the Civil Services Examination of the concerned year. While a substantial number of OAs filed before the Tribunal at Delhi were pending, a similar number of analo gous O.As filed by the petitioners before the Benches of Administrative Tribu nal at Patna, Jabalpur, Hyderabad, Jodhpur and Eranakulam were transferred to the Tribunal for the C.S.E. Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal. The Tribunal rendered its main judgment in O.A. No.206/89 Alok Kumar vs Union of India & Ors., and 61 other connected cases. The other judgments were passed on the basis of the conclusions arrived at in OAs Nos. 206 and 89 of Alok Kumar 's case, decided by this Court in Alok Kumar & Ors. vs Union o f India & ors., and the connected batch. Since the Tribu al has set out only the facts in the case of Alok Kurnar (O.A No. 207/89), the other two judgments were rendered on the same basis. The appeals filed by special leave against the judgment of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi are allowed and the cases of the petitioners are directed to be listed for final hearing in the light of the observations made herein. [972D E] In the instant case, the Tribunal has allowed the candidates who have been allocated to the I.P.S., or to a Central Services Group 'A ' and who has been permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to do so, will become eligible to compete for IAS, IFS, IPS and Central Services Groups 'A" and considered only for those appointments. The reasons attributed for such a classification on the ground of neglect of train ing, financial loss, unemployment situation, loss to service are all common to all the Central Service Group 'C ' listed in the CSCS.S./C.E., Rules, and therefore, the impugned second proviso is held to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed to the IPS and 16 Group 'B services and as such it is violative of Article 14.

The appellant challenged his order of detention under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, having been dismissed, he filed this appeal. The question relating to denial of fair hearing before the Advisory Board has not been noticed by the High court as a contention on behalf of the appellant, but counsel for the respondent did not dispute the allegation on the basis of record as also the papers available with him that the department was represented at the hearing before it and had stated in paragraph 9 of the special leave petition that he was formerly employed in the customs department and he would like to assist the detenu. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detaining authority had the assistance of the Deputy Collector of Central Excise and a Superintendent of Central excise. In the words of Chandrachud, CJ, "they play the role of legal advisers". The Board had no justification to refuse assistance of 793 Sundararajan to the appellant in such circumstances. [792F] 2.1 The rule in A. K. Roy 's case made it clear that the detenu was entitled to the assistance and of a 'friend '. The word 'friends ' used there was obviously not intended to carry the meaning of the term in common parlance. One of the meanings of the word 'content, according to the Collins English Dictionary is "an ally in a fight or cause; supporter". The term 'friending ' used in the judgments of this Court was more in this sense than meaning 'a person known well to another and regarded with liking, affection and loyalty. ' A person not being a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [788B C] 2:2 The detaining Authority had the benefit of the Advisory Boards 's order to permit the appellant to be assisted by the detenu before the Board through a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Central Board could have, if he was so minded, made a request to the Advisory board for permission to be represented by a lawyer. [789E F] 3:3 The rule is in A K. Gopalan etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; , referred to.

The Government of India issued a notice under sub r. (2) of r. 75A(2) Of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, to acquire the requisitioned goods and acquired movable property under the rules made under the Defence Of India Act, 1939. The owners of the jute mills were in possession of the mills and therefore the proper persons to be served with the orders of requisition in this case were the mills. The Government of india issued a notification on September 30, 1946, under sub rule (2), of r., 75A (2). The owners challenged the validity of the order of requisition by filing a suit in the High Court of Calcutta. The suit was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notice served on the owners of a property was not properly served and therefore there was no acquisition following on the service of the notices of acquisition. Held, that the order was valid and binding on the respective defendants. The notice of acquisition in this ease was effective service on the mills as owners for the purpose of r, 75A of the Defence Rules, and the property in the goods passed to the Government of the india on September, 30,1946. The notices of the acquisition were properly served on them through the managing agents and therefore these orders were validly and duly served on their respective defendants, and therefore they were not valid. Held further, that as the notice of the decision to acquire was given to the various managing agents of the Mills as such there could be no valid requisition for the service on them. The order of requisitioning was effective only when the property was actually appropriated towards the pucca delivery orders concerned and the notice was properly served.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Apprehending that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 6,52,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59 with the result that a sum continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. At the same time the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A. Though it failed at the earlier stages, it succeeded ultimately in the Letters Patent Appeal filed by it in the East Punjab High Court. In the said appeal decided on May 24, 1965, it was held that no action can be taken against the assessee. The Revenue obtained the aforesaid reference. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the asses following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, [1964] 65 I SCR 965. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a pro ceeding provision. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve. [113B] 2. In Metal Boxes, which has been followed in Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision and a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and, therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of tile proprietor 's interest. [114E F] 3. While approving the said statement it was stated in Vishan Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. that "In other words the broad distinction between the two is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be take into account, against gross receipt in theP.& L.

The petitioners, who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) (hereafter referred to as 'Engineers ' at places), challenged the validity of the classification on the ground that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds. The writ petitions filed by them before the High Court were dismissed. In the appeals preferred by the petitioners, it was contended that officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of their length of continuous service, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the date of the competitive examinations were placed above those appointed on the said basis of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The distinction and the classification of temporary Assistant Officers and members of the Indian Railways Service of engineers Class I fell clearly to be identified and marked. [1025B] 2.1 The scheme having met with approval of this Court cannot by mere passage of time be taken to have become vulnerable by subsequent exponence and dimension of Article 14 of the Constitution. This Court in Katyani Dayal 's case specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the then petitioners because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity or otherwise of the given weightage of half the length of service to Temporary Assistant Officers. subject to a maximum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [1125E F] 3.2 The rule of weightage also appears to be reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katakyani 's Case (supra), still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has already been decided finally. A dispute now sought to be raised under Article 32 of the constitution between the Officers in a Representative capacity and engineers across also in a representatives capacity across which stand arrayed the Union of India and the Railway Board as respondents. When this matter came up for hearing on 15th March, 1990 before a three judge Bench in which one of us (Punchhi, J.) was a member, it Was not permissible by means of successive writ petitions. [1109F G] 4.3 The contention of the petitioners that the State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably, falls to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's cases (supra). [1108A B] 5.4 The distinction between, the two services was well marked in Kattani Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., ; and Direct Recruits Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Ors. , referred to.

The Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, was passed by the Rajpramukh of Saurashtra on 9th February, 1950, which purported to amend the Saurashtra State public safety measures Ordinance (XLVIII of 1948), which had been passed "to provide for public safety, mainte nance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State". The appellant challenged the validity of the said Ordinance by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that it violated articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Consti tution. Held, that the impugned Act was not discriminatory as it purported to modify the procedure prescribed by the Ordinance and the notification which had issued thereunder offended against the equal protection clause of the Constitu tion. The State Government was in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court would not lightly interfere with the decision of the Government. Benoarilal 's case, (1923) L.R. 476 measure, referred to. Per PATANJALI SASTRI C.J., MUKHERJEA J. The impugned Act is in these terms: "A Special Judge shall try such offences or classes of offences or such cases as the State Govern ment may, by general or special order in writing direct". Section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance provides that a Special Court shall try all such offences and classes of offence or classes as the Government of the United State of Saurashtra may, under sub section (1) of section 9, be investigated, inquired into, tried and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and section 11 lays down that the Special Judge should try "such offences or class of offences". or classes thereof as the Govern ment of the former State may, in accordance with a special procedure devised for the purpose. The Act is not discriminatory and void under article 13 of the Con stitution.

The appellants were charged with the offence of theft and murder. The trial court acquitted nine accused persons, namely, the father of the deceased, PW 2, PW 3, PW 4, PW 5, PW 6, PW 8 and PW 9. The High Court dismissed their appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of PWs 1, 7 and 8 is not credible; (ii) the conviction of the accused persons for the offence under section 396 I.P.C.; (iii) the prosecution has failed to prove the presence of PW 2 in the tin shed of the house at the time of occurrence; (iv) the testimony of PW 3 that he saw the appellants in the light of lantern that was hanging in the eastern wall of the eastern kotha and that he had not sustained any injury during the occurrence, and (v) the presence in the western kotkha together at the same time at the scene of occurrence has been mentioned in the first information report Exh. Ka 1 by PW 2 or PW 8. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence of PW 1 is not reliable because he had stated that the appellants entered the house and assaulted her husband fatally and that some of them caused injuries to her and committed dacoity by looting properties worth about Rs. 2,700/ from her house. [573F] (2) It is not improbable that all the appellants were seen by PW 1 in the northern kothakha where the main part of the occurrence had taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify with the help of the lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her, and not strangers and she has received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the incident which had gone on for about 15 20 minutes. [574F] In the instant case, the evidence is corroborated by the evidence (PW 2) who had seized that lantern in the inner kothara where PW 2 was sleeping earlier to the western wall of eastern ketha of the said house and PW 8 had also received injuries, and PW 7 who had been believed by not only the Sessions Judge but also by the learned Judges of the High Court. [575B] (3) The argument that PW 3 had falsely implicated the appellants because she could not recognise the real culprits is unacceptable. It is true that the evidence regarding recovery of the stolen property from the house of the appellant was not accepted by the trial court and the Sessions Court, however, has rejected the evidence on the ground that it was admitted by PW 3 who had deposed that he did not claim to have seen the incident in the early hours of the day. [576C] (4) The fact that PW 2 had not mentioned the name of any of the persons to whom he entered the place of occurrence soon after the culprits left the place, is not a circumstance which could be relied upon because it has been deliberately made improvements in his version about the occurrence. [577E F] (5) It was not improbable nor improbable that PW 7 had stated the name or any of these accused to any other villagers who entered the scene house of occurrence immediately after the assailants left the scene, and also because he has not sustained injury during that occurrence and had not stated the names of any accused to other villagers whom entered the room of the scene soon after they left the places.

The respondent employer terminated the services of some of its employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that section 25F had no application to the effect that the discharge was invalid. The employer Corporation came before the High Court challenging the Award. A learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 25 FF. The appellant Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant employer that the employees were probationers at the time of discharge from service; there was no dispute that as a condition precedent to discharge the requirements of section 26F had not been complied with, and if the discharge of the employees would amount to retrenchment, appellant 's counsel did not dispute that the orders of discharge would be bad for noncompliance of section25F. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the discharge amounted or not was a case of voluntary retirement or retirement on reaching the age of superannuation or absence on account of continued ill health. [778C] 2.1 In the instant case the requirements were satisfied. The order of retrenchment was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. There would be one set of costs. [789E F] 3.2 The question of the correct interpretation of the definition of 'retrenchment ' in section2(oo)(of the Act was left open. [788F] 4.1 The view expressed by this Court in Hariprasad Shivshanker Shukla vs A.D. Divikar, ; and Mohan Lal vs Bharat Electronics Ltd., it was in terms held that the termination of service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice compensation etc. [781F] 3:2 The expression 'termination of service for any reason whatsoever ' is not defined in the Act. It is true that an artificial definition may include a meaning different from or in excess of the ordinary acceptation of the word which is the subject of definition; but there must then be compelling words to show that such a meaning differ from or In excess of ordinary accepted connotation of the expression which is a subject of defined definition. [783E F, 782A] 4:3 The underlying assumption of course, is that the undertaking is running as an undertaking and the employer continues as an employer but where either on account or of transfer of the undertaking or on account Of the closure of the Undertaking the basic assumption disappears, there can be no question of ' retrenchment, within the meaning of the term as defined by the Act; it is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court to both of which one of us was a party. Divakar, after referring to Pipraich Sugar Mills Mazdoor Union, the ratio of which was re affirmed by a Constitution Bench of this court in L. Robert D 'Souza vs Executive Engineer, Southern Railway & Anr., ; and State Bank of India vs N. Sundara Money, Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs The Workmen, [1971] 1 SCR 591; referred to.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore a sale of goods took place. The revision application was rejected on 27 January, 1960 on the finding that the sales effected by the assessee were sales under the Act and that the assesee fell within the scope of the Act. The High Court held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assesseee and that consequently a sale took place, and directed the assessing authority to accept the claim of the assesses as a 'dealer" and further held that the systematic and organised charac ter of business carried on by the assesses clothed him with the status of a "business" under section 2(c) read with C1 (g) of Section 2 of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, was a dealer within the meaning of the said Act. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the transaction of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment under the Indian Railways Act and therefore the assessee fell within its scope of section 2 (c) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposal of the Goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the t goods. [780B] 2. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway was a carrier of goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of such so disposing was adju tion to the Principal activity of carriage of Goods by the railway. It seems to South Eastern Rail Railway was an "dealer". for the purposes of the West Bengal Finance Act, 1950.

The appellants were convicted of the offence under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and all of them except Vishnu Prasad, were also convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants had acted in a manner which was known to him and was under his instructions, that he had authorised Chokhani to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the Insurance Company unless he was authorised by the Chairman; (ii) the evidence showed that the money was being received from the Insurance company for nothing which was due to Bhagwati Trading Company from that company and that therefore Dalmia did not include those securities in this letter. HELD : (i)(a) The prosecution had not proved that the moneys were being received by the Insurance Companies for anything which was payable to Bhagwati trading Company or the receipt of cash or the other transactions, his role having begun, according to the prosecution, after the offence was committed, i.e., after Chokhani had issued cheques on the Bank accounts of the insurance company with the Chartered Bank in favour of Bhagwati Trading Co. and therefore could know nothing regarding the diversion of funds of the Union Agencies to the Union agencies. [810 D] (b) The evidence showed the receipt and the entries did show the receipt or the entries of the amounts from Bhagwati Trading company, but the prosecution case was that the amount was received in cash and not through transfers which transactions had to be adjusted. [711 F G] (c) It is true that the funds of a Bharat Insurance Company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved by the prosecution. The introduction of Bhagwati trading Companies in the transactions was the first step to carry out deception about the actual payment of money out of those funds to the union agencies and therefore the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of the Corporation 's moneys to the Insurance Agencies and was with a view to deceive any such person in future who be traced to the source of the money received by it.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, the new State of Bombay was formed and by section 82 power was conferred upon the Central Government to give directions to the States. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new state of Saurashtra and Kutch. Under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, the States of Gujarat and Maharashtra were carved out of the territory of the former State of Saurashtra. By section 83 power was given to the Central Govern ment to give direction to the states that those provisions were applicable immediately before November 1, 1956, to the disadvantage of persons mentioned in sub sections (1) & (2) of section 115 of the Act. The respondents contended that r. 138 only dealt with the existing servants and did not prevent any additional members from being amalgamated in the Secretariat. HELD : (i) The order dated August 19, 1966 was contrary to the Recruitment Rules, 1957. If it be granted that the State was competent to transfer and did transfer the appellants to perform service in connection therewith, it is difficult to hold that when the State "regularised" the service of tho appellants in the secretariat with the consent of the Public Service Commission there was no absorption under the Absorption Rules. [519 E] (ii) The expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was any intention to absorb the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States personnel in the subordinate staff. [525 B C] Union of India & Anr. vs P. K. Roy & Ors., ; , referred to.

The petitioners of the second category purchase oil seeds for use in manufacture of edible oils. The surplus oil seeds are sold to other dealers, registered or unregistered, inside and outside the State. Both these commodities are essential commodities to which the Central Sales Tax Act applies. Certain provisions of these Amending Acts were challenged on the ground that they offend section 15 of the Central Act and were also unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that there was a possibility of tax being levied at more than one stage, the provisions of the first proviso notwithstanding. The State contended that since the tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase at the very first transaction, the stage was fixed and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 5(2)(a) (vi) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. HELD: (i) The question as to how far a party can ask for refund without the order of assessment being set aside by appropriate proceedings is highly doubtful; because at the time when the actual order of assess ment is passed, in certain eases, it may not be possible for a party to say whether he was entitled to exemption or not, under sub cl. (vi), of section 5 (2) of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act 1967, but if particular sales or purchase are exempt from taxation altogether they can never be taken into account at any stage, for the purpose of calculating or arriving at the taxable turnover and for levying tax. [539 F H] (ii) The matter is now in the hands of the dealer himself and it is for him to decide whether he would not claim the benefit of section 11AA and ask for a refund or in future transactions delete the sales from his taxable turnover when he is not the last dealer liable to pay the tax. In the case of local manufacturers if their cost of production varies, the net tax collected will be more or less in some cases but that does not create any inequality because inequality is not result of the tax but results from the cost of Production of the goods or the 'cost of their importation. [555 A B] (iii) The Central Act itself gives power to the legislature to choose a rate of tax at not more than 3 per cent of the taxable turn over. The Act has been amended in relation to the area of that State and it was inconceivable that this could not be within the competence.

The appellants were the representatives of three original plaintiffs who instituted a suit against the respondent for enforcement of a mortgage, against the present respondent. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No. 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of Rs. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No 1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties. The respondent contended that as the decree had already been passed by the High Court, it was not possible always to find logical solu tions. Held, that the view taken by the District Judge was right and should not have been disturbed. The fact that in the working of the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act alongside the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act several curious and novel situations had arisen for which it was no possible always open to find a logical sectation. Rainier vs Srinivasiah, (1940) 2 M. 39, 39 300 decisions referred to. Held further that the High COurt was right in holding that by virtue of the decree against defend ants 2 to 7 being satisfied, the entire mortgaged property would be freed from the debt and if the respondent gets any benefit thereby such benefit would be merely incidental or consequential in its nature. Raine vs Srinivasaiah, (1942) 1 M. 38, 39, 300 decisions of the High Courts relied on.

The City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The City Civil Judge, Bombay, was a tenant of the premises in question under the first defendant. The second and third plaintiffs were persons to whom the said premises were sublet by the first plaintiff. The first plaintiff as landlord of the said Premises gave notice to quit to the first appellant on December 6, 1947. Thereafter he filed suit No. 483/4400 of 1948 in the City Civil court on April 29,1948 whereby he sought to evict the first respondent and the third plaintiffs alleging that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The Small Causes Court held that the second and 3rd plaintiffs were not lawful sub tenants and the subletting by the First plaintiff to them being contrary to law the latter had deprived himself of the protection of the Act. It accordingly passed a decree for eviction of all the plaintiffs of the present suit. An appeal against the decree was unsuccessful and a revisional application to the High Court was summarily dismissed by that Court. Thereafter, the City civil court held that it had jurisdiction to try the suit but did not record any decision on the merits of the appellants ' case. The Act gave the first and third defendants an injunction restraining them from proceeding further with the execution of the decree in suit No, 2178/5400 of the City Court. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the City C court had no jurisdic tion to entertain a suit under section 28 on a question of title de hors the Act and as such the City Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable to the City City Civil Courts.

The respondent was a director of the appellant company. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for the appointment of the managing director as the managing directors of the company. It was contended that he had ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings and that the appointment by the appellant was void. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that section 312 of the , applied to the case. The word "assignment" in section 312 was not used in the sense of giving an assignment of his office by a director to another person under an agreement with the company void unless such assignment was approved by a special resolution of the Company. Section 317 of the Act did not prevent the appointment or appointment of any one of the directors. The section was intended to prevent that a managing director from appointing his successor when section 255 permits him to do that. The proviso to section 86B did not indicate that it was intended that the word "resign" in the main part of the section would include "appointment". The rule of construction applied by the High Courts, which enables by raising a presumption, something to be included in the present Act, was put in these words: "It is a well established principle of construction that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of section would have included the subject matter of the proviso. This rule would enable the court to hold in regard to section 484B at the most that an appointment by a directors to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment was not to be excluded within the word 'assign".

The respondent landlady filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart. The Trial Court held that the ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respond ent. The appel lants preferred an appeal to the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960 being the Court of Small Causes at Madras. The said appeal was numbered as H.R.A. 156 of 1979. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellants then preferred a Civil Revision Petition in the High Court against the aforesaid decision. This petition was dismissed by the then Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel tants that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of Order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 are directly applicable to the proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decisions is directly applicable. [420B] Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case, relied upon by Mr. Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly negatived by the Trial Court. [421C D] 2. The contention that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/S. Adarseshwar Glass Shop Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction petition was not maintain able at all. [416E F] Chhotal Pyarelal, the partnership Firm and others vs Shikharchand, , relied upon.

The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the imposition of a ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling limit. Section 2(n)(A)(ii) defines "vacant land" by providing that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess Of the ceiling area, the person shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. The Andhra Pradesh Act was amended by the Andhra Pradesh State (Telangana Area) Amendment Act, 1978 with effect from 1st January 1975 and it was provided that the imposition would not exceed two standard holdings. Section 3(f) of the Act provides for the constitution of a committee to be called the Andhra pradesh High Court consisting of five Judges of the High Court. The petitioners in these appeals were holders of certain lands situated in Andhra Pradesh to defeat an agrarian reform legislation enacted by the State or the benefit of the weaker sections of community. The validity of the said Act was challenged on the ground that it violated Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution inasmuch as it sought to impose ceiling on land in the whole of Andhra Pradesh including land situate in urban agglomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 2(m) of that Act was an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified to be an urban agglomerations, the whole Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Andhra State Legislature. The High Court held that the Andhra Act sought to imposed ceiling on lands in the entire State including land situated in urban commu nities and since it contravened Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) and (g) of Constitution, the provisions of the impugned Act were not applicable to "vacants land" falling within the ambit of the Central Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Andhra Act was intra vires and therefore void as having been outside the State of Andhra pra Pradesh Legislature. [1156 F] Union of India vs V. It was in pursuance of clause (l) of Article 252 that a Resolution 1150 was passed by the Madras Legislative Council on 7th April 1972 to the effect that "the imposition of ceiling on Urban immovable property" and acquisition thereof in excess thereof of the Ceiling and all matters connected therewith or ancillary thereto should be regulated in the State. [1106 F] The definition of 'family unit ' in section 3(1) is materially in the same terms as the definition of family unit ' In the Andhra Pradesh Act, a divided minor son was not liable to be included in "family unit" as defined in Section 3 (f) but it would be fully applicable in respect of land remaining with a person whether an individual or a family after the operation of the A.P. Act. [111 F] State of Madras vs Valluri Venkatrao, ; , referred to.

The workmen of the appellant company were dismissed from service by the respondent. The workmen 's case was that on a proper enquiry, they should be taken back in employment and the Union could take up the case on merits with the management of the Company. The Tribunal found that the workmen had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence and that was the reason why they were not taken back by the company. Held, that the Tribunal had misdirect ed themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders of the company and also as to its legality of the lock out declared by the Company and as to their legality of lock out. The two Tribunals below have misdirected themselves as regards the true nature of the strike declared by them and also the legality of their lock out held that they were guilty of unauthorised absence and insubordination, etc., and therefore, the company dismissed him. Held further, that on the facts of this case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the discharge and/or suspension of these workmen was justified if not to what relief those men were entitled. The fact that the notice dated August 23, 1953, terminating the services of the workmen and the second notice dated September 17, 1953 operated as a conditional revocation of the earlier notice did not signify an approval of that conduct which rightly came in for a good deal of criticism by the Industrial Tribunal. It was somewhat faintly suggested that if the notice had terminated the services Of the workmen, and the third notice, dated September 18, 1953 , operated as res conditional revocation. The order of suspension, which was certainly a valid order, did not imply an approval on the conduct of the workman prior to August 23.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Urea Kant was appointed as Professor in a department of the Department of Bastany. Dr Bhikalal, Dr. Shiv Sharma, Dr, Sudhakar Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant as well as the University have come in appeal by grant of special leave. The respondents submitted that the selection committee was properly constituted and that the appointment was rightly made as the life of the reserve list was initially for six months and subse quently extended to one year by a resolution of the syndi cate dated 3 12 1983. According to the University this was done in order to curtail the ad hoc appointments and also because the regular selections take a lot of time. It may also be noted that the Syndicate in its meeting held on 10th July, 1978 had resolved as under: i. Every Selection Committee may draw a Re serve List of suitable candidates upto a number not exceeding 50% of the number of posts for which vacancies exist (part vacancy be rounded or to the next whole number) and place them in order of priority; and (ii) The Syndicate by its resolution passed in its resolution dated 3rd December, 1983 decided that the reserve lists recommended by the Selection Committee shall be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extended to another year. According ly the University was done on the recommendations of the Selection Commit tee and appointed Dr. R.Nathawat as Professor. Section 3(1) of the Act of 1974 puts a restriction that no teacher in any university in Rajasthan shall be appointed except on the recommenda tions of the selection Committee constituted thereunder.

The petitioners, owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay, challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The petitioners contended that they had applied through their architect on January 2, 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose by which they proposed to construct on a portion of the land in section No. 9 of the Act. The respondents contended that the application was not bona fide but was mala fide. Held, that sections 4 and 11(3) of the Town Planning act were within the powers conferred by section 13 of the , and the provisions of sections 4 to 16 (both inclusive) would be applicable to the facts of each case. Section 14 of the does not in terms state the grounds on which the permission of the local authority to sanction development work may be withheld, it is clear that the authority had to proceed on the basis of the tentative plan. The preparation of a development plan for Greater Bombay was an immense task and the authorities proceeded with it in a manner to which no exception can be taken. Although section 12 does not state the ground on which permission of local authority could be withheld it is obvious that the Authority had to take into consideration all material available to it including the tentative plans and the final development plan and then make up its mind as to whether a commencement certificate should be granted or not. If the provisions are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases there was little or no scope for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under section 13 Of the Act to guide the competent authority in the exercise of their will and pleasure was met by saying that the restrictions imposed would not be held to be unreasonable. The State Legislature could not pass the Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the schemes were unauthorised and unreasonable and that the powers vested in the Town planning Officer and other authorities under the Act were unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled and as such infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioners under articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g) and 31 of the Constitution.

The petitioners who were displaced persons from Pakistan filed writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution in the High Court of Gujarat and three appeals against the decisions of the High Courts. The main contention was that there was no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which required to be demarcated on the ground. Held, that the claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the International Tribunal an attempt was made to cede any part of the territory which formed part of India before 1948 or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maharao of Kutch, was not legally valid. The dispute related to the boundary between the two States : it was referred as a boundary dispute, the respective claims urged were about the location of the boundary line, and the operative part of that award declared the alignment of the boundaries, which had under the terms of the agreement relating to the procedure for demarcation to be filed by pillars on the alignment. It was not evidence of the fact that it was territory over which the Maha Rao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the State became Indian territory. The area in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind, and apart from the survey maps there is no evidence that it is part of Great Rann or that it has been part of British India. In respect of the Kanjark Sector there was nothing on record to show that it had been part or that its territory was over which, the Mahamad of Kutch passed sovereign rights.
