The fact that the area in dispute was not a part of Kutch State did not affect the question whether the area was part of Part C State before 1948, or was, in any way different from that of the other States.

The mortgagor borrowed Rs. 5,500 from one Rabindra Nath Chakravarty and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount and encum bered his share in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr Bahaldih for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8 per mensem and further agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee did recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bansjuna, Simitan and Bahaldh. By the mortgagedeed the mortgagor also agreed to pay interest at 9% per annum from the date of dispossession of the mortgagees under the two deeds dated June 14, 1922, and August 27, 1922. The mortgagor 's right title and interest in the property was transferred by assignment, sale or otherwise to another person. On May 17, 1927, the mortgagor assigned his interest to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his share of the Zamindari land to one Narendra Nath Chakrabarty and on 10, 1927 the mortgagor conveyed his interest therein to one Moyee Devi. Thereafter in execution of a money decree obtained against the mortgagor ' his right title, title and interests in mauz Bahaldharih was taken by auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. By two deeds the mortgagor created a mortgage in favour of Sasindranath Chakravartity and Indra Nath Chakrawartyto secure payment of Rs, 5,000 advanced to him and interest thereon. The covenants of this mortgage deed were substantially the same as the covenants of the earlier mortgage deed dated June 15, 1922 and it was agreed that the mortgagees were to receive the instalment of royalty payable in Chaitra in respect of Mauza Bahaldpur. By paragraph 4 640 the mortgagor undertook not to transfer or assign Mauzhatas Banshora and simitanr to any person, and had merely assured the mortgagee that he had not assigned the rights in Mauza Bahaudih till the date when the money sued for becomes due. The terms of the two mortgage deeds are substantially thesame and such differences as there are in the covenants have no bearing on the questions to be decided in this appeal. The plaintiff 's suit was for enforcement of payment of money charged upon immoveable property and money sued on the later mortgage had become due on April 14, 1925. By para 13 of the mortgagor agreed that he would pay interest on the amount advanced by him towards the principal and interest due on or after April 14. The term "shall be deemed to be in possession" occurring in section 20 of the Limitation Act means a person liable to pay the debt, or by his duly authorised agent, a fresh period of limitation will be computed from the time when the payment was made. The words "the person liable" in section 2(1) are not defined in the Code but are used in the sense of persons who are actually in possession of the property and who have been in actual possession of it. In order to determine whether a particular person is liable to be proceeded against under section 20, the court must consider the nature of the document, its contents and the surrounding circumstances of each case. The Court has to see whether the document is admissible in evidence for determining the true nature of that document. If the document contains an endorsement on the mortgage deed that it was not possible for the mortgagor to pay a debt within the meaning of section 20 bind the person on whom the interest had devolved, and such payment having been made within twelve years from April 14 , 1925, the plaintiff ' 's claim to enforce the mortgage against the transferee of the equity of redemption is one for compensation and the period of Limitation for a suit to enforce a mortgage is governed by article 132 of the limitation Act.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport facilities which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TLCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month levied for the transported of employees from Chinchvad Village to TTELCo factory at Pimgra and back was levied for transport of employees of Chinchwad Village toTELCO factory at Pushpra and back, and for the Transport facilities provided by the employees of the company. Similarly, for the transportation facilities provided in the employees 's supervisory grades, the appellant averred that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of the arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman contended that even if a nominalcharge is realised from the appellants that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 defines 'public service vehicles ' as follows: "Private Service Vehicle" means any omnibus constructed or adapted to carry more than nine persons excluding the driver and ordinarily used by or on behalf of the owner of such vehicle for the purpose of carrying persons for or in connection with his trade or business, or otherwise than for hire or reward; but does not include a motor vehicle used solely for Police purposes. The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition Moreover, in the instant case, it is not disputed that the transport provided to employees by the appellant could be a public services vehicle in any sense of the term. [362C D] 2.1 In view of what we have already said, it was not necessary for this Court to go into such meticulous details because the legal position appears to be clear enough. As counsel for the appellants has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the employee for providing transport facilities and the point has now become more or less academic. [361E F] 2:2 The Commissioner appears to have dismissed the appeals of the appellants 5 978 SCI/78 as he felt bound by the judgment of the Bombay High Court which had held that the Transport vehicle provided to them by the company would be a 'public services vehicle '.

The appellants, who were the residents of the locality, applied for a licence for a temporary cinema and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate under his order dated 10th February 1976 for a period of six months. The appellants filed an appeal against this order before the State Government which by its order dated 27th December 1977 granted a licence to the third respondent for a quasi permanent cinema under the M.P. Cinemas Regulation Rules, to the fourth respondent Present appellants filed a petition under Article 226 questioning the validity of the aforesaid order of the State Govt conceding inter alia that they were the owners of the premises and that they had objected to the grant/renewal of licence on the ground that there was a mosque a madrasa and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house is to be constructed, and even though their objections were upheld by the licensing authority, the District Magis trate, they were not heard in the appeal preferred by the third respond ent. The State Government did not give any opportunity to the successful objectors and decided the appeal at their back. The order of first respondent State of Madhya Pradesh suffers from the vice of violation of principles of natural justice. The High Court was of the opinion that District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there had been a mosque, and a Temple in the nearby vicinity of the place when the proposed cinema house was to be built, but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a "temporary" licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the state Government, the State Gov ernment on being satisfied that there is no impediment to the granting of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and, therefore, it was not a fit case for interference of the High Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The rules envisage issuance of a licence in compliance with the restrictions or conditions imposed by such licence. Magistrate as the licensing authori ties. Section 5 provides for conditions subject to which licence may be granted. Sub rule (3) of Rule 3 provides that an application for a license shall be accompanied, amongst others, by a copy of the no objection certifi cates issued under Rule 6. Rule 101 confers power on the licensing Authority to grant a "no objection certificate" in respect of the site where the Cinema house is proposed to be located. The Act does not confer any right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing au thority against the grant of a noobjection certificate or a licence as the case may be.

The plaintiff instituted a suit against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated September 2, 1957 the defendant agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the plaintiff accepted the offer of September 2 by their plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 and that this acceptance was communicated to the defendant before November 6, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no concluded contract between the parties and that the suit was not an acceptance of the offer. HELD: The plaint in the present case was not a suit for specific performance. [584 F] Under section 2(6) of the Contract Act if the plaintiff desired to set up a new case that the contract was concluded in November 1957 they should have amended their pleadings accordingly. In re: Pellatt 's Case, , referred to. The defendant made an offer to assign a mining leases. No acceptance was made or communicated to him before hi withdrew the offer and there was nothing to show that the acceptance was not necessary. [585 F] In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. Ordinarily there is no contract unless there is an acceptance or communication of the acceptance.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G Sugar Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955 read with section 7 of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The said complaint was investigated and the appellants were objecting to that investigation on various grounds. They unsuccessfully sought their intervention under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court under article 227 of the constitution. The High Court held that there was no merit in this contention. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 3 of Act came up for consideration for the consideration of this Court in Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , followed. (ii) The power conferred on the Government under section 2(a) of the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 cannot be challenged as invalid. [677 F] (iii) The Central Government was well within its powers in issuing the Sugarcane Control Order, 1956 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III. [67 G H] Ch.Tika Ramji and Ors.v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., ; at page 432; referred to. (iv) The authority altered or amended that law is a competent one. The next contention of the appellants was that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order was issued on 12th January, 1977 which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966, issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order dated 12th December, 1977 inter alia provided as under: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new Industries in the State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. " By an order dated 11th August, 1975, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th February, 1977, the Government of Maharashtra issued another order which stated that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not been prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The aforesaid order dated December 12th, 1977 was challenged before the High Court by the appellants contending that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said order were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the ground that the concession granted by the said Order dated 30th June, 1969 were of no legal effect as there was no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order of 30th May, 1969 was ultra vires and bad in law. On appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) The doctrine of promissory estoppel was not attracted in the instant case because the Government was of Karnataka; (ii) The concession given by the Order dated 12st January,1977 was of no avail as there is no statutory provisions under which any refund could be grant ed; and (iii) The order dated 30.6.1969 was ultra rites and bad inasmuch as it was not mentioned in an order but could be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds is by way of refunds of sales Tax paid to the extent stated in the order. [949C] 1.2 In order to test the validity of the order dated 10th January 1977, one has to see the substance of the concession given under order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by virtue of refunds, although in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellants.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to A 6 were however found guilty for the offences punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 3. The appellants contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 149 and on applying 149 I 1.P .C. cannot be sustained. It was argued that the appellants being three in number, could not have formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.; that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime; and that the High court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction under Sections 149 and 302 on applying149 I.I.P., on the ground that they formed an assembly alongwith some unidentified person. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants acted in the forefront of their common intention of murdering the de ceased. [8C] 1.2 There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants that after acquittal of 4 accused persons, by the Courts below, the conviction cannot be sustain. It is not the prosecution case that apartfrom the seven appellants there were other unified persons who are involved in t he crime. The High Court clearly fell in error in confirmed the convic tion and sentence.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house for the same price of RS. 16500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was completed in the normal course and in this assessment no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by the assessee at the same prices at which it was purchased and no capital gain accrued or arose to him as a result of the sale. On 4th April 1968 however, the Income tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for that year. The assessee submitted a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice and contended that there was no under statement A of consideration in respect thereof in respect whereof the transfer was effected by the assesee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. 48,500 to tax on sub section (2) of section 52 and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration for the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transferred exceeds the full value of consideration declared by the assesses in respect Of the transfer by an amount of not less than 15% of the value so declared. The Income tax Officer rejected this contention and issued a demand notice under Section 148 of that Act seeking reopen the order for reopening the assessment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the view taken by him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the transaction in question was perfectly honest and bonafide; (2)(a) there should have been under statement in respect o the transfer or to put it differently, the actual consideration received for the transferred was 'considerably more ' than that declared or shown by the assis tant, but which were not covered by sub section(1), because the transferee was not directly or indirectly connected with the assessee; (b) there was under statement a consideration in regard to the transfer; and (c) there had been under declaration of consideration. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The object and purpose of sub section 2 of section52 is to avoid or reduce the liability of the asses see to tax for transferring his capital asset for a consideration lesser by 15% or more than the fair Market value and that would constitute unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the assesses under Article 19(1)(f) which fundamental right was in existence at the time when sub section was enacted. [653C D] 2. The two circulars of the Central Board of Direct Taxes referred to above must therefore be held to be binding on the Revenue in the administration or implementation of sub s.(2) and this sub Section must be read as applicable only to cases where there is under statement Of the consideration in question in respectof the transfer, and the burden of proving that there is such under statement is on the revenue. Once it is established by the Revenue, that the consideration for transfer has been understated or, to put the assessee differently, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gains or any other type of income. [557D F] 3.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P. Tambe and section P. Gaydhani. D.P. Tambbe (P.W. 2), a businessman, said that he had gone. to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination, he stated that he did not know whether it was a foodgrain shop. He said that there was some talk between the complainant and the accused. The appellant 's explanation was more credible, but the prosecution case was that the Til seeds sold were unfit for human consumption. The trial court held that the purpose for which the Til plants were kept was immaterial. On appeal by the State, HELD: (1) It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. Even if this be true, it is not so widely known a fact that we could take judicial notice of it. [330 D] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. (2) The use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. It is quite unsafe to base the appellant ' s conviction on such shaky foundations. [334 C E] Bhagwan Dass etc. vs Delhi Admn., ; , referred to. (4) In order to judge whether the Food Inspector 's version or the accused 's explanations was more reliable, it must be resolved (1 ) A. 1. R. , followed and (5) The appellant must get the benefit of that doubt.

The appellant, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to him on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17 6 1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; , in support of the contention that the suit was barred by limitation. The Division Bench dismissed the plaintiff 's suit on the ground that it has not been file within three year from the said date when the cause of Action first arose and as required by Article 58, the High Court could not exercise its jurisdiction or was it one pending at the commencement of the Constitution and the revisional order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. The appellant 's counsel placed before this Court the residuary Article 113 and has referred to a few decisions of some High Courts where in a 47 situation as reliance was also placed on that Article. It is unnecessary to refer to those decisions as on the authority of the judgment of this court in Sitaram Sahu vs The State of Orissa & Ors. , ; , it must be held that Article 113 of the Act of 1963, corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act, is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies. The fate of this appeal rests upon the finding as to when the right to sue first accrued. All the three Courts have accepted the position that on 1st March, 1966 when the order was made by the Collec tor, the right of sue first accrues and the appellant ' s suit was one to obtain a declaration of that the said order was inoperative. The appeal was therefore dismissed in limine. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: (1) Article 113 is a special kind and the reasoning in that case would not apply to the facts of the present case. [47F] (2) It is appropriate to notice the provision regarding limitation under Section 21 of the , which prescribes a period of one year for making of the application and power of condonation of delay of a total period of six months has been vested under sub section (3). The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father, and several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in them covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well. Held, that the decision of the High Courts was correct. The word "decision" in article 133(1) should mean not a part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision on that part of it must be considered as a whole. If there is a variation made in the appellate decree in the decision Of the trial Court, then such variation would not affect the character of the appellate judgment. The principle of affirmance on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance or variation by the appeal court as an act of adjudication and that necessarily means the decision. of the appeal Court on the merits is that a party aggrieved by a decree may appeal only against a part Of it and is not bound to file an appeal against the whole of the decree; but if there is no such variation in regard to the order as to costs such a variation would affect the nature of the original appellate decree. The applicant then applied for leave to appeal to the Privy Council and urged that the decree passed by the High court on appeal was not a decree of affirmence and since the test of the value of the subject matter was satisfied, he was entitled to go to the High ' Court even if there was a difference in favour of the intending appellant. Held further, that in construing the clause it is obviously necessary to bear in mind that the clause under discussion deals with the constitutional right of the litigant to make an appeal to this Court; and so it would be inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the material words used in the relevant clause. The decision of this Court undoubtedly supports the conclusion that the word "decree" must mean not only a partof the decree but the whole or of the judgment, then it would also be reasonable to hold that the words "judgment, decree or final order appealed from" denote that part.

The High Court of Allahabad, in revision petition under section 115 Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, held that a revision petition filed by the appellant against an order of the District Judge under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act was not maintainable against a revisional order under section 24 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court possesses revisional jurisdiction under section 114 in a case arising out of original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000 and above; and (ii) the District Court alone has jurisdiction under Section 115 in respect of cases arising out out of an original suit instituted before 20th September 1972. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was not vested with revisional jurisdiction by section 115, Code of civil Procedure over a revisional Order made by the District court under that section. [39B] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Courts were not vested in the District Courts. The hierarchy of remedies enacted in the Provincial Civil Courts Act represents a complete and final order of remedies, and it is not possible to proceed outside the Act to avail of a superior remedy provided by another statute. [40C D] 2:2 In determining whether the Legislature intended a further revision petition to the High court, regard must be had to the principle that the construction given to a statute should be such as would advance the object of the legislation and suppress the mischief sought to be cured by it.

The respondents, who owned Khasra No. 383 area 14 bighas 16 biswas situate in village Madrampura on the outskirts of Jaipur city, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for the acquisi tion of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose namely for implementation of a development scheme viz. Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The said notice was duly served on the respondents and they appeared before the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur and filed their reply dated September 8, 1975. In the reply, the respondents while denying the existence of a public purposes for acquisition of the lands under section52(1), asserted that they needed the said land to start new businesses in the State , to open a branch office at Jaipur and to construct residential quarters for their Director and other Senior Executives , but at a later stage they alleged that they wanted to construct a Three Star Hotel on the said lands. The Special Officer by his order dated April 9, 1976 held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really not needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition. The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section 53(1 ) of the Act could not be issued till February 8 , 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction ,of a Three star Hotel on an area of 6,000 square yards as their real objects was to get it released from the acquisition. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action neither wholly or in part arose within the territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court and therefore the learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition filed by the respondents under Article 227 of the constitution or to make the ad interim exparte prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the land acquired. [605C D] 2. The impugned orders passed by the learned single Judge of the High Court dated March 13 , 1984 issuing a rule on the application filed by respondents under article 226 of ' the Constitution and the ad hoc prohibitory order made by him are set aside and the proceedings before the Calcutta high Court are quashed.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction and for arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite. The appellant contended that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the new Rent Act, that it was covered by the new rent Act, and that the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Additional District Judge that the premises in question will be deemed to have been completed on 1st October 1971, the date of assessment of house tax and water tax held that the buildings were not ten years old on the date when the revision came to be decided by the High Court and, accordingly, the new Act had no application to the building. The Additional District judge negatived the defence and decreed the suit for ejectment as also for recovery of arrears of rents and damages. On appeal, the High court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about the arrears of the rent. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the new tenancy Act had not been applied to the premises during the pendency of the litigation and, consequently, the benefit of section 39 of the Act could be given to the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit under section 39(2), there was a change in the cause of action. [338B] 1.2 In order to appreciate the contention of the parties it will be relevant at this stage to refer to section 20 of the old Rent Act. It pertinently reads: "2. Exemption from operation of Act. (I) nothing in this Act shall apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores. After the works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948 they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 Of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held, that the copy of the Award which was sent to the Government would have been insufficiently stamped. The document in court was unstamped or insufficiently stampable document actually produced in Court and that the law did not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents. The law is no doubt well settled that the copies of an instrument cannot be validated, That was held in The State of Madras vs M/s. Karamchand Thapar & Bros., ; , referred to. Held further, also, that it was not necessary to examine whether the agreement which was executed by the arbitrator to refer to arbitration was covered by item 2 or item 12 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.

The respondent, a Superintending Engineer in the Public Works Department, Punjab was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase and sale of sign Boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In that meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The aforesaid First Information Reports were challenged by the Respondent in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 5837 M/85 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the respondent found favour with the High court which relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Haryana quashed the First Information report by its order dated February 12, 1986. Mangal Singh Minhas, the Respondent, in Criminal Appeal Nos. 423 24/1988 was posted in the Industrial Supply Section of the Directorate of Industries where various types of raw materials including wax and import lincences were dealt with. A First Information FIR was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the Respondents pertaining to purchase of the sign boards. vigilance inquiry was instituted against the respondents under sub section (1), and (ii) of section 5 of Prevention of corruption Act. In pursuance of these complaints, the Vigilance Department had initiated departmental enquiry against the Appellant for the offences punishable under sections 161, 165A, 165B, 165C, 165D, 165E, 165F, 165G, 165H, 165I, 165N, 165, 165 and 165A of the Indian Penal Code. The Respondents contended that Rule 2(2) was not applicable to the facts of the case because the same had been lodged after three years of his retirement; and that since the prosecution against the accused was quashed by the High Courts in view of Rule 3.2, the First F.I.R. was quashed. PG NO 919 The High Court allowed the Criminal Miscellaneous Petition filed by the Respondents.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 100 each and the issued and paid up capital was 2,500 ordinary and 3 1,000 equity share shares. Under the Articles of Association of the Company, both preference and ordinary shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the respondent company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the assessee company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on preference shares and 61 per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act. As it stood at the material time no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested, the respondent Company was one in which, the public are substantially interested. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order and the Tribunal also held that the respondent was one In which the Public were substantially con tended, but on different grounds. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) Where there is no individual member or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding fifty one per cent or more of the voting power, which controls the working of a company, it is from its very nature a company in Which there is any controlling member or group and therefore the public is substantially interested; (ii) where a shareholder holds or a Group of shareholders act in concert, the company would be regarded as one in whom the public arc substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the public, shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. (iii) Where not less than twenty five per cent Of the voting right are held by persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed percentage of the shares are vested in persons other not directly interested in such accumulation; it matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to the ordi nary shareholders or is accumulated and therefore in assessing whether the twenty five percent of the votes are vested In persons other, than the control group, shares yielding fixed rate have to he ignored. (iv) Where a shareholder holding or a member holds or group of shares acting in com prising concert hold fifty one cent or less of the controlling groups, the share yielding a specified rate of dividends has to be ignored; but for the purpose of ascertaining the voting powers, voting rights attached to all the shares must be taken into account. No investigation has been made by the Income 8 tax Department whether there is a group or persons controlling the working in the company. It is true that Ramayamma was holding 87 40 per cent share of the ordinary shares issued by the company and there is obviously no person who could hold twenty five% or more or less than 25 per cent, of the Ordinary shares. In order to attract section 23A it must be exercised only by the or dinary shareholders, and not by shareholders entitled to fixed rate Of dividend. The presumption under the Explanation cannot arise if regard be had to the terms of the Explanation. 51 section C 2 18 but even that argument is of no value, for twenty five one per percent of such voting power is not exercisable by the Public. (v) In the present case, as already observed, the preference shareholders were enti tled to vote in the meeting and the Articles had no application because no presumption on the facts found could arise thereunder.

The first appellant was a registered joint stock company. The first appellant 's selling agents were del credere agents and guarantee payment to the first appellant of all sales made and on the other side guarantee delivery to the purchasers with whom they deal direct. It was necessary for it to appoint a local agent in Bombay for making payments and receiving delivery. There was some confusion about the agent so appointed; at first one Dharsi Moolji was appointed and then P. C. The letter informed the first appel lant that he had effected a sale, (2) the selling agent had paid the first Appellant for the goods, (3) specific bales had been set aside and appropriated to the sale and consequently the property in the goods had passed, (4) the goods having actually left the Mills ' premises, and (5) they were in the Dady Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadas Khetan & Company. The appellant was convicted under sections 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act on two counts. Held, that the charge on the second count relating to the 6 bales is a similar one and the facts follow the same pattern. They have been detailed in the High Court 's judgment and they cannot be said to have concerned themselves with the question of actual physical possession because they say: " It would not be correct to say that there had been anything beyond a technical and unintentional breach of the law. Dwarkadash Khetan & Co. vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, A.I.R. (1954) S.C. 940, relied on.

The respondent was a Senior Lecturer in the Government College. He was alleged to have accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ other than legal remuneration for showing favour to a candidate Jayendra Jayantilal Shah by giving him more marks than he deserved in the Physics practical examination. It was stated that he had obtained that amount through Thakkar. Dwivedi was charged with offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with Section 114 of the Indian Penal code. The Special Judge who tried both these persons found them guilty of the offence with which they were charged. He imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1,000/ . Both the convicted persons filed appeals to the High Court. The High Court held that even an Examiner was a public servant and as regards section 161 Indian Penal Procedure Code it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public Servant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that (i) the ninth clause of section 21 of the Penal Code was wider when it came to the case of an officer who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty; (ii) the amendment made in 1964 and in particular the addition of the words "by the Government" in sub cl. (a) showed the legislative interpretation of the material portion of clause as it stood before the amendment under consideration; (iii) the omission of these words show that the clause was wider than when it had come to the respondent case of a University Examiner which, at every other appropriate Place, the word "Government" was to be found in the Ninth clause; and (iv) the use of corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1) case. HELD : (i). The words "corrupt" and "otherwise" refer to means other than corrupt or unlawful by which a public person may abuse his position. [327 C] (ii). The word "otherwise " refers to the other than "public servants". The word is not restricted to "any other kind of public servant". It is only used in relation to the obtaining of a bribe. [317 D E] (iii). The use of the word 'otherwise" in section 5 of the Act shows that the word is wider when the words are dropped "and every officer in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated By fees or commission or commission, for the purpose of any public duty by the Government who would fall within the definition of a "public servant". [317 E F] (iv). The expression 'corrupt ' is not defined in the Act. It has been used to denote a wide connotation and it includes all persons who are remunerated. The word ' otherwise ' refers to other than public servants. The words 'corruption ' and illegal means 'or 'by otherwise ' form a single clause and do not form two clauses. If that is so, the abuse of position as a public employee would be essential. [320 A B] (v).

The petitioners, who were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway, filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the claim of the petitioners. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents challenging the claims of the petitioner. According to them five out of forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasisis. One of them has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984 project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. A number of documents and circulars issued on January1, 1984 have been produced in support of their claim. The senior Signal and Telecom Engineer, (Powerignalling) filed a Counter affidavit on his behalf stating that they are project employees and do not belong to the Open line. According ly to him employees in the Open Line acquire temporary status on completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. That status is acquired on completion by casual labour in Project Works as provided in the scheme formulated under orders of this Court, though such status were acquirable by project casual labour on completionof 180 days of continuous employment previously. The respondents have placed reliance on the definition of 'Project ' which means: "a project should be taken as construction of new lines, major projects, restoration of dismantled lines and major important open line works, line doubling, widening of tunnels etc. which are completed within a definite time limit". The Senior Personal Signal& Telecom Engineer has filed an affidavit on the behalf of respondents challenging their claim of these petitioners. According tO them five Out of forty eight petitioners in the group of Writ Petitions had undergone Medical examination and they were granted permanent status asKhallasarsis. It is stated that out of the forty four Petitioners in this batch of writ petition have undergone medical Examination and were also granted temporary Status as Khalasis. The Junior Signal, & Telecom Engineers (Power) has also filed a rejoinder affidavit. At the hearing of the applications, counsel for the petitioners as also the learned Additional Solicitor General were given full opportunity of placing their arguments and documents. In addition, they have also furnished written submissions. 141 It is contended on behalf o the Administration that out Of forty four five petitioners in Writ Petitions have undergone Medical Examination and are granted temporary benefits as Koshallasamis.

The Forward Markets Commission, which was recognised by the Central Government under a. 6 of the Forward Markets Regulation Act 1952, issued a notification closing out all contracts of February 1956 and May 1956 Settlements at the rates mentioned in the said notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the grounds (1) that the Forward Market Commission could not, having regard to the terms of the statute under which it was created, be a proper recipient of the power with which it purported to do under the amended bye law 52AA; and (2) that it was beyond the powers of the Association to have conferred the power which it had purported to exercise under the unamended bye law. Held, that the notification dated January 24, 1956, by the Forward Marketing Commission was illegal and the appellants would be entitled to the issue of a writ of mandamus in the terms prayed for. The notification dated February 24, 1955, issued by the Board was illegal as it did not confer any power on the Central Govern ment under section 12 of the Act to make bye law with retrospective effect and, therefore, the new bye law made on January 21, 1956 in so far as it purported that it intended to operate retrospectively was invalid. The words "by or under this Act" in section 4(f) of the , are wide enough to include a rule made in exercise of the powers conferred by the Act, for if the said phrase takes in a rule, the word "prescribed" becomes redundant. If a rule was not comprehended by the phrase "under the Act", it would be illogical to hold that it would take in a bye law and would take effect only those contracts which were entered into after the date on which the byelaw came into operation and that if he was right in this construction, the impugned notification had gone beyond the power conferred on the Commission by the new Bye law.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts of dividend received by the assessee from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received, showed that the amount of compensation was deemed to be capital gain. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to land acquisition compensation received by it for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948, was not in the hands of the company receipt of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. HELD : (i) The assumption made that the entire amount of compensa tion is deemed to he capital gain cannot be sustained. [35 F] (ii) In appeals Nos. 737 to 739 of 1968 and 13 of 1968 which arose out of Reference No. 131 of 1961 and other references, decided by this Court on July 25, 1969, the only question of law raised was whether distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable. The scope of enquiry in this group of cases is more extensive. In appeals No. 737 of 1968, the High Court had to decide on the facts of each case 35 whether any amount of salami was capital gain and whether any part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains.

The Kerala Forest Act, 1961 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The Kerala Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to protect forest produce and regulates possession of the forest produce failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers, it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (or contravention thereof. As said earlier the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under Section 2(f)(i) of the Act. The High Court quashed the complaint holding that Sandals Wood Oil are forest produce within the meaning of section 2(g) (1). Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression wood oil is a technical and part of inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense and in an exhaustive manner. It cannot be restricted in a narrow circumference as was done by the learned Single Judge so as to defeat the object and purpose of the Kerala Forest (Amendment) Act, 1992. Extraction of tendu leaves even by mechanised process would nonetheless be a wood Oil. He laid emphasis on the word 'timber ' defined in Section 2 (k) of The Act is an inclusive definition. It is settled law that the word "wood oil" used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [503B C] 1.2 The expression ' wood oil ' is generally used as a word of extension. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning Of the words or pharases occuring in the body of the Statute. The restricted meaning sought to put up by the accused would frustrate the object of the statute and the literal interpretation would defeat the purpose. [506D E] 1:3 The Kerala Forests Act, 1963 incorporated in its definition of forest produce Sandal wood oil after the word `wood oil ' and the legislature in Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu, like the Act, do not specifically incorporate Sandal timber in the definition of Forest Produce. From this could it be concluded that if it be otherwise interpretable, that wood oil would not include Sandal trees as well. to mean wood oil oleo resin from Dipterocarpus alatus (family Dipteracumocarpuce), a tree of India and other regions of Southern Asia. Khori in his 'Materia Medica of 504 India and theirrapeutics ' and Pharmacaignhia Indica by Willim Dymock defined wood oil in the same strain. All these technical literatures were concerned in finding out physio chemical properties contained in wood oil and the source from which they are drawn for use in industrial purposes.

The prosecution alleged that the canal after a temporary closure restarted flowing on May 5, 1953. The diggi was filled up by 1 p.m. on the 7th and 8th of the village diggi (pond) with the consent of the two deceased who was in all probability not there. The accused were tried for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused but convicted them under section302 read with s 34 and awarded transportation for the life. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so. Surajpal Singh vs State of Punjab ; , referred to. The evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference could be drawn from it. The second point on which the judgment of the High court is assailed is the lack of compelling reasons, for setting aside the judgment Of acquittal. This Court has held that the view of this Court in Stephen Seneviratne vs The King (A.I.R. 1954 section C. 28 859 was not correct to say that the opinion of these authors were given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before it nor is this a satisfactory way of disposing of the evidence of an expert unless, the passages which are sought to discredit his opinion are put to him. This court has held in Stephen seneviratiatne 's case that the accused was guilty of the offence and convicted them.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Dhanbad, the com pany and the said workmen represented by their union called the Indoxco Labour Union, Jamshedpur, regarding the matters specified in their joint applications dated 7 9 1963 annexed hereto. The dispute was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said Indox co labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and Indox Co Labour Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the company wherever they may be stationed". The Tribunal also awarded that the union 's representatives should be given special leave to attend the law courts for matters connected with the workers and the management, to attend to annual conventions of their federation, to attending to Executive Committee meeting of the union federation and convention of central organisation i. e., INTUC." The appellant company challenged the award on the ground that it had amended its constitution on January 6 1963 and therefore as the reference was in October 1964, i. after the said amendment, the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal 's award would cover them also. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant special leave demanded by the Union. [522 D] (2) The company 's contention that it cannot be called upon to pay for overtime work anything more than its ordinary rate of wages if the workmen do work beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours a week, is without substance. The company would in that case be indirectly increasing the hours of work and consequently altering its conditions of service. If after taking into consideration the fact of comparatively higher scale of wages prevailing in the appellant 's Company the Tribunal fixed the rate for overtime worked at 1 1/4 times the ordinary rate. [544 E] (3) The workmen get various types of paid leave. As the figures of such leave are not correctly stated in the award, it is impossible to say that the Tribunal erred in doing so or acted unjustly.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1939 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into a partnership to carry on in the name of M/s Hakam Mal Tani Mal. The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44, the assessee contended that the firm had ceased to be a business at the commencement of the Indian income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 and that it succeeded to the business on April 1, 1943 after Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into force relief under section 25(4) was not admissible. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm was in March, 1943 and that firm alone was entitled to relief under s.25(4). On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the assessee was at the time of dissolution of the firm and that the business in timber which was carried on by that firm was taken over by the assesseee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The instrument of partnership in the first instance recites that the accounts were settled upto March 31, 1939 and upto March31, 1939. It is then recited that all the partners had become separate from April 1 1939. [655 B] (ii) The recitals in the instrument that the account were settled up to March 31 1939, and that, the partners have become separate would imply that the partnership was continued for the whole or a part of the day on April I, 1939, or it may mean that from the end of March 31. 1939 there had been separation.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. The Secretary to the Regional transport Authority called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the issue of the permit, respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the appeal holding that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the issue was made beyond the prescribed period of time under rule 119; and (ii) the grant of the permits was made within the prescribed time of limitation. HELD: The appeals before the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the further appeal to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order granting the permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State Road Transport Appellate tribunal. [641 D] The High Court was, therefore not right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. Although arguments were addressed on behalf of counsel with regard to old rule 151 and rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules 1963, it did not appear that there is any error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunal in interfering with the grant or granting the permits.

The appellant was the sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates, Prakash Vir Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 34,274 votes. The Congress candidate respondent No. 1 filed an election petition challenging the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. At the hearing of the appeal the appellant appeared in person after counsel on his behalf had obtained leave of this Court to withdraw and to allow the appellant to appear in person. The various corrupt practices on which the appellant relied relate to occurrences at six places. The appellant did not press the other occurrence. The first occurrence relates to a meeting held at Hapur Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on 7 February 1967. The respondent was not called upon to state as to whether there was a meeting on 6 February, 1967. On the question whether there is a contract between the parties and it was alleged by the appellant with reference to two letters that the letters would indicate some of the terms of the transaction. HELD : (i) There was no evidence that the assault was by the workers of Prakash Vir Gandhi. The allegations were that on 2 February,1967 an election meeting was organised in support of the candidature of the appellant 'and the supporters of respondent No 1 Prakash Vir Singh created disturbance with the result that the meeting could not be continued and the supporters were alleged to have chased the appellant. [895 F G] (ii) The publication in the newspaper 'Vir Arjun ' Exhibit 22 was an appeal on behalf of respondent Prakash Virar Shastri. As long as the publication is not tainted by corrupt practice, such an appeal will not be an infraction of the provisions as to corrupt practices. [900 D E] (iii) There is no evidence of any report having been made by the respondent to the Election Commissioner or the police about the alleged occurrence. The publication was in the newspapers 'Vilir Arjun Exhibit 22 is to the effect that differences between Hindus and Harijans were being spread by the supporters. The statements in exhibit 22 do not make any reflection on the moral or mental nature of the respondent. [901 F] (iv) There are no evidence to show that the appellant was made by respondent No 2 to be published with the consent of the candidate or his election agent. It is highly improbable that two meetings of the two rival candidates were held at the Hapur Town Hail Maidyan at Hapur. The witnesses on behalf, of the respondents were D.W. 25 and D. W.D.W., who spoke of the report of 3 February 1967 and a report of 9 February 1967 relate to the alleged incident of 2 February 1967 at Chhajjupur. It was highly improbable, that two meeting of 898 the two contesting candidates, namely, Prakashvir Shastri and his supporters would both be held on the same date and at the same place. Fifthly, the reports which were lodged by the appellants with regard to the attack on the office of the Republican Party do not mention or refer at all to any meeting on behalf or of respondent Ram Vir Shastri on 7 2 February1967 at the Town HallMaidan Hapur throw light on this aspect. These three documents indicate that the meetings which was held on 7th February 1967 were a meeting organised by the leaders of the Congress party.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh, since deceased, the predecessorin interest of the appellants, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and by another judgment debtor Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an appli cation under Order XXII Rule 95 of the C.P.C. for setting it aside the order dated December 12, 1980 of the executing court, which was opposed by the judgment debtors on the ground that as the application was filed more than two years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . The District Judge held that in view of Article 136 of the , an application for setting t aside the auction purchaser auction purchaser for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him was maintainable and not barred by time. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the Judgment debtor under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code. In this appeal on certificate granted by the Court, it is contended that Article 136 would apply to an application made under Order XX1 Rule 95 CPC by one Nagammal who claimed under a possessory mortgage and that claim was allowed on June 14, 19, 13, 20 and 21 respectively. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The period of limitation prescribed by Articles 136 and 134 is for two different purposes, the former being for the execution of a decree for possession in respect of which decree is passed and the latter for an applicationfor delivery of posses sion of immovable property which is purchased in the course of execution of decree. An application for deliv ery of possession can be made within one year from the date on which sale became absolute as prescribed by Article 180 of that Act, but under Article 136 such an application can be filed within one ye ars from the day on which the sale becomes absolute. [362F] Chandra Mani Mani vs Shri Chandra Mani, ; , referred to. 2.1 The period for delivery Of possession of property purchased at the court sale has been reduced to a considerable extent but that also cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of interpretation of the provisions of the Limitation Act. [361G H; 362A] Chandramani Mani vs Sri Chandra Mani & Ors., ; , relied on.

The appellant was the candidate of a political party. The first respondent filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that he had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The High Court held that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the ambit of Section 100(1)(d) of Act and were sufficient to uphold the election. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the first respondent had stated in his petition that the pamphlet was printed and distributed with a view to create false impression among the elector ate that he was a murderer; (ii) the evidence showed that the poster was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the appel lant with his knowledge and consent; and (iii) the High Court had erred in holding that both the acts amounted taults within the mischief of Section 83(4). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The first Respondent and his workers would not have failed to do so had the posters been pasted at the time alleged by them. [776F] 1.2 In the petition there is no reference to the Election agent in this connection anywhere and the reference to Chief Agent cannot be construed as a reference to him. What is further, he has also in his examinatiOn in chief gone to the extent of saying that even when exhibit P1 was pasted near exhibit P 14, a day prior to election, he had seen the actual pasting. This, of course, he retracted in his cross examination when he stated that he has not seen the said act of pasting and that he did not know who pasted exhibit P 1 at exhibit P14 though in examination chief he has categorically stated that it was done with the knowledge and the consent of the election agent.

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, Byramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., in 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown in the residential zone and a contiguous parcel of land was entered as green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the respondent Corporation submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star hotel on an tract of Land measuring 44.820.50 square yards. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. The appellants contended that the whole of the land should be kept reserved for a green belt or recreational ground in the interest of general public; that the entire land should he kept reserved to be kept open for a Green belt or recreation ground in its interest of the general public and that the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of section 46. The Respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of Municipal Corporation rejecting the plan submitted by the Respondent Company after hearing the appellants as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the Plan on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the Planning Authority. The respondent No 2, however filed a writ petition challenging the legality of the order dated 25.7.1978 granted sanction of plan submitted for the constructions of a hotel on the said plot. The Writ Petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that in granting exemption to the respondent Company, the authority concerned has violated the relevant guidelines and also the provision of section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act; that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors; that in giving exemption on the ground of availability of 75,000 sq.

The respondents, who were in service of the appellant employer, filed two complaints against the employers for alleged unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court dismissed the complaints. The Union thereupon filed these appeals by special leave. 66 At the hearing of the appeals, it was contended on behalf of the employers that the industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. Dismissing the appeals ^ HELD: 1. When it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure of an industrial activity, the Industrial Court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practices must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [68H; 69A] 2. When the suspension of work is ordered it would constitute lock out. On the other hand closure implies closing of industrial activity as a consequence of which workmen are rendered jobless. 22(2) of the ID Act prohibits an employer in a public utility service from locking out any of his workmen without giving notice as provided therein. 23 prohibits an employee from declaring a lock out in any of the eventualities mentioned therein. [69B] 3. The closure implies closure of industrial activities as a result of which workman are rendered jobsless. [70C D] 4. When once it is alleged that the respondent has resorted, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a deviceor pretence. Therefore the correct approach ought to be that when it is sought claimed that he is not guilty of imposing a lockout but has closed the industrial activities, the industrial court before which the action of the respondent is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the stage of closure decide and determine whether such closure was bona fide one or was a devices or a pretence to determine services of the workmen. [71E F] 5.

The assessee company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which were set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The Income tax Officer rejected the plea of the assessee company that it was a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties under a misapprehension and without appreciation of the correct facts. On appeal by the assessee to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal and upheld the order of the Income tax officer. The assessee company then applied to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act for a reference of the following questions of law: " (i) Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the assessee Company can be treated as a dealer or an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and (ii) whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, security and immovable property of the asses company can be taxed as business profits. The High Court rejected the assessee 's plea that it had never carried on any business in the purchase or sale of share securities, securities or properties in support of its contention. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (i). It is only in regard to a finding of fact that the question can be properly framed "as to whether there was material to support the said finding. [52 E] (ii). The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law and what was the legal effect of the facts found by the Tribunal and whether as a result, the asses see can be termed a dealer. [53 F G] In dealing with the findings on such questions of mixed law and fact the High court must not have taken into account the primary evidentiary facts but its ultimate form is determined by the application of relevant legal principles. To put it differently, the proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore the claim of the assesses that the profits or losses arising therefrom from the sales of shares etc., cannot be taxed. [54 F] G.
