On the last occasion it was pointed out by this Court that the questions actually framed by this court on the last occasions are not appropriate and (1) 54 do not reflect the real controversy between the parties. It is therefore, expedient in the interest of justice that the High Courts should modify the questions framed by the High courts on the first occasion and call upon the Appellate Tribunal to make a fresh statement of the cases.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On August 22, 1950 when judgment was still pending, the Government passed an order placing the appellant on suspension until further orders. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953 and the enquiry into the charges against him was without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the order passed by the High court on January 28 of 1954, was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 of the Constitution. It was also not correct to say that the High Courts had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final order of the Government. The order passed on January 29, 1954 was merely an one of suspen sion pending final proceedings by the State Government and such order was not one of dismiss ment or removal from Service within article 310 of the constitution. It could not be said that the conclusion reached by the Tribunal in the present case was erroneous. Rule 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Rules, which came into operation on October 1. 1953, was as follows: " In rule 4 of these rules, the proviso occurring after sub rule (2) shall be omitted and in lieu thereof, the following sub rule shall be inserted, namely: (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub rule(1) or sub rule 2), the following cases shall not be referred to the Tribunal, namely : (i) cases arising in the Judicial Department; (ii) Cases arising against Government servants in the subordinate ranks of the Police forces of the rank of Sub Inspector and below, unless the cases are against them together with officers of higher ranks. " By reason of this amendment which is expressly retrospective in character, the main ground of objection on which the application of the appellant was founded, was no longer tenable.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. was a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The National Bank of India Ltd., obtained probate of Gannon 's will in theUnited Kingdom and appointed the respondent as the executor to administer the estate in British country. It applied for and obtained in India on August 14, 1946, letters of administration "durante absentia" to the estate of Gannonka and the name of Gannonrani reciting that he had reason to believe that Anderson 's income assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949 had escaped assessment. The Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed in respect of the shares held by a shareholder, but included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeals, the Tribunal held that the respondent was not liable to pay tax on receipt of income due to the deceased, notwithstanding that he died while assessment proceedings were pending, because the proceedings could not be continued and the assessment could not therefore be made after the tax payer 's death. The High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. With special leave, Held: (i) The legal personality of a deceased person cannot vote on behalf of the shareholder and may not become a director of the company on the strength of the representation alone; (ii) where the income was notional as under section 23A the legal personality or of the deceased must be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed to have been received by the legal representatives of the dead person. [557 D] (iii) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax or any other tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died. [511 E] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City II vs Shakumtala and others, ; , followed.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State of Baster to the Government and to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government was of the opinion that it fit. The appellant was not assessed to land revenue but this was denied on behalf of the State. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler for purposes other than the Constitution. The ordinary dictionary meaning of maufi is "Released, exempted, exempt from the payment of rent or tax, rent free" and maufidar is "A holder of rent free land, a grantee". It was common ground in the High Court that the villages in question were exempt from payment of 'rent or tax. The burden was on the appellant to prove this fact which he never attempted to discharge. It was impossible therefore to accept this contention on behalf Of the appellant. The onus was on him to prove the fact which the appellant never attempted and which he had never attempted. The High Court rightly held that the contention of the appellant in this respect could not be accepted. The question whether the villages mentioned in Schedules A and B of the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution fell within the category of Estates or Alienated lands but they did fall within the categories of Mahals.

The respondent was a Garden Curator in the Office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Bastaghatti. The respondent challenged his transfer before the Central Administrative Tribunal. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the Central Government, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He contended that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. The learned Single Member of the Tribunal recorded the following finding: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the transfer order No. BSI. 80/5/80 Estt. dated 29.1.1991 in respect of applicant S.L.Abbas was malafide and liable to be quashed". The Union of India preferred this appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued by the Government on the subject do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order of transfer is vitiated by mala fides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued on the Subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees." [419H; 432A B] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306, followed. Bank of india vs Jagjit singh Mehta [1991] 1 SCC 305, referred to.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A4 armed with lathis, A1 armed with an iron rod, A6 with a lathi (bil hook), attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [3B] 2. The intention of the appel lants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., read with section 34, IPC.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs 3.00,000, Rs.7,00,00 and Rs.80,000 advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. It may be noticed that the Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, and the sum of RS.80 lakhs was admittedly advanced by way of loan by the bank after its nationalisation. The respondent firm owned certain motor vehicles which were mentioned in A and Schedules to the plaint of the said suit. The Bank had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, also created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of E Schedule properties of the plaint. Section Doranna Choudhary, since the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, while denying the creation of the mortgages contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank had been nationalised or formed under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 promulgated on July 19, 1969 and the present Banking Companies Act only ratifies the already created Bank under the said Ordinance, the appellant Bank was not, therefore, formed or created under any special Indian law. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements denying the existence of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos.4 to 12. The trial court decreed the suit against them but the High Court in appeal held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour by the respondent Bank and, accordingly dismissed the suit filed by the appellant bank. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even assuming that the expression `special Indian law ' means a law enacted by the British Parliament specially for India, that the Banking companies Act is a special law enacted under the British parliament; that the said words mean a special Indian Law enacted by an Act of British Parliament for India. It was not disputed that the banking Companies Act is not a `special law ' but by or under a `Special Indian law, that is, the Banking Corporations Act. It is also not disputed in this case that the loans were advanced by Bank to its firm under the cash credit Account opened in favour and by Nagpur Pioneer Insurance Company Limited, Bombay, admittedly before the creationof the Corporation under the and it was held by this Court that the words `special ' Indian law" are placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom ' and before the words "Royal Charter or Letters Patent" it must be held in view of the setting that the expressions `specialIndian law ' refer or relate to a special Law enacted under an Act Of Parliament for the India. 965 The respondents contended that even if the expression 'special Indian ' means `a law enacted ' by the Indian Legislature and that the ' Banking Companies Acts is such a law, still the provision of section 4(e) of the Act will not apply inasmuch as the appellant Corporation was not formed in pursuance of any `special Iary Indian law but by and under a special 'Indian law. It would be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by orunder a special Iary ', it will not come within the purview of section 3(27)(a) of The Act.

The Central Government by a notification dated July 30, 1958 fixed ex factory prices of sugar produced in Punjab Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The Central Government was also authorised by that Ordinance to fix quotas for the wholesale and retail sale of sugar manufactured in the State of Uttar Pradesh. In exercise of these powers the Central Government promulgated the Sugar Export Promotion Ordinance No. V of 1958 empowering it to appoint an export agency for carrying out the work of buying sugar in the Indian market and exporting the same to foreign markets and fixing the quantity of sugar for export. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it did not fix any price at which the persons purchasing sugar from the mills would sell it, so that it was open to the middleman who bought sugar from factories to sell it at any price, thus creating discrimination between factories and factories and between the producers selling sugar and the middlemen who buy sugar selling the same in their turn. Held, that the impugned notification did not subserve the purposes of the Act and the order made thereunder was bad as it was discriminatory because it fixed exfactory prices only for factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and North West Bihar and not for factories In re : The Central Provinces and Berar (Control) Order, 1958, which was passed in the interest of general public in order that sugar might be available at fair prices, did not contravene article 19(1)(g). Re. 1 (b), and Re. 2, referred to. The impugned notification was therefore beyond the authority conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 3 of the Sugar (Control ) Order, 1955.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , and directed that such dispute shall be adjudicated and the proceedings disposed of by that Tribunal after the commencement of the Amending Act as if that Act had not been passed. The Company preferred an appeal against that award to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta which was dismissed on August 30, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the previous award made by the Tribunal between the same parties on April 26, 1951 and confirmed by the Labour appellate Tribunal by its orders dated August 30. 1951 had not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act; (2) the Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuating rate in the index between that date, i.e., August 30; and (3) the tribunal went wrong to take the rise In the cost for living index by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise. Held: (1)(a) The Government made the order transferring the dispute pending before the Second Tribunal, i., after section 2 of the amending Act 18 of 1957 was deemed to have come into force. It must therefore be held that the Government acted well within its powers in transferring the disputes pending before it. Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras, ; , followed. (b) In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of live index in the year 1957. The Tribunal, on the consideration of the entire material placed before it came to the conclusion that full neutralisation of the deficiency as a result of rise in cost of the living index could not therefore be permitted; and therefore allow them only 76 per cent of the increased dearness allowance on the ground that there was a rise in prices of living Index.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Sri Gavi Mutt was a religious Institution dedicated to it. It appears that on 6th September 1939, the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments constituted under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 (Act II of 1927) framed a scheme under section 63 of the said Act for the proper administration of the Mutt and its endowments. The predecessor in office of the appellant then filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights guaranteed by article 1 9(1)(f ), and so, it could not be enforced. The District Judge dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the petition holding that some provisions of the scheme contravened the fundamental right under article 19 (1) (f) and so it couldnot be enforced on the grounds that some of its provisions contravened the petitioner 's rights guaranteed under article 1(1) of the Constitution. Held, that the scheme was not consistent with the provisions of section 103(d) of Act II of 1951 and as such, it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the schemes on the basis of the fundamental rights under article 14 of the Constitu tion. The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the administration of a Mutt and properties, it would be open to him to challenge on the said grounds that they contravened the Matadhipati 's right under Article 19(1).

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. Although the period of summer vacation during all these years was not approved by the educational authorities, the appellant continued to work as Hindi teacher in the school under the orders of the Managing Committee. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational Authorities of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 1982. On this notice the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teachers with effectfrom July 121982. The only argument raised before the Orissa High Court was that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989 on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.7.1982 and continued till 18.7 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the Validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validation Act does not arise. " The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appel lant was not entitled to the benefit of the validating Act on the above reasoning. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that on the plain reading of Section 2(1) of the Validating Act, the period during which the appellant continues to serve as Hindi tenant in the School under the order of the management committee, is continuous for a periods of atleast one year without any break or with a break or breaks in one or more aided schools; and 3. Is continuing as such teacher or his services were terminated after the 31st December, 1984 save for misconduct or. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. [992G] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, ; , followed. Rattan Lal & Ors. vs State Of Haryana, [1987] S.C. 478, referred to.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The respondent challenged the election of the respondent in an Election Petition inter alia on the ground of disqualification based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1952. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under rules 3 to 6 made the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti an office was in addition to the payment under r. 3 and payment of two sets of aLlowances must necessarily result in profit to the payee. HELD : The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member, and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him. [427 B] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, ; , referred to. Ravanna subanna vsG.S., Kaggedgeerppa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 654 and Ravanna vs C.B.I., A.R, 1954 S C.C., 653, distinguished. Ravna Subanna v G.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later, they filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. The disputed construc tions included a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the order of the first appellate Court on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration warranting appellant ' s eviction under sec.14(c). Since the constructions had been made with out permission of the respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. The High Court held that since two sides of the tin shed were resting on the pucca wall it constituted a material alteration and dismissed the respondents suit. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court should not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether the constructions materially alter ed the accommodation was a mixed question of fact and law which should be determined on the application of the correct principles. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The nature of construction, whether they are permanent or temporary is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '. A permanent constructio l tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis, while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affect the form or structure of the building, as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the building.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent Firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the Company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte judgment. The respondent firm filed a revision petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which was allowed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since Navlakha was an employee of the company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta the summons will be deemed to have been duly served and that the summons purported to have had been served on one Shri Navlakh on 17 3 1975. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was clearly wrong in upsetting the judgment of the trial court. There was no error in that judgment much less any error of jurisdiction entitling the High court to interfere with it. [1031E] 2. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Case that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the C.P.C. may kindly be perused. [ 1031F] 3. The judgment by the Trial Court setting aside the decree was correct. In any event no error of Jurisdiction was committed by it.

The appellant filed a complaint against the respondents on the basis of a police report. After passing a preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate had recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed and such a finding was implicit in the final order passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order in the finally order also. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) A finding of existence of breach of peace is not necessary at the time when a final order is passed nor is there any provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure requiring such a declaration in the Final Order. Once a preliminary decree drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a contravention of the law existed, it is not required that the breach of law should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145 of the Code. [95 H] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to. (2) The High court was right in holding that the final Order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of 'the peace existed at the date the order was passed. [96 F G] R. H. Bhutani vs Sita Ram & Anr., ; and Hari Ram vs Banwari Lai Lal & ors.

The assessee company was a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Agents were its partners. The company carried on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits arose for the most part from the sale of cotton. According to the account books of the company, its profits from business for the account year 1941 42 were Rs. 9,25,364, for 1942 43 Rs. 2409,832 and for 1943 44 Rs. 291388 1. In its returns, the assessee showed these amounts as its income chargeable to tax for the respective years. The Department did not accept the correctness of the figures as shown in the accounts. It contended that the company had earned more profits than were disclosed in its accounts and that it had contrived to suppress them by resort to certain devices. Held, that the question whether the sales entered in the books of account were genuine and if not, to whom the goods were sold and for what price are all questions of fact. The Tribunal was right in holding that the sales were real or genuine and that the inference drawn from these facts was one of mixed law and fact. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., ; , referred to. Held further, that on the findings of the Tribunal that it was not a pure question of law, the High Court was right. The finding of the Commissioner was that it wag not open to the reference under section 66(1) was one which was not supported by any evidence or that it is perverse but that where there was evidence to consider, the decision of the tribunal was final even though the court might not, on the materials, have come to the same conclusion if it had the power to substitute its own judgment. The mere fact that the Tribunal considered the question as one of fact did not make any difference whether the assessee was an individual or a company, both of them being equally liable to tax under section 14(2)(c) and that on such findings the question could not arise either.

The appellant carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager, Shri J.P. Vaish, which had been disallowed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court answered the question against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of the case the amount of Rs., 37,733 paid to Shri J, P. Vaish was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922; that the amount was not a real or that it was not incurred by the assessee in the character of a trader or it was therefore not laid out entirely and exclusively within the meaning of section 10 (2) (xv) and that the income tax Appellate Assistant Commissioner had wrongly taken this circumstance into consideration. HELD : The question of law referred to the High Court must be answered in the manner indicated and this appeal is accordingly allowed with costs. Appeal allowed. C.I.T Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Pvt. Ltd., ; , followed. Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C. I.T., U.P., ; and Swadeshy Cotton Mills co. Ltd vs C., U P. , referred to. The question whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for purposes of the assessee 's business, business profession or avocation as required by section 10 of the Act has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances established by the asses see. [532 D] Swadeshani Cotton Mills Ltd.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, he submitted a written reply denying the charge and asking to be excused. The management made an order terminating his services with effect from January 18, 1954. An industrial dispute was raised on this question of dismissal by the Union and was referred along with a number of other disputes to the Industrial Tribunal, Bihar. After the written statements were filed by both the parties stating that all the disputes were going to be compromised. On November 16, 1956, the present appellant made an application praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957, by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union. The High Court dismissed this application summarily. It was against that order of dismissal that the present appeal by special leave has been preferred. Held: (i) The appellant was at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the union. (ii)The terms of the compromise of the dispute regarding the appellant 's dismissal were that he would not get reemployment but by way of "humanitarian considerations the company agreed without prejudice to pay an ex gratia amount of Rs. 1,000/ . The terms of a compromise of a dispute regarding an individual workman was that he should be entitled to be represented by an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. (iii)The appellant ' s Secretary of Union had no authority to enter into any compromise on behalf of the appellant company in preference to Fateh Singh the Secretary, of the respondent Union.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against two defendants on the allegation that defendant No. 1 was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2. The suit was decreed by both the courts below. On appeal by defendant No, 2, the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No 1 and confirmed rest of the decree against defendant Nos. 2 and 3. In view of rr. 3 and 11 of O. XLI, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the appeal abated so far as Kedar Nath was concerned as no application for bringing his legal representatives on record was made within the prescribed time. On October 1, 1956, two applications were filed in the High Court one under section 5 of the Limitation Act for the condonation of delay in filing the application for substitution of the heirs in placecec of Kedar Nath. The other was an application under section 6 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 for the condone of the delay in filling the application. The High Court allowed the appellants time for filing an affidavit stating that the deceased was a member of the joint Hindu family and other relevant facts. On September 8, 1958, an affidavit was filed by defendant Nos., 2 and 4 stating that he was not a member or Karta of the Joint Hindu Family. The application was on the basis that Kedar Nath and the surviving appellants formed a joint Hindu Family, even though time had been given to them for filing the affidavit stating such a fact. The appellants contended that the appeal could not be said to have abated in the particular circumstances. Held: (i) Rule 4 of OXLI empowered the Court to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made in the proceedings before it and thus could have reference only to the nature of the decrees or Order in so far it affects the rights of the appellant. The appellate court cannot, in any way modify that decree directly or indirectly. The reason is plain. It is immaterial that the modification which the Court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. No question of its provisions overriding those of r. 9 of O.[554 C] (ii) Rule 33 really provides as to what the Appellate Court can find the appellant entitled to. It empowers the Appellate court to pass such decrees and make such further or other decree or Order as the case may require. The Court is thus given wide discretion to pass orders such decrees, and Orders as the interests of justice demand. Such a power is to be exercised in exceptional cases when its non exercise will lead to difficulties in the adjustment of rights of various parties. A case like the present is not a case of such a kind. When the legal representatives of the deceased appellant and the contesting respondents were negligent in not taking steps for substitution, the Court is not to exercise its discretion in favour of such an party. The discretionary power cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of the abatement of the appeal so far only as Kedarnath was concerned.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument has arisen). At the time of the lease the appellant had not been extended to Delhi although later on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord filed a petition for eviction under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that no notices terminating the tenancy under section106 were needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination can be availed by the landlords even in its absence of notice as envisaged by section III(g). The High Court held that no opportunity was given to the appellant to defend his case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111 (g) and no notice terminating the lease under section 107 was needed and that further that forfeiture of tenancy caused in contravention of the terms Of the deed of demise could be avail of by him even in his absence of any notice as prescribed under those sections; that the appellant 's case was that the TP act did not fall within the meaning of section 111 of the Act because no notice had been issued nor notice terminating tenancy under Section 106 was needed, and further, that the forfeited of the contractual tenancy caused contrary to terms of lease could be utilised by the tenant even in absence of the notice as required by those Sections; that since admittedly no notice in writing had been sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux or by forfeiture following the breach by the appellant, equity and good conscience; that even if the Rent Controller held that the termination of the contract was bad in law, he could not evict the tenant unless he satisfied any one of the grounds set out in section 3. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement as to written notice provided in the section is intrinsic evidence of the fact that the formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. [913C] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant presses the position that since the admittedly no notices in writing, as laid down in the Section, had been issue ed, the eviction proceeding could be shot down by that legal missile alone. The statutory law, as it now stands, is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease, by giving notice in that behalf. [936C D] 2:2 The requirement of a written notice is no part of equity or justice but a technical or formal statutory requirement. If the purpose of the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine, the lease and to avail himself of the tenant 's breach of covenant it could, as effectively, be achieved by an oral intimation as by a written one without in any way disturbing the mind of the chancery judge.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that Shri P. K. Hore, Superintendent, P.W.D.F.C., and Wing against whom more charges had been received was unfit to be retained in the public service and that he ought to be dismissed from service. The Governor made these two orders in terms of article 311(2) as it existed before its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963 which came into force on October 6, 1963. The amended Article 311(1) was amended by the Fortyfourth Amendment Act, 1964 with effect from October 6. In the case of P.K. H.ore, the Governor made two orders dated April 1, 1965 and May 5, 1965, in terms thereof: "It is not expedient to give the said Shri P K.Hore an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above". The order of dismissal was passed in violation of article 31(2). The appellant challenged the validity of these two Orders on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the Governor had no power under sub clause (c) of the proviso to clause (2) of Article 311 of the Constitution to give him an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed; and (2)(a) that in the present case the satisfaction recorded by the Governor was not recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311 stood prior to its amendment. HELD : The satisfaction recorded under sub cl.(c) is not a mandatory one and it cannot be said that the satisfaction of the Governor under sub el. (c), has the effect of depriving a government servant of a very valuable right ofhaving an opportunityto prove his innocence as well as opportunity to make a representation against the penalty proposed to he inflicted on him. [488 F] Khem Chand vs The Union of India and Others, ; , followed.

The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi is a Sunni community of the said property. The Shia Waqf Board and Sunni Central Wakfs Boards constituted under the U.P. Muslim Waqf Act, 1960, were constituted in pursuance of an order dated December 12, 1978 passed by the Chief Commissioner of Wakfs, Uttar Pradesh, in respect of certain plots and structures thereon. The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6 as representing the Sunni community filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Shia Community of Mohalla had a right to perform their religious ceremonies and practices on the said nine plots and the structures thereon and there were considerable gaps and inadequacies in the documents and material before the court in that behalf which could only be filled in by trial and by recording evidence and in the absence of adequate material no declaration as to the title to the plots or structures or even as to rights in or over the plots and structure could be granted in favour of the Shias community. The present appeal is against the said judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order passed by a Magistrate under section 144 Cr. P.C., by the Sunni Board is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of Shia Muslims to perform religious ceremonies or functions on the other plots and constructions thereon. Apart from the finality attaching to the Chief Commissioners 's Report (together with the Appendices X and XI annexed thereto) dated 28th/31st October, 1938, the petitioners have also claimed that the aforesaid plots and buildings structures thereon had been registered as Shia Wakfs for purposes of performing their religious rites and functions under section 38 of the 1936 Act by the Shiana Central Waqf Board after making full inquiry and following the procedure prescribed by that section as early as in 1952 and the Board had issued the requisite Sanads in that respect.

The assessee, a limited company, disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10 lakhs but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs 3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. The assessee challenged the rejection of its claim before the Appellate Tribunal and reiterated its claim. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the Income Tax officer had clearly disallowed the assessee"s claim of set off by it. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue, it was contended: (1) that the benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was in error in holding that the provisions in Section 24(3) regarding intimation of losses deter mined by the Income tax Officer do not apply to the loss falling under the head capital '; (2) that in view of the provisions of Section 80 of 1961 Act, it could be said that the loss claimed for the assessment was admissible in law. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court reached the correct conclusion and there is no merit in the appeal. [1165B] 2.1 In the order for assessment year 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: "Section 74(1)(a) Where an assessee sustains a loss such as is referred to in sub section (2A), and the loss cannot be wholly set off in accordance with the provisions Of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. Their 22 services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween the three units, and all the service conditions of the persons working in the three Units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In 1979, the Defence Scientific and Technical personnel (Gazetted) of D.R. & P became a member of DAQAS. When the trifurcation was made, the Service Rules governing the three unit had a common Rule which was rat ing Rule 12 in DAQAAS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DQDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of serv ice of the members of the Service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect o the service be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. At the time the present controversy arose, and the respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, he was holding the post of Deputy Chief Scientific Officer. By an Office Memorandum dated July 10, 1986, the said decision was conveyed whereby Scientific & Technical personnel were (gazetted) ofD.R., D.S. and P became member of DQ. The appellant who was working in DTD &P became a Member of DA QAS. The Tribunal held that respondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years his superannuation being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. It is this decision which is challenged before this Court by the appellants. On behalf of the appel lants it was contended that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of services for the members belonging to the different units, but merely because the superannuation age of the member of the DQS was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz., DAQ. QAS, was entitled to the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The first of these were to the effect that the appellant had published all the phmphlets mentioned in the petition and distributed the same amongst the voters and the petitioner had come across the first pamphlet during the process of distribution. There could be no doubt that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June, 1967 and the petition which was filed on 24th June 1967 was beyond time and should not have been entertained. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968 and the appellant has now come up before this Court by special leave. It was contended for the appellant that the trial court had wrongly allowed the election petition holding in favour of the appellant on the first issue. Held: (i) The order of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution is not called upon to go into this question. There is certainly some substance in the grievance raised on behalf of the respondent that the second issue was rather confusing and misleading. Instead of framing a separate issue with regard to each charge of corrupt practice raised in the Petition, the learned Judge framed the issue in a manner which leaves much to be desired. The issues should further have specified the different heads of corrupt practices committed in respect of each of the pamphlets. (ii) There is no difference between the two Gazettes with regard regard to the names of the successful councillors. The appellant might have, if so minded, set up the first Gazette publication as the one fixing the period of limitation in which case the trial Judge would have been required to go to the matter. But the appellant precluded himself from doing so by his unconditional acceptance of the statements in paragrapbs 1 and 2 of the petition.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The validity of this notification was challenged by the petitioner under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the constitution. Held, that the Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The impugned notification dated April 31, 1957, was intra vires as it was issued before section 3 A was in operation. That Act received the assent of the President on August 31,1957 and was published on September 3, 1957. The State Legislature derives its authority to enact a law with respect to tax on the sales of goods under entry 52 in List I of the VII Schedule to Constitution. It has been held that a sale for the purpose of entry 54 must be what in law is recognised as sale. That the power conferred on Parliament under article 286(2) is a legislative power and such a power conferred by a Sovereign Legislature carries with it authority to legislate either prospectively or retrospectively, unless there can be found in the Constitution itself a limitation on that power. The fact that the 1947 Act after the amendment permitted the seller who was a registered dealer to collect the sales tax as a tax from the purchaser does not alter the real nature of the tax which, by the express provisions of the law, is cast upon the seller. The power of a legislature to enact an Act with reference to a topic entrusted to it, is, as already stated, unqualified subject only to any limitation imposed by the Constitution, comprehended the power to impose a tax thereon is plenary and unrestricted subject only only to such limitations which the Constitution might impose. In the exercise of that power, it will be competent for the legislature to impose sales tax with retrospective operation even for a period prior to the constitution, and in the exercise Of that power it will not be competent to the legislature, to impose any tax on sales conditional on its making a provision for sellers to collect tax from purchasers.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Court, and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [591 F] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [592 F G] Sunil Kumar Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. In jail treatment must therefore be geired to psychologistaling, released of stresss, restoration or restoration of Self respect andagricultural normalisation, apart from experience to adapt mentself to life outside; the functional failure in prison administration of our prisons cannot be simplistically assumed by award of long incarceration, for, otten that remedy aggravates the malady. Punitive therapeutics must be more enlightened than the blind strategy of prison severity where all that happens is sex starvation, brutalisation, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio environmental pollution, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological conditions and emergence, at the time of release, of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully ' processed into a hardened delinquent, thanks to the penal illiteracy of the Prison system. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be steritimitated by humiliating or harsh treatment, but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed Jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment.

The assessee, a limited company dealing in land, maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assesse. The assessee was not satisfied with the amount of compensation and preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator. The Arbitrator made an award on July 29, 1955 whereby he fixed the amount at Rs.30,10,873 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount of compensa tion by Rs.513,624 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8 1953, the date of acquisition to the date when payment was made till the date the date on the date it was actually determined and had become payable. The State Government then appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal on April 25, 1956 it deposited Rs.736,691 which the assessee was permitted to withdraw on May 9, 1956 on furnishing security. On receipt of the amount credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Rs. 7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the sum of compensation payable and the amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesses on the dates of the award. The assessment was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax on first appeal. In second appeal by the assessee before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal two contentions were raised by it. It was urged that the amount received by the assesee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was therefore a trading receipt of business carried on by the assesses, and therefore a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax; and that in any event the amount did not accrue to the assessees as its income during the relevant previous year ended April 31,1956. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by it related to acquisition of lands which was stock in the trade of assessee, but was a trading receipts of the business carried out by the assessees, and that therefore a ' receipt of revenue nature could not be said to have accrued to it as income during that previous year ending March 31. 1956 relevant to the assessment years 1956 57. It allowed the appeal accordingly by its order dated February 22, 1964. At the instance of the Revenue the Appellate Tribunal referred the question of law set out earlier to the Calcutta High Court for its opinion and held against the Revenue.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The terms of the compromise petition were clear and definite especially in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section 12(1)(f) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act 1952. [881E F] (2) In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act, the suitor must make out a ease for eviction in accordance with the provisions Of the Act, and when the suit is contested the issue goes to trial. [888H; 880A] (3) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the context of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances, is entitled to have such a decree under the law. It is too late in the day to contend that the provisions in order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [868B] (4) The object of section 13(1) of Delhi and Rent Control Control Act is to protect the tenant against protracted litigation expenses, which may be granted to them against the defendants.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs, 91,116/ . The Income tax Officer however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs 60,761/ . In appeal, the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he accordingly cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A(1). The High Court answered that question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income tax Officer took an erroneous view of section 21(1), and the High Court was right in holding that the assessee had incurred a capital gain of Rs 12,00,000/ as a result of the depreciation of the value of the shares of Elphinstone Mills Ltd. [864 D] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee & Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., ; , referred to. (ii) The question is not whether the value or the value distributed as dividends is judged by business considerations, such as the previous losses, the present profits, the availability of surplus money and the reasonable requirements of the future and similar others.

The appellant filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge allowed the objection and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. On appeal by special leave: Held, that section 37 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, read with sections 46 and 47 of the , is intra vires. Section 12(6) must be read with section 37 Of the Act and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made final is the decision of the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings, if any, have been taken under the provisions of the . The effect of section 46 and section 47 of ' the is that all the provisions Of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. Section 37 of 'the Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15 of the Act. Attar Singh vs The State of U.P., [1959] Supp. 1 All. 66, followed. Atttarar Singh 's case, ; , referred to. Attarsar Singh v The State Of U. P., [1962] Supp I S.C.R. 928, approved. Attaram Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh, [1959], Supp. 2 S. C.R., referred to and distinguished. The effect Of section 46 is that the provisions in sections 15, 16 and 30 of the are applicable to arbitrations tinder the Consolidation Act.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, a corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said resolution by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Two contentions were raised before this Court. (i) that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post; and (ii) that if at all such a discrimination was permissible, it could be done only by a statutory rule or regulation framed under section 64 of the Act. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulations the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [Emphasis supplied]. 1.2 In the absence, of rule, or regulation the authority could prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was taken till the years 1988 and was also sought for to be achieved since 1988. [1H; 2. The proposition in the instant case neither the practice adopted till 1988 nor the resolution passed by the respondent corporation in 1988 nor resolution passed in accordance with section 64, of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. It is well settled that for the purposes of promotion, a valid classification can made among members holding the same post on the ground of their qualification. In State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , relied on. The Court then referred to Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of India, ; and distinguished it on the facts by pointing out that it was a case of the direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. Once they were integrated they lost their birth marks, viz. the different sources from which they were recruited. [2H; 3.1 In view of the above, the petition stands dismissed.

The petitioners, an advocate practising in this Court, filed the present writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country and ancili al orders of directions in regard to the same. The petitioners contended that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. It was further contended that there was no justiciable matter, and that the filing of these writ petitions and proceedings of the Court had helped the Union Government to fill the vacancies to a considerable extent by making the various constitutional authorities con scious of the urgency of problem and of their responses. Dismissing the petition, this Court HELD: 1.1 The primacy of the Chief Justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [439C] 1.2 In practice there appears to have been a distortion of the scope of the observations of the majority even to the extent these observations go. The State executive initiating the proposal must first forward it to the Chief Judge of the High Court who would be better informed about the practising advocates as well as the District Judges subordinate to the High Courts, and seek the views of the chief Justice. So far as the executive is concerned, the `right ' to initiate an appointment should be limited to suggesting appropriate names to the chief justice of the Supreme Courts or the Chief Justices of the States and that of the Judges in position was apparently due to the fact that vacancies in that post were not filled in as soon as they occurred. [454E F] 1:3 The primacy is to safeguard the independence of the judiciary and to ensure selection of proper persons. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. There are preponderant and com pelling considerations why the views expressed by the Chief Ministers of the State and that in the case of the high Courts of Calcutta, should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. [453F] 2.1 In practice, there appears, to have had been a serious distortion between the sanctioned strength and the number of judges in position. The primacy over the very significance of the `consultation ' is to protect the independence and ensure selection by proper persons.[454E G] 2:2 It is clear on a plain reading of clause (2) of Article 124 that it is the President, which in effect and substance means the Central Government, which is empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the said Supreme Court. [449F] 1 :3 The recommendations of the two Judges shared in Gupa 's case, do not recognise the special and pivotal position of the institution of the District Judge or the High Chief Minister of the state concerned. It is, therefore clear that where there is difference of opinion amongst the constitutional functionaries in regard tO appointment of a Judge in a High Court, the opinion of none of the constitutional functionary is entitled primacy but after considering the opinion on each of the Constitutional functionaries and giving it due weight, the Central Govern ment is entitled to come to its own decision as to which opinion it should accept in deciding whether or not to appoint the particular person as a Judge.

The respondent, a Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the Bank availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by him. No reply was received from the said firm but the respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found to be satisfactory. Some correspondence ensued between the respondent and the appellant in this connection but finally the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. The Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental enquiry against the respondent. However, during the pendency of the departmental inquiry he retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against him by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and thereafter passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14, 1980. The respondent 's departmental appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980 and he did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon at any time during the penden cy of the inquiry. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition, quashed the order of punishment but directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order of the Single Judge. The Division Bench dismissed it by a single line order: "no ground for interfer ence is made out" and held that on retirement Shri U .B. Shah was nobody in the hierarchy of authorities to impose 201 punishment on the respondent, and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. The learned Single Judge allowed the appeal of the appellant by a Single Judge 's order dated January 18, 1988 holding that since the initial appoint ment of Shri U B. Menon was valid, his actions and decisions could not be invalidated by his subsequent retirement. The Letters Patent Appeals filed against the aforesaid order were also dismissed by a Division Bench. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent will be paid 50% of the consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders was bad in law.

The respondents are owners and are in possession of the building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent and extensive repairs on October 16, 1965, the respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial". A controversy arose between the parties regarding the construction of the Master Plan and the Zonal Development Plans. The High Court held that the Commissioner could decline the sanction only if there was a contravention of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 or any other provision of the Corporation Act or of any other law in respect of land use. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 332 prohibits the erection or commencement of the erection of any building or execution of any work specified in section 334 except with the previous sanction of the Commissioner. [171 E] (2)(a) The Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi which has statutory force, has come into operation under section 11, in the area concerned. [172 F] (b) Though section 8 contemplates the preparation of a Zonal Development Plan simultaneously with the preparation and the Master plan, or as soon as there may be thereafter, no such Zonal Development plan has been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal development Plan under section 8(2)(c) which will show the approximate location and extents of land uses proposed in a zone for roads; further, under sub cl. (d) of sub s.(2) Of section 8, the said Zonal Development plans will also contain provision regarding the allotment or reservation of land for roads. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Planning Plan then section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted because any user of a land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Master Plan will be hit by that section. [173 F G] (3) The provisions of section 7 of the Development Act clearly indicate and that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the Master plans that the Master Plans will only give a very broad outline of DeLhi as it will look in future. Though there is an obligation on the Authority to prepare the Zonal Plan simultaneously alongwith the preparation, of the master plan or as early as there can be thereafter no such zonal Development Plan has been made. That assumed considerable importance because it was the ZonalDevelopment Plan under s 8(1) (a) which would show the estimated location and the extents thereof of land used in a Zone for roads, section 14 would not have any application whatsoever.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2 was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code and the appellants were tried in the Court of Special judge at Rewa under the Vindhya Pradesh Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Ordinance, 1949. The Judicial Commissioner acquitted both of them but convicted the appellants of various offences with which they were charged. On appeal by the State to the Supreme Court it was contended that the statement made by the appellant to him was not recorded under section 164 of the Code and was therefore inadmissible in evidence. Held: (i) The statements made by appellant No 1 to the two witnesses being admissible in evidence there is no doubt that the appellants had not exactly remembered what transpired on that night in the bedroom of the appellant 's wife, the Additional District Magistrate took in this affair. (ii)The statement made to them was not a confessional statement and was, therefore, inadmissible in character. (iii)The statements were admissible under section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The statements were not admissible under s. 164 of Criminal Procedure. The statement was admissible under S.164 of the Evidence Act. The Magistrate was entitled to take into consideration the statements made to him by appellant Nos. 1 and 2 as evidence in regard to the statement. (iv)The evidence of these witnesses being thus worthy of credit and the statements were inadmissible in material particulars.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the respondent along with Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On appeal, the Additional District Judge dismissed the plaintiff 's suit holding that the order of dismissal was void on the ground of arbitrariness and there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. In the second appeal before the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed, and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Serious objection has been taken against the observations of the first appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the respondent in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties, we agree that the question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High 824 Court in the manner it has been done.

The appellant company was carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessment year in question is 1959 60. In the relevant previous year which ended on June 30, 1958, the assessee entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B T will was with two parties M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd., for 500 bales and M/S. Mahadeo Ramkumar for 600 bales. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its Income for the assessment year 1959 60 on the ground that there were no speculation profits in that year he held that the loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profits. The Income tax Officer held that these transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya & Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; , D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; and D.M. Wadhwani vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra) overruled. In appeal to the Tribunal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction was speculative in nature as contemplated in Explanation 2 to section 24(1) read with explanation 2 and restored the order of the Income tax officer. HELD: The question referred to the High Court in the present case had been correctly answered by this Court in D. P. Wadhwai vs Commissioner, Calcutta; , followed. In view of the decision of this court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar 's case it was correctly stated in D G. M., Wadhwana 's Case and Manalal M. Verma & Co. (P.)
