Ltd. vs Commissioner for Income tax [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 891 that a delivery order being a document of title to the goods cover cd by it, possession of the document not only gave one the right to recover the goods but also to transfer them to another by endorsement or delivery and that there being two separate transactions of sale, one between the mills and the original purchasers, and the other between the original purchaser and the third parties, tax was payable at both the points. [184 D F] In the present ease the question referred for determination in the instant case had not been considered in Raghunath Pras Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner Income tax Calcutta, , relied on.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an Election Petition challenging the validity of the nomination on the ground that it was not accompanied with the required attestation under section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Held, that the attestation in the prescribed manner is required in the case of illiterate persons unable to write their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that their signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way. The words " signing" are not used in the same sense in the Act because a special meaning has been given to the word " sign". The words ' signs " in relation to a person who is unable to writing his name means authenticate in such manner as may be prescribed. The prescribed manner of attestation in section 36 is required to be found in rule 2(2)of the Representation Of the People (Conduct of Election and Election Petitions) Rules, 1951, and it runs as follows: " For the purposes of the Act or these rules, a person, who is able to write his name shall, unless otherwise expressly provided in these rules be deemed to have signed an instrument or other paper if he has placed a mark on such instrument or another paper in the presence of the Returning officer or the presiding officer or such other officer as may, be specified in this behalf by the Election Commission and such officer on being satisfied as to his identity has attested the mark as being the mark of such person. " In view of this attestation in prescribed manner it cannot be held that the nomination paper was not invalid.

The appellants, who were employees of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given to the Company by their registered union called 'the Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Unions leaders who had been dismissed by the Company. On September 7, 1972, the appellants wrote to the company returning the cheques sent by the company and stating that its letter dated September 7.1972 which had reached them only on September 20, 1972 had already been replied by letter dated Sept. 21, 1972 that they were interested in the service of the company. The Assistant Commissioner thereupon summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts at conciliation did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellant made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result as stated above. On October 23, 1972 the appellants ' union wrote a letter to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of service of 25 workmen including the appellants and emphasising that they had not abandoned service. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants intimating that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they are no longer interested to continue in service of that company and have totally abandoned the Company 's service" their names had been struck off from the rolls of the appellant from that date. Along with its communication, the Company sent a cheque to each one of the appellants for the amount due to him on account of gratuity, leave salary and one month 's salary. On July 5, 1973, the union made a formal demand calling upon the company to re instart the appellants, and 10 other workmen informing them that since by not reporting duty they have confirmed its presumed presumption that their services were no longer useful to continue In service of Company and had totally abandoned their service" the appellant 's names had be struck off. The Labour Commissioner thereupon summon the parties to discussion on the aforesaid points but his attempt at conciliation failed. Thereafter the appellants made the said complaints before a Industrial Tribunal, with the results as stated in the letter dated October 23. 1972. The appellants ' Union made a draft demand calling for re settlement of the dispute concerning the re instation of 16 employees including the appellant. The Tribunal dismissed the complaint holding that the action of the respondent Company in removing the names of the appel lants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary, that the appellants had not terminated the services of the respondents and that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the workmen 's standing orders and since the Standing Orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the action was manifestly illegal and invalid. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no abandonment of service on the part of the respond ent Company and that the appellant had voluntarily abandoned the services. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 In Express Newspaper (P) Limited vs Michael Mark & Anr., ; , Express Newspapers (P.) The respondents were trustees of a public trust. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree, and in an application for execution by the mortgage, the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 5,000 by the executing court. The respondents applied under 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 being 5 % of the purchase money for payment to the appellant and Rs. 6 for payment of the mortgage amount. The Subordinate Judge passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs.250 out of the amount deposit, by the trustees be paid over to the respondents. In appeal against that order by the appellant, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 88 of 0.21, Code of Criminal Procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction sale. The High Court in exercise of powers under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code set aside that order and directed the District Judge to decide on all the points correctly arising out of it. In an appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) A judgment delivered by a Single Judge of the High Court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that court on the view that every Judge is entitled to take such view as he chooses of the question of law arising before him as Venkatarama Aiyar J. [459 F] (2) A single Judge of a High Court, who is a member or of a Division Bench of that High Court and who has no existence in law, cannot by himself refer the matter to the Full Bench for decision. Such a judgment according to Raju J. would "Dot be a judgment at all" and "has no existence In law". [459 B] (3) A Single Judge does not by himself referring the matter referred to the Division Bench. He only requests the Chief Justice to constitute a Full Bench to examine the question. That is the proper and traditional way to deal with such matters and it is founded on healthy principles of judicial decorum and propriety. [460 C] (4) A decision delivered by the Single Judge after due considerations of the point before it was liable to he regarded as invalid by Judges.

The Government of India, in exercise of its power under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, retired a Government servant at any time after he had completed 30 years of qualifying service. The appellant challenged the order of retirement by way of a writ petition before the High Court. The single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and that there Was no in the firmity. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that the Government had issued instructions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule II(j) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and the memorandum dated February 8. 1956 are not statutory rules. [800G] 1.2 The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2 of Pension Rules. A Division Bench of the High court came to the conclusion that Rule 2046 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ed by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. [801B] Union of lndia & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. 1.3 The Memorandum is in nature of execu tive instructions but it is similarly couched as Rule 2047 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code. Even otherwise para 6 of the memorandum could not and did not add anything to Rule 2.(2)of Pension Rules which is a statutory rule.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1. Phool Chand and the sale of Kat Phechu were effected by M/S BiharilalBalkishan at their shops in Kanpur. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/ s Biharilal, Balkrishnan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee 's firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechku from October 1940 to September, 1941. The sales in this case were effected between 26th July, 1943 and March 31st, 1944, failing in the financial year ending March 31, 1944 and no part of it was sold. April 1, 1941 to March 31. 1944, falling in the financ tion year ending 31st December, 1941, sales took place from May 30, 1941 and April 1. 1944 to April 4, 1944 falling in their financial year ended March 31th March, 1943. The dispute in this appeal is with regard to the set off of deficiency of profit relating to the periods 20th October, 1940 to 17th October. The Excess Profit Tax Officer held that business carried on during October, 1941 was completely differ ent from the business carried out during the chargeable accounting period under consideration and that the same business of manufacturing Katechin in Nepal and selling the finished products at kanpur was carried On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the assessee that there was no profit or loss during the relevant accounting period, and therefore, the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting periods which should have been allowed set off. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question must be answered in the negative and in favour of the revenue. [610E] 2.1 In order to work out the scheme of the Act, there must be proper devetailing of the concept of "accounting period", "chargeable accounting period" and basic scheme of Income Tax Act bearing in mind that excess profits are excess of profits which were intended to be mopped up during the war period intended to he taxed separately and differly.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the KPSC Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the K PSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions, in Mechanical Engineering. Petitioners who were qualified in Civil Engineers had to answer the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified in Mechanical engineering and answered questions indicated in Category 11 in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government of Kerala and the K.PSC to prepare "two lists, namely, one for Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner & R will implement the orders forthwith. " The petitioner challenged the judgment and order dated 23rd March 1979 passed by a Division Bench of the said High Court dismissing a number of writ appeals. The petitioner contended that the applicants who had been appointed in Civil Engi ne Engineering or Electrical Engineering of Kerala University were one of the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court, contending that the applications who had appeared in Civil Engineer lank was not entitled to be directed to effect selection and prepare and publish separate rank lists of selected applicants holding Civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. The respondents contended that they had qualified according to the separate lists for Civil and Electrical Engineering prepared on the ground that they were qualified under the separate list for Civil Engineering graduates and answered the questions indicated therein in Category 1 on the One hand and these candidates who had already been appointed, had not yet been appointed. Allowing the special leave petitions, this Court HELD: 1. The order as it appears, also refers to a common list although no common list was directed to be prepared or was prepared by the Kerala Public Services Commission. [749E] 2. In pursuance of the directions given by the learned Single judge in his judgment in effect upheld by the Division Bench, the Government and the Public Services Commis tioner of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in view of the observation of this Court in its order dated 11th November 1980 quoted above, the State of Kerala filed a petition before this court for clarification. This Court passed the following order on 11th Nov. 1980: "We have heard learned Advocate General and Shri A.S. Nambiar on the modification or clarification sought. The actual position has already been explained in the order by this Court dated 28th April, 1980 quoted below. [750F H] 3.

The respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership firm, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm and for accounts. The valuation was put as Rs.150 being the sum of Rs.50 for declaration, Rs. 50 for rendition of accounts and another sum of profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal by special leave it was contended that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the respondent in the suit. It was further submitted that the respondent had laid claim to a sum of about Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax Department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint and it was, therefore, preposterous on his part to suggest in para 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.49 only. According to the defence case which is challenged as incorrect by the plaintiff, the respondent requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. The "Ruksell Exchange", building is a very valuable property near Park in the city of Calcutta. A copy of the Profit and Loss Account for the calendar year 1979 attached by the appellant to the additional affidavit filed on his behalf before this Court mentions figures in lacs. Mr. Arun Prakash, the counsel for the respondent No 1, contended that it was manifest that relief could be given an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, and that the court is bound to accept that ' made on behalf of the respondent plaintiff before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849 was rejected after observing that there was some authority for the extreme view as urged in two Calcutta decisions but later a different view was taken by the said Court as also by the Allahabad Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by Mr. Chatterjee helps him. It is true that in a suit to recover accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, (1946) Nagpur Law Times 916, this court while taking note of the appellant 's right to give a tentative value on the suit he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It cannot be said that the valuation put by him appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable. [512C D] Smt. Tara Devi vs Sri Thakur Radha Krishna Maharaj, ; , referred to.

On behalf of the assesses it was contended that this Court had refused leave against the Full Bench judgment on account of certain special facts which were considered sufficient to dis tentwine the assesses in those cases from claiming the exemption. The High Court took the view that these rules and instructions had no relevance to the claim for exemp tion put forward under the notifica tion of 23.10.1981 and that, in any event, the executive instructions could not override the provisions of the statu tory notification. It was further contended that, since the exemption granted earlier was only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption and the former is not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above, the same should be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. Allowing the appeals of the State, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question of grant of eligibility certificate by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate the Industries Depart ment has to see whether all the requirements as con tained in the instructions are fulfilled and complied with or not. But, here: "as pointed out earlier, column 3 of the 1981 Notification (Annexure B) does not contain any guidelines or a procedure in the matter of grant ing of eligibility certifi cate or refusal thereof by the industries Department and as the grant or refusal of such certificate cannot be an empty ritual formality and, therefore, in order to avoid the possibility of arbi trariness and injustice to any one the State Government was justified in issuing executive instructions laying down the guidelines and procedure for the same. No. To answer these contentions, one has to look first at the statutory instruments in this case viz. section 12 of the Act and the notification thereunder. Section 12(1)(i), with which we are concerned, lays down four requirements for grant of exemption from the provisions o the Act: (a) that any exemption to be granted under the section has to be by a notification; (b) that the dealer should continue to furnish the pre scribed returns under the Sales Tax Act; and (c) that they should produce, at the time of their assessment, a certifi fate from the Director of Industries certifying that such dealer is eligible to claim exemption and has not opted for the scheme of deferred payment of tax under the rules framed for the purpose. [609E F] 1.2 The new industrial unit shall be entitled to defer the payment of the tax for a period of ten years. No further notifications are required to be issued. Special provisions relating to deferred payment tax by Industrial Units Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Act, a registered dealer, who is (a), registered as a small scale industrial unit with Indus trial Department of the Government of Madhya Pradesh;or (b), registered under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 (No.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were direct recruits to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The recruitment of promotees is dealt with by Rule 5(1) according to which, recruitment of persons to the service from the Delhi Judicial Service shall be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High Court. In other words, promotees are appointed to temporary posts in the service while under Rule 17 they are appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the Service. It is only when they are recruited in a substantive capacity to a post in the Services that they become members of the Service and their seniority inter se between them and direct recruits is determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the services or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in the permanent capacity. The petitioners who are directly recruited in the Delhi High Court, challenged the validity of Rule 5 on the ground that they had not completed ten years of service in accordance with the qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) and (b). The respondents contended that seniority between promotees and direct recruit must be determined in accordance With the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges and that, direct recruits who are appointed as Additional Distt. & Sessions judges after the promotees are so appointed, cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority of members of Delhi Judicial service promoted to the Service shall, be determined according ly the respective date of their actual officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Delhi judicial Service is appointed in substantive capacity or to a temporary post of Additional District and Sessions Judge by national placement at a time when he did not even reach the age at which he or she would have become eligible for appointment. [362E F] 2.1 The seniority list which is impugned in this case has been prepared on the basis that the rule of `quota and rota ' will continue to apply notwithstanding the fact that appointments are made to the Services under Rules 16 and 17. It would be incongruous to do so because, if the quota rule is adhered to in conjunction with Rule 8(2), it will result in manifest injustice. [361F] 2:2 The seniority lists which are impugned in the present case have been prepared by the Full Court of theHigh Court and appointments were made on merit cum seniority basis so much so that persons found not fit for promotions were ignored as in the case of Shri C.D.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The Tribunal referred the questions to the High Court which answered the first question in the negative. On appeal by Debi, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the orders of the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner. In further appeals by certificate, HELD : (i) Section 31(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, provides that where as the result of an appeal, any change in the assessment of a firm or association of persons or new assessment of the firm or associa tion of persons is ordered to be made, the appellate Assistant Commissioner may authorise the Incometax Officer to amend accordingly any assessment made on any partner of the assessee or any member of the association. All the returns have been filed by Debi parshad but in dif ferent capacities. The said instances are only illustrative. It is not necessary to pursue the matter further. [391 D] (ii) Section 34(3)(b) of Income Tax, 1922 provides that an order of assess ing or re assessment may be made after the expiry of four years from the end of the year in which the income, profits or gains were first assessable. But to this rule there are several exceptions. If the assessment had to be flied on the assessee and any person 'm consequence of or to give effect to any findings or direction contained in an order or a reference made in a reference, the assessment could be made even after the expiration of the four years. [392 E F] Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed.

The appellant, who was the son of Subbiah Chettiar, filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by him. The respondent claimed that he had been adopted by Lakshmi Achi in 1922 and that as Subbiah 's son, the appellant claimed to have a share in the joint Hindu family properties. The appellant contended that the said rule merely contemplates the levy of certain specified court fees as indicated in the provisions of the Act which are expressly made applicable to the Original Side. Held, that the suit was not maintainable under section 7(iv)(b) of the Madras Court Fees Act and it could not be reopened at this stage. The question whether the High Court was justified in directing the appellant to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the memorandum of appeal must be answered against him. Section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act provides that in all suits falling under section7(iv) the plaintiff shall state the amount at which he values the relief sought is valued in the plaint or memorandum of Appeal. The value for court fees and the value for jurisdiction must no doubt be the same in such cases; but it is the value of court fees stated by the plaintiff that is of primary importance. The result is that it is not possible to apply any of the provisions contained in Chapter III of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, either to the suits filed on the Original side of the High 'Court or to the appeals arising from judgments and decrees in such suits.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal against the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987, declining to sanction the Revised Plans for the construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before the 5th day of May, 1989. The NDMC assailed the decision by way of a Writ Petition in the High Court. The main contention of the appellant was that the sanctions for the multi storeyed high rise buildings, as envisaged in the Building designs, were allayed by the Chief Fire Officer 's clearance and held that thereafter there was no impediment to the sanction. During the course of hearing, the standing counsel for the NDMC raised the issue of applicability of Bye law 16.4.8 of the applicable Building Bye laws of the Delhi Municipal Act 1911 and submitted that the clearance of the Chief fire Offi cer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. However, the Court in the light of the statement of counsel for respondent No. 1, allowed the Writ Petition and directed NDMC to conveyed its formal approval of the plan on or after the 5 th day of April, 1989, and that the permission of the proposed construction for sanction except on the point of adequacy of "Refuge areas" in the requirement of a "pedestrian walk way" and "Podium/pedestreet walk way". The NDMC challenged the decision before this Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the prescriptions in bye law 16, 16.8.1 and 16.2 would detract from the validity of the first Respondent 's claim and establish that the clearances from the Chief Level ing Officer were one of the conditions and not the sole or conclusive test of the adequacy of fire safety measures in terms of the relevant Bye laws. On the other hand, it was urged that the approvals in byelaw 16.9.1 were not inflexible and wherever more liberal and better standards of fire precaution were incor porated in the designs, the bye laws did not prohibit such better measures being adopted by the licencing authority. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The clearance from the chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 17.1 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the DDA to satisfy itself that the building plan provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. The exemption by the chief fire officer which is expected to involve and follow a technical assessment and evaluation, obliges the NDMC, to give due weight to it but, having regard to the scheme and language of the Bye laws the decision in the NDMC are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the bye law.

The plaintiff was running a liquor shop, and the business carried on by him was that of a grocery shop. The plaintiff was maintaining his accounts upto March 31, 1946, and he filed an application before the Civil Judge praying for accounts of the motor transport business. The application was dismissed as barred by res judicata. On appeal to the High Court it was contended that the cause of action in the two suits was identical with the cause in the previous suit and that the suit was therefore barred by Order II, rule 2, of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that on a fair reading of the compromise arrived at between the parties in the circumstances then existing, the only legitimate conclusion is that the parties had agreed to confine the taking of all accounts upto the date of the final decree. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake or misunderstanding as held by the trial Court a finding which was not interfered with by the High court it follows that a matter once concluded between the two parties who were dealing with each other at arms length cannot now be reopened. Held further, that the compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the joint family businesses including the motor business after the 31st March 1946 and the plaintiff was bound by the terms of the agreement and the consent decree following upon it. The obvious effect of this finding is that a consent decree is as binding on the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum. The true effect of the finding is to divide all the property by metes and bounds and to award monies as found on examination of accounts right up to the date when the final judgment was passed, and for the compromise which limited the period of account the plaintiff would have obtained the relief he is now seeking, in the partition suit as accounts would have been taken of all the businesses up to March 31 1946.

The Salt Works were extended over an area of about two hundred and fifty acres. The appellant was employed in the Salt Works and was working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process was being carried on without the aid of power or was ordinarily so carried on, but did not include a mine subject to the operation of the , or a railway running shed. The salt works were carried out in the salt Works and described above, came within the definition of the word " factory " under cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act. The Salt Works extended over the area of two hundred & fifty acres, but the appellant was prosecuted for having carried on the salt works without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the said Act read with r. 4 of the Rules framed under the Act and was convicted by the High Court. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the Salt works were not "factory" within the meaning of the expression " factory ' in cl. 2 of section II of the Bombay Salt Works Act, 1948, and as there were no buildings except temporary sheds on the Salt Estates, the Salt work could not be said to be a " factory ". Held: (i) The word " premises " is not restricted in scope to buildings alone. of course, the building referred to in this clause is the building which is referred to In section 93 of the Indian Factories Act. (ii)The process of converting sea water into salt carried on by the appellant 's Salt Works comes within the expression ' manufacturing process ' in el. (k) of s 2 of tile Act.

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State in 1935 as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. He was reverted to his parent department on June 11, 1956, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the then State of Mysore set up the Department of Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere became part of that Department. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the Department. On June 11. 1956, the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor under the rules then in force and as his reversion at this distance of time for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him, the Commission were of the opinion that he may be absorbed as Tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as had been ordered in the ease of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty. In 1956, he was again appointed on deputation to the Polytechnics and joined duty thereafter there on 12th June 1956, when he initially resumed duty on deputation. His specific grievance was that in any case, he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on deputation with effect from November 28, 1949, which was the date on which he originally came on his deputation. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the Respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailor Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, Sri K Narayanaswamy C: Chetty who is his junior and possessing similar qualifications was transferred as tailoring Instructor in that Department." The respondent 'reversion to the parent department in 1955 56 was not justified. Ultimately, the Government by order dated February 19, 1964 ordered the absorption of the respondents in the department of Technical education in the grade of Rs. 150 with effect on the date from November 1, 1956 when he originally resumed duty as Instructor and appointed as Tailores Instructor under Rule 9(7) of the Mysore State Reorganization Act, 1957. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing his absorption in the respondent Department of technical Education from the dates of his initial appointment therein, namely November 28th, 1949 and to give him benefits of revisions of pay scales effected in 1957 and 1961 and weightage benefits thereunder. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption should be given effect from 11th November, 1949 when he was working subject to these conditions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed; (2) the case was fully covered by the decision of this Court in K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty and Anr. vs State of Karnataka ; , that the respondent did not stand on the same footing as that of Narayanaswamy Chettiar because the order of Chetty 's absorption was passed by way of increments or weightage benefit accruing thereunder, (3) the appointment of the employees which came on : deputation from a particular date, was a concession which could not he claimed as of right and consequently, a writ for mandamus should not be issued; (4) the State Government had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The respondent was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the respondent. [259 F] K.V.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail", and alleged that not only Indian children of tender age were under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. " The petitioner accordingly sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies "from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad" and directing the Govern ment of India to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children by foreign parents, and directing that the Indian Council of Social Welfare and the Indian council of Social welfare should carry out its obligations in respect of adoption. The Court issued notice to Union of India, the Indian Law Council of Child Welfare and Indian Council for Child Welfare or any other independent, reputed and publicly recognised social welfare agency to which notice was issued by the court would have to scrutinise the application for guardianship made on behalf of the foreigner wishing to take the child in adoption and after examining the home study report, the child study report as also documents and certificates forwarded by the sponsoring social or child welfare agency and making necessary enquiries, it must make its representation to the Court so that the court may be able to satisfy itself whether the principles and norms laid down by this Court have been observed and followed.

The appellant company employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its accounting year is from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the (hereinafter to be referred as the Act). For the year 1965 66, it calculated a sum of Rs. 23,68,785 as available surplus. This amount represented 13 51% of the wage bill. The workmen were dissatisfied with this offer of bonus at 1351% and demanded payment of bonus on the balance 6.49%. The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute " What should be the quantum of bonus payable to the Workmen of the Indian Cable Company Limited Calcutta for the accounting years 1965 66" and the Unions contended before the Tribunal that the computa tion of allocable surplus by the Company has not been properly made in accordance. The Unions further alleged that the Company had spent large amounts for payment of liability for future years with a view to reduce the available and allocable available surplus, which in consequence has resulted in reduction of percentage of bonus. The company on the other hand maintained that it has kept proper accounts which have been audited by a reputed firm of auditors, Lovelock & Lewes and that the computation of allocables has been properly arrived at having due regard to the provisions Of the Act. The Tribunal computed the available surplus at Rs. 2.65 lakhs as per the profit and loss account as expenditure had to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. The appellant, a Sales Tax officer in 1953, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for the State and Subordinate Services. His service book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him react his good record of Service. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax officer it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner that he was a very intelligent and capable officer who kept the entire district under his control in perfect discipline. On enquiry by the Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department, charges were framed against him by the Board of Revenue. The explanation of the appellant was obtained. The Full Board of revenue (CT) was therefore requested to frame charges straightaway as for a major penalty against the appellant on the basis of allegations levelled against him. The Board accepted the report of the Directorate and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and anti Corruption. Out of eleven allegations levelled in the confidential file of the Appellant in 1969, seven allegations were not substantiated, in the enquiry made by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption. The Government examined the report and considered that there was a primafacie case in respect of certain allegations and this was sufficient to proceed against him as for major penalty. " The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the petitioner including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. Sometimes, past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. [80F] 2.1 The previous service history of Government servant would be completely overlooked, once the appellant is promoted and he paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled to his costs.

The appellants who were operators of the two transport operators whose permits were liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the , challenged the validity of three Schemes framed under Chapter IV A of the nationalising motor transport in certain areas in the Kumool District of the State of Andhra Pradesh which for convenience was to be taken over, while under the 2nd and 3rd, 17 and 13 routes respectively were proposed to be nationalised. The appellants contended that (1) the provisions Of the schemes (and this applied both to the draft schemes published by the Corporation as well as approved schemes published under section 68 D(3) did not conform to the statutory requirements of section 68 C; (2) the Regional Transport Authority which is specifically mentioned in section 68 F(1) is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter IV" and that the section rendered the provisions applicable to cases covered by section 68F(1); and (3) the approval by the Transport Minister must be held to be vitiated by mala fides of the Chief Minister. Held, that the Regional transport Authority which was specifically mentioned as in section68 F(I) is competent to issue a permit to transport undertaking ' notwithstanding anything to this contrary contained therein. The Regional Transport Authori ties for the purposes of the Art are not entitled to issue permits under Ch. IV of the Act. The scheme framed by the State Government under section 58 of the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950 was in conformity with the requirements of that Chapter and the rules made thereunder.

The appellant company was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 in the return for the year the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,928 10 0 and claimed exemption under two heads, namely, (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) thereof Rs. 69,65,979 9 6; and (ii) under s.5(2) (a)(iii) thereof the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The Commercial Tax Officer disallowed the assessee 's claim for exemption on the ground that the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed the order of the single Judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i). Section 5(1) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1947, provides for the exemption in respect of certain sales to a dealer if the sales are made to a registered dealer for the purposes mentioned therein. But the said exemption is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. The proviso cannot be construed as laying down a condition for giving the exemption, but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded in a case where the proviso cannot he strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purpose mentioned in the said sub clause. [629 H] (ii). The expression "on demand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration forms are to be produced; otherwise, the rule would be inconsistent with the section and would defeat the express intention of the Legislature. Nor does r. 27A support the contrary construction. The expression 'on demand ' in r.27A of the Rules is not helpful to the appellant. They provide only safeguards against abuse of the declaration form by the purchasing dealers; they do not enable the selling dealer to either directly apply or to compel the purchasing dealer to apply for duplicate forms; nor do they enjoin on the appropriate authority to give the selling dealers a duplicate form to replace lost one. [ 630 A C] State of Orissa vs M.A. Tulloch and Co. Ltd., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a Deputy Inspector General of Prisons, was convicted under section 395 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The petitioner challenged the conviction on the grounds that (i) the State had assured him in his affidavit that several steps regarding different directions given by the Court were being promptly implemented but due to shortage of time it has not been possible complete the same; (ii) the requirement of the proviso was complied with and (iii) the failure to comply with the proviso to section 167(2), Cr. P.C., was fatal to the petitioner 's case. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the State Government had failed to furnish particulars as to what were the dates on which these under trial prisoners were remanded from time to time by the Magistrates and directed the State of Bihar to furnish them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail, and rejected the contention. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the High Court had failed in its duty to comply within the provisions of section 167 (2), Criminal Procedure Code, 1973; (2) the proviso had not been complied with as the State was not in a position to try them within a reasonable period of time. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The requirement of proviso to Section 167(1) is complied with in their case. [529 F] (b) The State Government cannot avoid its constitutional obligation to provide speedy trial to the accused by pleading financial or administrative inabilitiy. The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It is also the constitutional obligation of this Court as the guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing the necessary directions to the State which may include taking of positive action, such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery setting up new courts, building new court houses, providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure expeditious trial. [540 F G] (c) The Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. [541 A B] (d) The obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trials is an essential element of any 'reasonable, fair and just procedure for a person accused of an offence and it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21. This is a constitutional right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty indigence or incommunicado situation and the State isunder a mandate to provide a lawyer to an accused person if the circumstances of the case and the 540 needs of justice so required, provided of course the accused person does not object to the provision of such lawyer. [543 B] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (e) The right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trials in some countries but it is in ours that it is In ours. Equal justice and free legal aid: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal assistance, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (2 A). The tenancy was to terminate from March 31, 1953. The landlord made an application on April 7, 1953, under section 29(2) of that Act for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2A) to section 34 by the Amending Act No. XXXIII of 1952 which came into force on January 12, 1953 and by this amendment certain restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protected tenant. The appellant contended that the notice having been given before the Amending Acts came into operation, the further limitation put on the rights of the landlords by subs. (2) A), introduced by the amending Act, would not apply to notices issued before the amendment came into effect. Held, that the view taken by the High Court was correct and sub section 2A would apply to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending act. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (I.L.R. LXVII) referred to. The words of sub s.(2 A), are on the date on which the right to terminate matures, that is, the date of termination, of the tenancy. In order to exercise this right to terminating the tenancy, the crucial date is not the date or the date when the right is to be enforced. Nor are we impressed by the argument that by applying sub section(2 A) to notices given before Amending Act came into existence, it would be taking away the vested right of landlord. Durgibbhai Amabhai vs Jhavarbhai Bhikbhai Bhikubhai (I L.R., Cal. 1037), relied on.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali, filed a petition raising a question of violation of the fundamental right to hold property guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The Custodian held that the properties had already been acquired under the , and therefore the petitioners had no longer any claim to them. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to declare the entirety of the two houses evacuee property and deprive the petitioners of their rights in them. The acts of the Custodian in so far as they deprive the appellants of their property cannot be upheld. It was well established and not disputed that no property of any person can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act. The act of the custodian in so much as they deprived the petitioners ' right of property cannot therefore be upheld, Held, further, that on the admitted facts, the petitioners could not maintain this petition. It is well established that no appeal by him against that order lay or was necessary. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction so far it affected the rights of the petitioners in the properties concerned. There was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the houses. If, as was conceded, Zafar Ali had filed an appeal to the Custodian against the order of January 11, 1952. The order of December 10, 1953, was without jurisdiction inasmuch as it remained so in spite of the appeal. In view of the decision of this Court in the case of Nizam 's case, the orders of February 10, and March 31, 1952 were without Jurisdiction so far that they deprive them of their properties cannot be sustained.

The assessee company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving of yarn. The second Department carried on the operations of spinning of cotton yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952. The assessee company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. Subsequently on December 15, 1953 the assessee Company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the principal selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000/ and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to make payment of 6% commission on net sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with Mis saligram under which they were appointed the sole sell agents on specified conditions. The selling agents M/S. Saligrams Premnath advanced a sum of Rs, 6,26,847 and Rs. 871,873 and received Rs. 37,157/ and Rs . 37, 157/ and RS. 37. The case of the assessee was that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by the company in order to earn profits and would therefore fall within the ambit of section 10(2) (xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax officer however disallowed the deduction and held that the deduction claimed was actually a division of profits after the profits had come into existence and had been ascertained. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the contention of the Revenue and held in favour of the asses company. On further appeal by the Revenue the Tribunal held that there was no agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses which were a provision peculiar to the present transaction and was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court, that itself was proof positive of the fact that the transaction amounted to a joint venture with a view to division of profit between the assessee and the selling agent after the profit had come in existence and that it was therefore a case of no assistance to the assessee.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The respondents contested the suits and pleaded that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that they had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them and that the entry in the record of rights published during the settlement in 1931 was correct. The District Judge held that the documents on which the defendants claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title were not proved to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree in ejectment could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that on the facts found a lost grant could not be presumed in favour of the respondents. Held: (i) The entries in the Record of Rights in 1931 were made in compliance with that Rule and that what it imports is not that there was a rent free grant but that that the person in possession was not actually paying rent. It was well settled that it is beyond the powers of a manager of a Hindu religious institution to grant perpetual lease binding the institution for all times to a fixed rent, unless there is a compelling necessity or benefit therefor. In the light of these principles, it has now to be seen whether on the materials found a had been established by them, and that they were in possession without payment of rent for a considerable length of time, but it has not been established precisely for how long. In their written statements they pleaded that they bad been holding under a Lakhearaj grant made prior to 1931, and had been in possession by virtue of that title for over 200 years. The defendants had in their written statement denied the title of both the Maharaja and the Asthal, and having failed in that plea, cannot fall back on a presumption of lost grant by the very persons, whose title they have repudiated. (ii) The suit properties formed part of Mouza Mauza Nala within the Zamindari of Burdwan and if a grant had been made in favour to the predecessors of the defendant, it must have been made by the Maharaja or by the Rajgunaj Asthal. But before raising such a presumption, it should be established that the grant was one which could have legally been made, by him. It is well settled law that it cannot be the duty of a Judge to presume a grant of the non existence of which he is convinced" Farwell J. in Attorney General vs Attorney General, , referred to.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land. The respondent pleaded that the land which was the subject matter of the contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 ( 'Tenancy Act ') and as the intending purchaser, the appellant was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the said Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit in respect of specific performance and while considering the main issue whether specific performance should be granted or not, civil Court will have to consider whether there are prima facie any facts on account of which granting of specific relief would result into a transaction forbidden by law and, consequently, civil court will have jurisdiction to decide the subsidiary issue whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist. In appeal to this Court it was contended that if the Court does not take note of Ext 78, an issue on the pleadings would arise whether the appellant is an agriculturists or not and, in view of the provisions in section 85A, the Mamlatdar alone would have exclusive jurisdiction under the Tenancy Acts to decide that issue if it arises before it in a civil suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decided or deal with any question which is by or under the tenancy Act is totally ousted. [595C] 1.2 In an appeal by special leave, the appellate court reversed the finding that a suit on title for possession alleging that the defendant was a trespasser was a properly constituted civil suit and if in such a suit defendant raises a contention that he is a protected tenant it would be a subsidiary issue and would not oust the jurisdiction of Civil Court. [596D] 1:3 The question whether an acquisition in excess of the ceiling would be invalid would be within the exclusive jurisdiction of Mamlatdar under section 70 (mb) and that the civil court has no jurisdiction to determine whether the acquisition would become invalid but there is nothing in section 71 or any other provision of the Land Revenue Act which excludes the Civil Courts 's jurisdiction to decree specific performance. [597E] 1 :4 The question as to whether an acquired excess of ceiling would not be valid would be outside the exclusive jurisdic tion of the Mamlatdar under Section 70 (b) of the and that it is in the context of these facts that it was held that even though civil court had no jurisdiction, to decide or deal With this question and a reference ought to have been made to the Mamlatdar.

The assessee, a heavy engineer in the erstwhile Indian Iron Foundry Division, was manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. For the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60, the assessee claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of the profits and gains derived from its steel Foundry division for the year 1959 60. The assessee had previously in the earlier years bought from outside the castings manufactured in the Steel Foundry Divisions which was started in the assessment year 1958 59, and continued thereafter. Again in the year '1959 60, in addition to the manufacturing of cast ings in the steel Foundries Division, the asses see 's claimed exemption under section15C of that Act in respect thereof in respect o f its profits and gain derived from it for the years 1959 60 and 195960. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under Section 15C(2)(i) of the Act. The Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee and accepted the claim for exemption under s.15C. The High Court held that even though the manufactured products of the new industrial undertakings were mostly used in the assessee 's other business of manu facturing boilers, wagons, etc., the element of profit was there and the extent of the same could be ascertained as the assessee is maintaining separate books of account.

The inam lands were granted by Hindu kings for performance of services of watchman, palanquin bearer background music player, mason, blacksmith carpenter, potter, was connected with the temple. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars. By an order passed on April 10, 1947 under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, the Revenue Divisional Officer resumed the inam lands and regranted them to the temple, but the orders were confirmed on appeal by the District Collector. The revenue Divisional Officer and the District Judge held that the inams comprised both melwaram and kudiwaram rights in the land. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (1) the inam grants did not comprise the kudiarwaram; (2) the inams did not constitute the kaiwaram, and (3) the right of resumption could not be extinguished by adverse possession. HELD : (i) The Inam lands were originally granted to the office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them in connection with the Temple. There was a well recognised distinction between the grant of the land burdened with a condition of service and the grant Of land as remunerationfor an office, see, forbes vs Noor Muhammad Tuquee, [1870] 13 H.I.A. 438, referred to. (ii) The inams in the present case were not personal inams. They were inams granted to office holders on hereditary offices as remuneration, for services connected with a math or temple as also to an inam granted to them and were within the purview of section 44B(2)(a)(i). [547 B] (iii)The inam was not forthcoming. The plaintiffs and their predecessor in title were in continuous possession of the lands for over 80 year under the cowle lease. The original cowle granted a permanent lease and the inams had been granted as inams. The amount of the assessment or melwar was very low and could not therefore be an ade quate remuneration. [547 D] (iv)The Inam lands did not come within the definition of section44 B(2) (a)(1). The inam lands comprised both the warams. The inam were originally granted, to the temples before fasli 1212 corresponding to 1862 and that in 1863 the inam was being enjoyed by Verrabadra Mudali, Periasami Naidu and Andiappa Mudali.

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax 127 at the rate of 7% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The respondents who were trustees of a charitable trust were the owners of certain houses situated in Indore City. Prior to January 26, 1954 the Indore Municipality was governed under the Indore city Municipal Act 4 of 1909. Under section 2(c) of the 1954 Act the municipality had imposed the tax on houses at the rates of 7%. The respondents claimed refund on the ground that under the 1954 act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The difference came to Rs. 1,461 and of this the trustees claimed refund of the excess amount paid by them under pain of distress. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant Corporation could do so because the rules made under the repealed Indore City Municipalities Act, 1950 were saved by section 2 (c) and therefore the rate at 7% was saved and secondly that under section 79(1) of 1954 Act, the Corporation need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year. HELD: The tax imposed on the appellant was inconsistent with section 73 of the Act. [130 E] Section 76(2) provides expressly that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular official year it can be done subject to the provisions of sections 75 and 76. In other words, an assessment list being for a specific official year even when an assessment List prepared in accordance with the provisions Of section 73 it has to be published and time has to he fixed for lodging objections against the entries therein. After such objections are heard and disposed of the assessment list has to have been authenticated as provided by section 76(6). Sub sec. 6 lays down that such assessment list when authenticated becomes conclusive evidence for purposes of all taxes. of the valuation or annual letting values and of the amount of tax leviable on such buildings or lands or both in any official year in which such list is in force.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions, and the assessee company started to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of association. On May 9, 1943, the assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The purchaser was allowed sixty days for the payment of the balance of the price, Rs 57,500 having been already paid at the time the agreement was 'entered into. The purchasers made a default in payment, and on August 9, 1944, a fresh agreement was entered into between the parties, this time for a consideration of Rs. 7,35,000 and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944 to the shareholders, the 963 Directors stated that the prices obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and that the sale was of the entire assets including goodwill, and not a business profit, which was liable to tax. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the assessee was liable for income tax on a profit of Rs 36,498 6 4. The Commissioner of Income tax on appeal, however reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259. On an appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that by the sale no business was done and that there was legally a single transaction of the whole match factory inclusive of raw materials. It further held that there could be a sale in the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, but that the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not liable to income tax. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transaction was not during the carrying out of the carrying On the business of manufacture and sale, a realisation sale, or whether trading was going on in spite of the winding up, so as to attract tax on profits made. [966 F] (ii)The transactions were of the same nature that the sales were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading in chemicals and raw materials, but to close down the business and to realise the assets. There was no identifiable price for the chemicals and the raw materials except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals, and raw material and the price with them. From that alone, however it was impossible to infer that the chemicals or raw materials were sold in a particular way, because the evidence clearly showed that clause was never used and the two sales of chemicals through the years were too trivial in themselves not afford evidence Of a continued trading or sustained trade in chemicals.
